item.title: 单图生成「能按的」资产：PhysAg3D 把动作、机构与局部柔性一起生成，还能在仿真里验证 ｜ PhysAg3D: Bridging 3D Generative and Agentic Models for High-Fidelity and Physically-Interactive Assets
item.description:
一句话：要的不只是「长得像」：资产要能被操作、机构要能动、局部要能软，且落在可仿真的表示上。

要点：

  • 任务定义很工程：从单图生成交互式 3D 资产，要求同时满足三件事——视觉上像、几何与材质细节保留、对动作的响应符合该物体（笔记本支架会调倾角与支撑臂、耳机刚性支架配局部可压缩耳罩）
  • 做法是把 3D 生成模型与 agentic 模型接起来：把「需求—机制—具体实现」串到生成表面上，用视觉与执行证据驱动局部修改，同时保留有用的几何
  • 物理侧落在可仿真基座上（MuJoCo / PyBullet / Isaac / 可微仿真器），因此生成物不是「看起来能动」，而是能在里面真的跑起来

为什么值得看：「AI 造资产」到「AI 造可交互资产」之间隔着一层机制：铰链、滑轨、软垫这些必须在几何里被显式表达，否则进引擎只能当摆件。这条给出了可操作的路径——生成 + agent 迭代 + 仿真验证，正好是引擎侧资产管线该补的一环。

中文摘要：从单张图生成交互式 3D 资产，是给虚拟环境与具身仿真批量「填物件」的可扩展路径，但一个有用的资产要同时满足三件事：捕捉到图中这个具体实例、保留真实感的几何与材质细节、并且对动作的响应方式符合该物体。PhysAg3D 把 3D 生成模型与 agentic 模型接起来：把需求、机制与具体实现关联到生成的表面上，用视觉与执行证据驱动局部修改并保留有用几何，再在 MuJoCo、PyBullet、Isaac 等可仿真基座上验证。文中给出的例子包括可调整托盘倾角与支撑臂高度的笔记本支架、以及刚性支架加局部可压缩耳罩的耳机，说明「可交互」被落实成了几何与机构层面的约束。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-11-01

PhysAg3D:

1  Introduction

Generating interactive 3D assets from a single image offers a scalable way to populate virtual environments and embodied simulations with objects from the real world [(Mildenhall et al., 2020; Kerbl et al., 2023; Mo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020)]. A useful asset should capture the depicted instance, retain realistic geometric and material detail, and respond to actions in ways appropriate to the object. These goals concern different aspects of quality: a visually convincing reconstruction can remain static, while a functional mechanism can belong to an asset that no longer resembles its reference. The task therefore requires bringing appearance, instance alignment, and physical interaction into a coherent realization.

Recent advances provide strong foundations for this task. Image-conditioned generators synthesize detailed geometry and materials [(Poole et al., 2023; Jun and Nichol, 2023; Nichol et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a; Shi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Hong et al., 2024; Long et al., 2024; Tochil and others, 2024; Xu and others, 2024; Du et al., 2024a; Voleti et al., 2024; Tang and others, 2024; Xiang et al., 2025b; Xiang et al., 2025a)]; articulated and physical generation methods infer part structure, motion, and material behavior [(Mo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026; Makoviychuk et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2020)]; and agentic systems construct and revise assets through executable programs, visual grounding, and feedback [(Ahn et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2023a; Driess et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023; Valmeekam et al., 2023; Le et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)]. A remaining challenge is to maintain agreement between what an object is expected to do, how that behavior is implemented, and which visible surfaces actually respond. A single image underdetermines hidden mechanisms and physical parameters, and a generated mesh need not expose the semantic parts required for interaction. Furthermore, a valid joint or deformable simulation does not ensure that the corresponding detailed surface moves with it. Addressing these discrepancies can require changes to geometry and physical structure, creating a further tension between functional construction and preservation of the depicted appearance.

We introduce PhysAg3D, a framework for single-image interactive asset generation through generative–agentic coupling. Our central idea is to combine the instance-specific geometry and appearance supplied by a pretrained 3D generator with an agent’s ability to reason about object behavior and construct executable physical models. The generated asset provides a detailed visual foundation; agentic reasoning turns this foundation into an interactive realization and revises it in response to observed behavior. This division of capabilities allows physical construction to make use of rich generated surfaces while remaining responsive to the structure and interactions of the depicted object. Figure 1 illustrates this goal through mixer-head articulation, compass-lid closure, telescope reorientation, and local ear-pad deformation. The examples associate actions with specific moving or deforming regions while retaining recognizable object structure and surface detail.

Specifically, a vision-language agent first infers revisable semantic and physical priors from the image, and a 3D generator produces a textured whole-object mesh from the same image. We propose a hierarchical interaction representation for this coupling, connecting semantic requirements, physical mechanisms, and concrete asset realizations. Explicit correspondences associate intended interactions with the structures and visible surfaces that implement them. Guided by these relationships and observations of the mesh, the agent uses geometric and physical tools to construct parts, joints or compliant regions, and surface bindings while retaining useful generated geometry and materials. Rendered interactions and execution measurements then guide targeted revisions with bounded construction and validation attempts. The representation expresses both rigid articulation and compliant deformation through their respective relationships between physical state and visible appearance. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A generative–agentic framework that grounds interaction construction in image-derived priors while retaining useful surfaces and materials from detailed whole-object generation.

  • •

    A hierarchical interaction representation that connects requirements, mechanisms, and concrete surface realizations to organize construction and feedback-guided refinement.

  • •

    Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks, assessing appearance, image alignment, and interaction attributes, with ablations of bounded refinement and source-surface preservation.

    • 2  Related Work

    Image-conditioned 3D asset generation.

    Early text-to-3D systems distilled diffusion priors into 3D representations [(Poole et al., 2023; Jun and Nichol, 2023; Nichol et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2026)]; feed-forward and multi-view methods improved single-image consistency and speed [(Liu et al., 2023a; Shi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Hong et al., 2024; Long et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024b; Tochil and others, 2024; Xu and others, 2024; Voleti et al., 2024; Tang and others, 2024)]. TRELLIS introduces structured 3D latents, and TRELLIS.2 supports detailed geometry and physically based materials [(Xiang et al., 2025b; Xiang et al., 2025a)]. UniLat3D unifies geometry and appearance in a shared latent space for single-stage image-to-3D generation [(Wu et al., 2026)]. SINGAPO conditions articulated parts on images and part relationships [(Liu et al., 2025)]; PAct jointly generates geometry, composition, and articulation [(Liu et al., 2026)]; PhysX-Omni covers rigid, deformable, and articulated objects [(Cao et al., 2026)]. Shape, surface, and texture reconstruction further improve appearance [(Gao et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2023c; Cao et al., 2023; Chen and others, 2024; Guo et al., 2020; Müller et al., 2022; Laine et al., 2020)]. More recently, SUPRA-TEX generates relightable materials faithful to reference images by anchoring visible-surface observations in material latent space while completing unobserved regions [(Yang et al., 2026)]. PhysAg3D studies agent-driven construction and revision around a detailed whole-object reconstruction, linking image-derived requirements to mechanisms and visible surfaces.

    Articulation and physical modeling of 3D assets.

    PartNet, PartNet-Mobility, GAPartNet, and Shape2Motion support research on parts, affordances, and mobility [(Mo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019)]. Articulate AnyMesh segments movable parts and refines joints for open-vocabulary meshes [(Qiu et al., 2025)]. Particulate predicts segmentation, kinematics, and motion constraints in one pass [(Li et al., 2025)]; Instruct-Particulate adds semantic and point-prompt conditioning, combining 3D generation with vision-language inference for image-to-asset articulation [(Li et al., 2026b)]. PhysAg3D focuses on connecting intended interactions, physical entities, exported bindings, and observed surface responses, including compliant regions whose simulation and visible geometry differ.

    Agentic 3D modeling and refinement.

    Articulate-Anything uses vision-language reasoning and actor–critic refinement for articulated modeling [(Le et al., 2025)]. Language-guided robotics connects instructions to executable actions and closed-loop spatial reasoning [(Ahn et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2023a; Driess et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2023)], while planning studies emphasize replanning and verification [(Singh et al., 2023; Valmeekam et al., 2023)]. ArtiCraft provides a part-and-joint SDK, object-specific tests, and structured execution feedback [(Zhou et al., 2026)]. aDSL unifies hierarchical modeling and spatial relations for planning, execution, and critique, combining procedural scaffolds with TRELLIS through SpaceControl [(Wang et al., 2026)]. Shape programs and CAD languages offer related compositional abstractions and persistent references [(Jones et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2025; Cascaval et al., 2023)]. PhysAg3D links requirements, mechanisms, and concrete realizations to generated surfaces. Visual and execution evidence guides local revision while preserving useful geometry.

    Simulation and visual grounding substrates.

    MuJoCo, PyBullet, Isaac Gym, and differentiable simulators provide complementary dynamics and contact substrates [(Todorov et al., 2012; Coumans and Bai, 2016; Makoviychuk et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2020)]. Segment Anything, DINOv2, and CLIP provide visual grouping and image–text alignment primitives [(Kirillov et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2024; Radford et al., 2021)]. These form contextual foundations for PhysAg3D’s explicit interaction-to-surface representation.

    3  Method

    3.1  Task Definition and Framework Overview

    Given a single image I, PhysAg3D generates a textured 3D asset with object-specific interactions. An asset contains visible geometry and materials, physical entities and parameters, controls, and bindings from physical state to visible surfaces. We evaluate appearance, image alignment, and physical behavior separately; construction targets the declared interactions, since hidden structure, scale, and material parameters are not determined by one image.

    Figure 2 summarizes the workflow. Image interpretation produces revisable semantic and physical hypotheses, while a pretrained generator provides a detailed whole-object mesh. Mechanism reasoning connects these sources through interaction intent S (what should happen), physical structure K (which mechanism produces it), and concrete realization X (the implementing asset entities and bindings). Asset construction realizes these mechanisms and bindings; evidence attribution links observations to the responsible regions for local revision. These are functional roles in one agentic loop. Appendix A details the interaction representation, construction procedures, validation checks, and candidate-selection policy.

    3.2  Generative–Agentic Coupling

    Image priors and generated geometry.

    A vision-language agent infers provisional hypotheses Π₀=Φ(I) about parts, materials, connections, candidate interactions, and scale, while retaining ambiguities. A pretrained generator produces a textured whole-object mesh M₀=G(I); our implementation uses TRELLIS.2 [(Xiang et al., 2025a)]. The agent inspects rendered views and geometry of M₀ before fixing partitions or mechanisms. Priors guide construction but do not condition G, so the coupling occurs through interpretation, construction, and feedback without joint training.

    Hierarchical interaction representation.

    For candidate version v, we define

    ℝᵥ=(Sᵥ,Kᵥ,Xᵥ,Γᵥ,ρᵥ), Hᵥ=(ℝᵥ,Eᵥ),

    		(1)

    where S, K, and X encode semantic requirements, mechanisms, and concrete realizations; Γ links their entities; ρ records correspondence to visible regions of M₀; and E stores candidate observations. The revision index v is distinct from execution time t.

    A requirement is

    r=(Uᵣ,aᵣ,Oᵣ,ψᵣ,Dᵣ),

    		(2)

    where Uᵣ is the target region, aᵣ the action protocol, Oᵣ the observation, ψᵣ the response test, and Dᵣ the initial conditions and scope. Thus, lid opening is measured relative to its support, while local compliance is measured after removing common rigid motion. Material compliance and articulation are separate attributes.

    The mechanism level K specifies rigid or compliant domains, supports, connections, degrees of freedom, joint frames, limits, and material assumptions. The realization level X identifies actual meshes, materials, scene nodes, controls, simulation entities, and exported bindings, while retaining construction or loading failures. An intended mechanism can therefore remain valid even when its realization is incomplete. In Figure 2, “Interaction intent” denotes S, “Physical structure” denotes K, and “Visible surfaces” depicts the surface component of X, whose full scope includes the implementing entities and bindings.

    Correspondences across levels and surfaces.

    The relations Γ connect requirements to mechanisms, mechanisms to realized entities, semantic parts to visible regions, and physical drivers to bindings. The source map ρ records retained, modified, added, deleted, and unresolved surface/material regions relative to M₀. In Figure 2, the inter-level links illustrate Γ, the native surface and material anchors illustrate ρ, and attributed observations contribute to E. These maps distinguish intended relationships from exported ones: an intended hinged panel may be found attached to the base. Topology changes require an updated correspondence rather than reuse of obsolete face indices. The hierarchy expresses progressively stronger commitments about one candidate, not a fixed sequence of agent roles; requirements can select mechanisms, and observations can retrieve the associated entities for inspection.

    3.3  Physical Construction with Appearance Preservation

    The agent grounds semantic parts and compliant domains in image evidence, rendered views, and measurements of M₀. Connected geometry can contain multiple moving parts, and texture boundaries need not be mechanical boundaries, so every actionable surface selection is recorded in a declared frame. Construction uses Blender for geometry/material edits and physical assembly tools for simulation entities. Rigid construction sets body ownership, parent–child connections, joint frames and limits, collision geometry, and controls. Compliant construction sets a physical discretization, material assumptions, supports, loads, and a map to the visible skin. Both preserve useful source geometry, UVs, and materials while recording the purpose and source correspondence of bounded edits.

    For an executable realization X,

    zₜ₊₁=F_X(zₜ,uₜ), Vₜ=B_X(zₜ;Vᵣₑₛₜ), y_r,t=O_r,Γ,ρ(Vₜ,zₜ).

    		(3)

    Here F_X is the implemented transition, B_X the exported binding, and y_r,t the observation used to assess r. A kinematic playback and a physics simulator may produce similar visible states, but only the latter supplies dynamics evidence. Rigid vertices follow their assigned body transform; for a compliant region, one valid binding is

    Vₜ=Vᵣₑₛₜ+W(Pₜ-Pᵣₑₛₜ),

    		(4)

    where Pₜ are physical-node positions and W maps their displacements to visible vertices in a shared frame. Binding checks verify node identities, dimensions, weights, and rest geometry against the export. A correct rest pose or moving proxy alone does not establish the intended surface response.

    3.4  Refinement with Visual and Physical Feedback

    Each candidate is evaluated with complementary evidence: renders assess image alignment, retained appearance, part separation, and visible response; source checks assess preserved surfaces and materials; execution checks assess actions, ranges, contacts, supports, and applicable deformation or recovery. MuJoCo [(Todorov et al., 2012)] is used for supported physical models. A moving proxy, a joint reaching a target, and the intended visible surface responding are distinct observations. Each Eᵥ record stores the requirement, target entities, candidate identity, action, initial state, runtime, and assessment configuration, with outcomes marked unassessed, pass, fail, or inconclusive. Errors without trajectories provide no measured response, and earlier dynamic evidence is invalidated after a build change.

    For an unmet requirement, feedback combines the discrepancy or missing evidence with the related mechanisms, realized entities, and bindings obtained through Γᵥ. Given remaining allowances bᵥ, the agent proposes

    oᵥ∼π(I,ℝᵥ,Eᵥ,bᵥ), Xᵥ₊₁=Apply(Xᵥ,oᵥ),(5)
    ℝᵥ₊₁=Reconcile(ℝᵥ,oᵥ,Xᵥ₊₁;M₀).

    Correspondences localize inspection but do not guarantee a causal diagnosis: failures may arise from partitions, frames, supports, controls, material assumptions, bindings, or observation definitions. Reconciliation records the actual export and keeps unresolved discrepancies; accepted requirements remain traceable across revisions, so a reduced motion range cannot silently satisfy a full-closure requirement.

    A declared policy bounds construction and validation and preserves prior candidates when revisions fail. The system returns the best eligible candidate under a fixed evidence-based selection rule, together with its interactive preview and unresolved requirements. A preview may be useful without a valid simulation trajectory, while its dynamics remain unverified. Appendix A gives the implementation budgets, checks, and selection policy.

    4  Experiments

    4.1  Experimental Settings

    We evaluate single-image interactive generation on real photographs and external benchmarks, and ablate bounded refinement and source-surface preservation. Implementation and scoring details appear in Appendices A and B.

    Common protocol.

    All comparisons fix input lists, method versions, and inference configurations; image-conditioned methods receive the same source image. We record auxiliary conditioning, output support, and computational cost. Candidate selection uses only within-run evidence, without benchmark annotations or final evaluation scores. Refinement permits at most two Builder repairs after initial construction and returns the best available candidate. All attempted inputs remain in the outcome accounting. Static assets are evaluated for input consistency; missing or invalid interaction videos count as failures within the fixed action denominator.

    Qualitative development examples.

    Figure 1 shows separate development examples: mixer and compass articulation, approximate compliant ear pads, and telescope poses specified by joint parameters without dynamic validation.

    4.2  Single-Image Interactive Generation in the Wild

    Benchmark and comparisons.

    Our benchmark contains more than 200 real-object photographs; evaluation uses a fixed subset of 50 objects with 110 predefined semantic actions, spanning rigid, compliant, and mixed objects. Development cases are identified separately, and method-specific preprocessing is documented. We compare PhysAg3D with Particulate, PhysX-Omni, PAct, ArtiCraft, and aDSL [(Li et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)]. Additional qualitative comparisons appear in Appendix C.

    Evaluation metrics.

    For input-view consistency, a fixed spatial grid search selects the rendered camera view closest to the input; foreground IoU, PSNR, and CLIP similarity are computed on the aligned pair. Action Completion Rate (ACR) measures correct semantic completion. Strict Mis-Motion Rate (MMR) counts missing, incomplete, incorrectly related, structurally broken, or spuriously coupled actions. Video-based Range Achievement Rate (RAR) scores the maximum valid visible range in {0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1} after the ACR semantic gate. These three metrics are macro-averaged over objects. Function-and-Visible-Stability Pass (FVSP) is the fraction of objects completing all expected actions without video-visible instability. It assesses rendered video evidence, not simulator-log stability.

    PhysAg3D leads all reported input-consistency and interaction metrics in Table 1, reaching 91.3% ACR and 88.0% FVSP versus 66.8% and 42.0% for aDSL, the strongest baseline on these two measures. Figure 3 compares appearance and visible interaction states under consistent rendering conditions.

    4.3  Evaluation on External Benchmarks

    Reference-based evaluation.

    PhysXVerse and PhysX-Mobility provide reference assets for appearance, geometry, and attribute evaluation, with the dataset split reported by PhysX-Omni [(Cao et al., 2026)]. In Table 2, PhysAg3D achieves the best reported score in every column on both datasets, improving PSNR over the strongest baseline by 2.74 and 2.76 dB, respectively.

    Reference-free evaluation.

    PhysX-Bench evaluates generated assets using image and behavior evidence [(Cao et al., 2026)]. We use its released evidence-generation and scoring pipeline with fixed judge configuration and prompts. In Table 3, PhysAg3D ties MonoArt on CLIP, ranks second on RQS and MCS, and leads DQS, APS, KPS, MPS, and DCS. These results show strong attribute scores alongside competitive visual quality. The articulation score uses joint playback and does not establish dynamic contact stability.

    Qualitative comparison on PhysXVerse.

    Figure 4 compares five selected inputs with PAct, Particulate, ArtiCraft, and aDSL [(Liu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)]. PhysAg3D preserves patterned headphones during earcup rotation, camera housing during lens extension, and ornate cart surfaces during wheel rotation; the microscope and butterfly show localized mechanism and wing motion. ArtiCraft and aDSL simplify fine geometry or patterns, while some PAct and Particulate outputs show fragmented surfaces, misplaced parts, or implausible motion.

    4.4  Human Perceptual Evaluation

    We evaluate six methods for input-image consistency and motion plausibility. First, second, third, and last place receive 5, 4, 3, and 1 points; unranked methods receive 2. First and last place are required, whereas second and third are optional. A separate multi-select question records visible motion collapse.

    Across 102 valid evaluations (Table 4), PhysAg3D leads in mean input-consistency (4.63 versus 2.98) and motion-plausibility scores (4.38 versus 2.84), and first-place selections. Collapse is flagged 7 times versus 11–47 for baselines. These judgments measure perceived fidelity and motion plausibility, not calibrated dynamics or contact stability.

    4.5  Ablation Study

    Ablation settings.

    The three settings share PhysX-Bench inputs, cached TRELLIS.2 reconstructions, image priors, model and decoding settings, construction tools, and final scoring. Full pipeline preserves useful source geometry, UVs, and materials while allowing evidence-guided edits and up to two Builder repairs using visual and physical feedback. One-shot construction returns the same initial build without repair, but still undergoes final evaluation. w/o surface preservation removes the construction-time geometry, UV, and material preservation constraints while retaining the initial reconstruction, physical-to-visible bindings, repair budget, and candidate-selection rule.

    Results.

    Table 5 shows that Full pipeline improves KPS and MPS over One-shot by 19.68 and 17.26 points. Removing surface preservation reduces CLIP by 0.16 and RQS by 17.68. These results support bounded refinement and source preservation; failed and inconclusive runs remain in the evaluation.

    5  Conclusion

    We presented PhysAg3D for generating interactive 3D assets from a single image. Its hierarchical representation connects interaction requirements, physical mechanisms, and visible surfaces to guide construction and feedback-based refinement. Experiments support appearance preservation and plausible interactions, with ablations indicating benefits from refinement and surface preservation. Recovering hidden structure and material properties remains a limitation.

    Supplementary Material

    This supplement provides implementation details, evaluation protocols, and an extended qualitative comparison accompanying the main paper.

    Appendix A Method and Implementation Details

    A.1  Interaction Representation

    The representation in Section 3.2 separates interaction intent, mechanism design, and concrete assets. The semantic level S identifies the target region, action, expected response, and observation frame. The mechanism level K specifies bodies or compliant domains, connections, degrees of freedom, supports, and parameter assumptions. The realization level X identifies the meshes, materials, scene entities, controls, and exported bindings. The relations Γ connect these levels; ρ records the origin and modification of source surfaces; and E associates observations with the candidate that produced them. These correspondences link interaction requirements to mechanisms, realized entities, and surface bindings for construction and feedback-guided revision, as defined in Section 3.2. The following subsections detail the associated construction and validation procedures.

    For example, a lid-opening requirement refers to the lid region and measures its motion relative to the base. Its mechanism identifies the hinge axis and permitted range, while its realization identifies the moving body and the visible lid faces assigned to it. This correspondence allows the hinge configuration and visible-surface assignment to be inspected separately; it localizes the relevant entities without by itself establishing the cause of a failure. For a padded region, the corresponding records identify the load, support, physical discretization, and visible skin. These examples explain the representation without assuming that hidden mechanisms or material parameters are uniquely recoverable from the input image.

    A.2  Geometry, Materials, and Surface Binding

    The initial TRELLIS.2 reconstruction supplies the detailed visible geometry and materials. Geometric refinement uses rendered views and measurements to identify actionable regions: mesh connectivity alone does not determine which parts should move, and a texture boundary need not be a mechanical boundary. Bounded edits preserve useful source faces, UV coordinates, and material assignments. When topology changes, source correspondence must be updated rather than inherited from obsolete face indices.

    For rigid articulation, visible vertices follow the transform of their assigned body. Correct body ownership, local transforms, parent–child relationships, joint frames, and limits are all needed to produce the intended visible motion. Collision geometry can differ from the detailed render mesh, but motion of a collision proxy alone does not verify motion of the visible part.

    For compliant regions, the physical discretization and visible skin may also differ. The displacement binding in Eq. 4 transfers physical-node displacements to visible vertices in a common frame. Its node identities, dimensions, weights, and rest geometry are checked against the exported asset. Supports and loading conditions are specified separately from the skin binding. A local deformation observation removes common rigid motion before assessing shape change; otherwise, movement of the entire object could be mistaken for local compliance. The ear-pad example uses an approximate compliance model rather than a material calibration recovered from the image.

    A.3  Feedback and Candidate Records

    Rendered observations assess appearance, part separation, and visible response. Execution observations assess the requested action, achieved range, contacts, supports, and applicable deformation or recovery. Each record identifies the requirement, candidate, target region and entities, action, initial state, runtime and assessment configurations, and assessment outcome. The four outcomes are unassessed, pass, fail, and inconclusive. An execution error supplies no measured trajectory, and a changed build requires renewed dynamic evidence.

    Feedback associates a discrepancy with the relevant mechanism, realized entity, or binding. Local repairs can address motion range, tracking, surface assignment, or assembly; structural replanning addresses topology, ownership, joint-axis, or material contradictions. Previous candidates remain available when a revision fails. The budgets and selection procedure below bound this loop.

    A.4  Runtime Configuration and Budgets

    Table 6 summarizes the documented v0.2.0 runtime configuration. Blender handles geometry and material editing; MuJoCo executes supported physical models. The reasoning model is accessed through the local Codex interface. The configured generator seed identifies the initialization setting, without implying deterministic agent execution.

    Invalid returned messages consume their role-response allowance. Host validation attempts are reserved before execution, so an interrupted simulation also consumes an attempt. Candidate history and cumulative counters persist across continuations; selecting an earlier candidate does not reset them. Simulator calls made inside construction tools are not covered by the host-attempt limit. These counts therefore describe distinct resources rather than an aggregate computation budget. The initial construction and at most two repairs constitute the Builder budget in Section 4.1; structural replanning does not reset this budget. As in Section 3.4, a modified build requires new dynamic evidence, and a preview does not turn an unverified simulation status into a pass.

    A.5  Motion-Range Adaptation and Physical Checks

    For a hinge or slide with original interval [ℓ₀,h₀] and neutral coordinate q₀, the documented range helper tests

    ℓₙ=q₀+(ℓ₀-q₀)(2/3)ⁿ, hₙ=q₀+(h₀-q₀)(2/3)ⁿ, n∈{0,1,2}.

    		(6)

    The original interval remains the reference across repairs. The retained span must be at least 0.2(h₀-ℓ₀) and, for a hinge, at least 10^∘. A reduced interval is considered only after a completed failed sweep with a valid rest pose. The checks include rest and both motion directions where applicable. A colliding rest pose, missing clearance information, incomplete sweep, or execution error terminates this search. The achieved range is retained explicitly; reducing travel does not satisfy an unchanged full-closure requirement.

    Let D be the positive asset diagonal in meters. The documented acceptance profile uses a contact-proxy penetration tolerance of 0.005D, an angular endpoint tolerance of 5^∘, and a translational endpoint tolerance of 0.005D. Additional checks cover finite states, solver warnings, joint limits, measured interaction, and applicable compliant-region requirements. Geometric sweep checks apply to sampled configurations and do not replace dynamic execution.

    For a declared compliant region, a least-squares rigid alignment removes common motion from the simulation nodes. Let d_\max be the maximum residual over recorded samples and phase endpoints. The response criterion requires d_\max≥0.001D together with a pairwise-distance-change check. When recovery is required, the residual after unloading must not exceed \max(0.001D,0.35d_\max). These criteria are deformation heuristics on simulation nodes; exported-surface response is assessed separately through the binding and visible observations.

    A.6  Output Selection

    Selection excludes unloadable, empty, nonfinite, externally dependent assets and detected source-identity conflicts. In autonomous runs, eligible candidates are ranked by appearance evidence, native retention, semantic evidence, absence of unsupported additions, display checks, declared bodies, supported physics acceptance, and recency, in that order. Native retention includes source identity, face accounting, geometry, and UV/material checks. As specified in Section 4.5, Full pipeline and w/o surface preservation use the same selection rule. In the latter, source-geometry, UV, and material preservation constraints are removed from construction, while the shared ranking criteria and physical-to-visible bindings remain. This intervention therefore tests the construction constraints under a fixed output-selection policy. Supported physics acceptance requires a passing report, at least three trajectory states, and matching asset and trajectory identities. A preview can be returned without a valid dynamic trajectory, with that status kept distinct. If no refined candidate is eligible, the native reconstruction can serve as a static fallback. Such a fallback is not evidence that the requested interaction or dynamic validation succeeded; failed and inconclusive attempts remain in the outcome accounting.

    Appendix B Evaluation and Comparison Details

    B.1  Evaluation Scope and Aggregation

    The in-the-wild collection contains more than 200 photographs; the fixed evaluation subset contains 50 objects and 110 predefined semantic actions. Following Section 4.2, ACR, MMR, and RAR are macro-averaged over objects. For normalized object-level scores sᵢ⁽ᵐ⁾, metric m is reported as 100N⁻¹∑ᵢ₌₁^Nsᵢ⁽ᵐ⁾, with N=50. Thus, each object contributes equally, regardless of its number of rendered frames.

    ACR measures correct semantic action completion. Strict MMR counts missing, incomplete, incorrectly related, structurally broken, or spuriously coupled actions. RAR scores the maximum valid visible range in {0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1} after the ACR semantic gate. FVSP is the percentage of objects that complete every expected action without video-visible instability. It is a joint functional-and-visible-stability criterion based on rendered videos, not simulator logs.

    Support marks indicate declared or evaluated capabilities, not successful outputs. Static assets remain evaluable for input consistency; missing or invalid interaction videos count as failures within the fixed action denominator. Failed and inconclusive attempts remain in the outcome accounting, with unsupported output types distinguished in the records. Development examples remain separate from the benchmark comparison.

    B.2  Inputs, Baselines, and Scoring

    Section 4.1 specifies the common comparison protocol. Image-conditioned methods receive the same photograph; mesh-conditioned methods require an identified reconstruction and any auxiliary conditioning. Format and coordinate conversions are distinguished from geometry repair or inference of missing physical parameters, which would change the evaluated method. PhysXGen denotes the framework introduced in PhysX-3D [(Cao et al., 2025a)]. aDSL reports image-to-shape generation and articulated creation as a downstream application, motivating its inclusion in the single-image comparison.

    Reference-based comparisons use compatible alignment, pose, sampling, distance normalization, and scoring settings. Shape normalization must preserve the separately assessed absolute-scale error. Table 2 follows the PhysXVerse/PhysX-Mobility split reported by PhysX-Omni; its kinematic score is not a dynamics success rate. Missing scores, marked by a dash or NR, are unreported entries rather than measured zeros.

    PhysX-Bench uses fixed evidence generation, evaluator configuration, and prompts across methods. Joint playback supplies articulation evidence, while material response and static appearance are separate observations; playback does not establish dynamic contact stability. The selected states in Figure 4 likewise demonstrate visible articulation and surface appearance. Table 7 summarizes the evaluation settings.

    B.3  Ablation Configuration

    The three variants in Section 4.5 share inputs, cached reconstructions, initial priors, model and decoding settings, construction tools, and final scoring. Full pipeline and w/o surface preservation share the two-repair limit and candidate-selection rule. One-shot returns the initial candidate and receives final scoring without feeding it back for repair. All attempted inputs, including failed and inconclusive runs, remain in the outcome accounting.

    The source-preservation ablation removes construction-time geometry, UV, and material constraints while retaining the initial reconstruction and physical-to-visible bindings. It keeps output selection fixed, including the native-retention ranking criterion. The One-shot comparison measures refinement as a whole, including additional repair and candidate-selection opportunities; it does not isolate an individual feedback signal.

    Appendix C Additional Qualitative Comparisons

    Figure 5 extends Figure 3 with additional cases and methods, showing geometry, materials, and texture continuity alongside input-image agreement in proportions, parts, colors, and patterns. No additional aggregate score is introduced.

一句话：要的不只是「长得像」：资产要能被操作、机构要能动、局部要能软，且落在可仿真的表示上。

要点：

  • 任务定义很工程：从单图生成交互式 3D 资产，要求同时满足三件事——视觉上像、几何与材质细节保留、对动作的响应符合该物体（笔记本支架会调倾角与支撑臂、耳机刚性支架配局部可压缩耳罩）
  • 做法是把 3D 生成模型与 agentic 模型接起来：把「需求—机制—具体实现」串到生成表面上，用视觉与执行证据驱动局部修改，同时保留有用的几何
  • 物理侧落在可仿真基座上（MuJoCo / PyBullet / Isaac / 可微仿真器），因此生成物不是「看起来能动」，而是能在里面真的跑起来

为什么值得看：「AI 造资产」到「AI 造可交互资产」之间隔着一层机制：铰链、滑轨、软垫这些必须在几何里被显式表达，否则进引擎只能当摆件。这条给出了可操作的路径——生成 + agent 迭代 + 仿真验证，正好是引擎侧资产管线该补的一环。

中文摘要：从单张图生成交互式 3D 资产，是给虚拟环境与具身仿真批量「填物件」的可扩展路径，但一个有用的资产要同时满足三件事：捕捉到图中这个具体实例、保留真实感的几何与材质细节、并且对动作的响应方式符合该物体。PhysAg3D 把 3D 生成模型与 agentic 模型接起来：把需求、机制与具体实现关联到生成的表面上，用视觉与执行证据驱动局部修改并保留有用几何，再在 MuJoCo、PyBullet、Isaac 等可仿真基座上验证。文中给出的例子包括可调整托盘倾角与支撑臂高度的笔记本支架、以及刚性支架加局部可压缩耳罩的耳机，说明「可交互」被落实成了几何与机构层面的约束。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-11-01

PhysAg3D:

1  Introduction

Generating interactive 3D assets from a single image offers a scalable way to populate virtual environments and embodied simulations with objects from the real world [(Mildenhall et al., 2020; Kerbl et al., 2023; Mo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Xiang et al., 2020)]. A useful asset should capture the depicted instance, retain realistic geometric and material detail, and respond to actions in ways appropriate to the object. These goals concern different aspects of quality: a visually convincing reconstruction can remain static, while a functional mechanism can belong to an asset that no longer resembles its reference. The task therefore requires bringing appearance, instance alignment, and physical interaction into a coherent realization.

Recent advances provide strong foundations for this task. Image-conditioned generators synthesize detailed geometry and materials [(Poole et al., 2023; Jun and Nichol, 2023; Nichol et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a; Shi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Hong et al., 2024; Long et al., 2024; Tochil and others, 2024; Xu and others, 2024; Du et al., 2024a; Voleti et al., 2024; Tang and others, 2024; Xiang et al., 2025b; Xiang et al., 2025a)]; articulated and physical generation methods infer part structure, motion, and material behavior [(Mo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019; Xiang et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Cao et al., 2026; Makoviychuk et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2020)]; and agentic systems construct and revise assets through executable programs, visual grounding, and feedback [(Ahn et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2023a; Driess et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2023; Valmeekam et al., 2023; Le et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)]. A remaining challenge is to maintain agreement between what an object is expected to do, how that behavior is implemented, and which visible surfaces actually respond. A single image underdetermines hidden mechanisms and physical parameters, and a generated mesh need not expose the semantic parts required for interaction. Furthermore, a valid joint or deformable simulation does not ensure that the corresponding detailed surface moves with it. Addressing these discrepancies can require changes to geometry and physical structure, creating a further tension between functional construction and preservation of the depicted appearance.

We introduce PhysAg3D, a framework for single-image interactive asset generation through generative–agentic coupling. Our central idea is to combine the instance-specific geometry and appearance supplied by a pretrained 3D generator with an agent’s ability to reason about object behavior and construct executable physical models. The generated asset provides a detailed visual foundation; agentic reasoning turns this foundation into an interactive realization and revises it in response to observed behavior. This division of capabilities allows physical construction to make use of rich generated surfaces while remaining responsive to the structure and interactions of the depicted object. Figure 1 illustrates this goal through mixer-head articulation, compass-lid closure, telescope reorientation, and local ear-pad deformation. The examples associate actions with specific moving or deforming regions while retaining recognizable object structure and surface detail.

Specifically, a vision-language agent first infers revisable semantic and physical priors from the image, and a 3D generator produces a textured whole-object mesh from the same image. We propose a hierarchical interaction representation for this coupling, connecting semantic requirements, physical mechanisms, and concrete asset realizations. Explicit correspondences associate intended interactions with the structures and visible surfaces that implement them. Guided by these relationships and observations of the mesh, the agent uses geometric and physical tools to construct parts, joints or compliant regions, and surface bindings while retaining useful generated geometry and materials. Rendered interactions and execution measurements then guide targeted revisions with bounded construction and validation attempts. The representation expresses both rigid articulation and compliant deformation through their respective relationships between physical state and visible appearance. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A generative–agentic framework that grounds interaction construction in image-derived priors while retaining useful surfaces and materials from detailed whole-object generation.

  • •

    A hierarchical interaction representation that connects requirements, mechanisms, and concrete surface realizations to organize construction and feedback-guided refinement.

  • •

    Quantitative and qualitative evaluations on real photographs and external benchmarks, assessing appearance, image alignment, and interaction attributes, with ablations of bounded refinement and source-surface preservation.

    • 2  Related Work

    Image-conditioned 3D asset generation.

    Early text-to-3D systems distilled diffusion priors into 3D representations [(Poole et al., 2023; Jun and Nichol, 2023; Nichol et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2026)]; feed-forward and multi-view methods improved single-image consistency and speed [(Liu et al., 2023a; Shi et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Hong et al., 2024; Long et al., 2024; Du et al., 2024b; Tochil and others, 2024; Xu and others, 2024; Voleti et al., 2024; Tang and others, 2024)]. TRELLIS introduces structured 3D latents, and TRELLIS.2 supports detailed geometry and physically based materials [(Xiang et al., 2025b; Xiang et al., 2025a)]. UniLat3D unifies geometry and appearance in a shared latent space for single-stage image-to-3D generation [(Wu et al., 2026)]. SINGAPO conditions articulated parts on images and part relationships [(Liu et al., 2025)]; PAct jointly generates geometry, composition, and articulation [(Liu et al., 2026)]; PhysX-Omni covers rigid, deformable, and articulated objects [(Cao et al., 2026)]. Shape, surface, and texture reconstruction further improve appearance [(Gao et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2023c; Cao et al., 2023; Chen and others, 2024; Guo et al., 2020; Müller et al., 2022; Laine et al., 2020)]. More recently, SUPRA-TEX generates relightable materials faithful to reference images by anchoring visible-surface observations in material latent space while completing unobserved regions [(Yang et al., 2026)]. PhysAg3D studies agent-driven construction and revision around a detailed whole-object reconstruction, linking image-derived requirements to mechanisms and visible surfaces.

    Articulation and physical modeling of 3D assets.

    PartNet, PartNet-Mobility, GAPartNet, and Shape2Motion support research on parts, affordances, and mobility [(Mo et al., 2019; Xia et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2019)]. Articulate AnyMesh segments movable parts and refines joints for open-vocabulary meshes [(Qiu et al., 2025)]. Particulate predicts segmentation, kinematics, and motion constraints in one pass [(Li et al., 2025)]; Instruct-Particulate adds semantic and point-prompt conditioning, combining 3D generation with vision-language inference for image-to-asset articulation [(Li et al., 2026b)]. PhysAg3D focuses on connecting intended interactions, physical entities, exported bindings, and observed surface responses, including compliant regions whose simulation and visible geometry differ.

    Agentic 3D modeling and refinement.

    Articulate-Anything uses vision-language reasoning and actor–critic refinement for articulated modeling [(Le et al., 2025)]. Language-guided robotics connects instructions to executable actions and closed-loop spatial reasoning [(Ahn et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2023b; Huang et al., 2023a; Driess et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2023)], while planning studies emphasize replanning and verification [(Singh et al., 2023; Valmeekam et al., 2023)]. ArtiCraft provides a part-and-joint SDK, object-specific tests, and structured execution feedback [(Zhou et al., 2026)]. aDSL unifies hierarchical modeling and spatial relations for planning, execution, and critique, combining procedural scaffolds with TRELLIS through SpaceControl [(Wang et al., 2026)]. Shape programs and CAD languages offer related compositional abstractions and persistent references [(Jones et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2025; Cascaval et al., 2023)]. PhysAg3D links requirements, mechanisms, and concrete realizations to generated surfaces. Visual and execution evidence guides local revision while preserving useful geometry.

    Simulation and visual grounding substrates.

    MuJoCo, PyBullet, Isaac Gym, and differentiable simulators provide complementary dynamics and contact substrates [(Todorov et al., 2012; Coumans and Bai, 2016; Makoviychuk et al., 2021; Hu et al., 2020)]. Segment Anything, DINOv2, and CLIP provide visual grouping and image–text alignment primitives [(Kirillov et al., 2023; Oquab et al., 2024; Radford et al., 2021)]. These form contextual foundations for PhysAg3D’s explicit interaction-to-surface representation.

    3  Method

    3.1  Task Definition and Framework Overview

    Given a single image I, PhysAg3D generates a textured 3D asset with object-specific interactions. An asset contains visible geometry and materials, physical entities and parameters, controls, and bindings from physical state to visible surfaces. We evaluate appearance, image alignment, and physical behavior separately; construction targets the declared interactions, since hidden structure, scale, and material parameters are not determined by one image.

    Figure 2 summarizes the workflow. Image interpretation produces revisable semantic and physical hypotheses, while a pretrained generator provides a detailed whole-object mesh. Mechanism reasoning connects these sources through interaction intent S (what should happen), physical structure K (which mechanism produces it), and concrete realization X (the implementing asset entities and bindings). Asset construction realizes these mechanisms and bindings; evidence attribution links observations to the responsible regions for local revision. These are functional roles in one agentic loop. Appendix A details the interaction representation, construction procedures, validation checks, and candidate-selection policy.

    3.2  Generative–Agentic Coupling

    Image priors and generated geometry.

    A vision-language agent infers provisional hypotheses Π₀=Φ(I) about parts, materials, connections, candidate interactions, and scale, while retaining ambiguities. A pretrained generator produces a textured whole-object mesh M₀=G(I); our implementation uses TRELLIS.2 [(Xiang et al., 2025a)]. The agent inspects rendered views and geometry of M₀ before fixing partitions or mechanisms. Priors guide construction but do not condition G, so the coupling occurs through interpretation, construction, and feedback without joint training.

    Hierarchical interaction representation.

    For candidate version v, we define

    ℝᵥ=(Sᵥ,Kᵥ,Xᵥ,Γᵥ,ρᵥ), Hᵥ=(ℝᵥ,Eᵥ),

    		(1)

    where S, K, and X encode semantic requirements, mechanisms, and concrete realizations; Γ links their entities; ρ records correspondence to visible regions of M₀; and E stores candidate observations. The revision index v is distinct from execution time t.

    A requirement is

    r=(Uᵣ,aᵣ,Oᵣ,ψᵣ,Dᵣ),

    		(2)

    where Uᵣ is the target region, aᵣ the action protocol, Oᵣ the observation, ψᵣ the response test, and Dᵣ the initial conditions and scope. Thus, lid opening is measured relative to its support, while local compliance is measured after removing common rigid motion. Material compliance and articulation are separate attributes.

    The mechanism level K specifies rigid or compliant domains, supports, connections, degrees of freedom, joint frames, limits, and material assumptions. The realization level X identifies actual meshes, materials, scene nodes, controls, simulation entities, and exported bindings, while retaining construction or loading failures. An intended mechanism can therefore remain valid even when its realization is incomplete. In Figure 2, “Interaction intent” denotes S, “Physical structure” denotes K, and “Visible surfaces” depicts the surface component of X, whose full scope includes the implementing entities and bindings.

    Correspondences across levels and surfaces.

    The relations Γ connect requirements to mechanisms, mechanisms to realized entities, semantic parts to visible regions, and physical drivers to bindings. The source map ρ records retained, modified, added, deleted, and unresolved surface/material regions relative to M₀. In Figure 2, the inter-level links illustrate Γ, the native surface and material anchors illustrate ρ, and attributed observations contribute to E. These maps distinguish intended relationships from exported ones: an intended hinged panel may be found attached to the base. Topology changes require an updated correspondence rather than reuse of obsolete face indices. The hierarchy expresses progressively stronger commitments about one candidate, not a fixed sequence of agent roles; requirements can select mechanisms, and observations can retrieve the associated entities for inspection.

    3.3  Physical Construction with Appearance Preservation

    The agent grounds semantic parts and compliant domains in image evidence, rendered views, and measurements of M₀. Connected geometry can contain multiple moving parts, and texture boundaries need not be mechanical boundaries, so every actionable surface selection is recorded in a declared frame. Construction uses Blender for geometry/material edits and physical assembly tools for simulation entities. Rigid construction sets body ownership, parent–child connections, joint frames and limits, collision geometry, and controls. Compliant construction sets a physical discretization, material assumptions, supports, loads, and a map to the visible skin. Both preserve useful source geometry, UVs, and materials while recording the purpose and source correspondence of bounded edits.

    For an executable realization X,

    zₜ₊₁=F_X(zₜ,uₜ), Vₜ=B_X(zₜ;Vᵣₑₛₜ), y_r,t=O_r,Γ,ρ(Vₜ,zₜ).

    		(3)

    Here F_X is the implemented transition, B_X the exported binding, and y_r,t the observation used to assess r. A kinematic playback and a physics simulator may produce similar visible states, but only the latter supplies dynamics evidence. Rigid vertices follow their assigned body transform; for a compliant region, one valid binding is

    Vₜ=Vᵣₑₛₜ+W(Pₜ-Pᵣₑₛₜ),

    		(4)

    where Pₜ are physical-node positions and W maps their displacements to visible vertices in a shared frame. Binding checks verify node identities, dimensions, weights, and rest geometry against the export. A correct rest pose or moving proxy alone does not establish the intended surface response.

    3.4  Refinement with Visual and Physical Feedback

    Each candidate is evaluated with complementary evidence: renders assess image alignment, retained appearance, part separation, and visible response; source checks assess preserved surfaces and materials; execution checks assess actions, ranges, contacts, supports, and applicable deformation or recovery. MuJoCo [(Todorov et al., 2012)] is used for supported physical models. A moving proxy, a joint reaching a target, and the intended visible surface responding are distinct observations. Each Eᵥ record stores the requirement, target entities, candidate identity, action, initial state, runtime, and assessment configuration, with outcomes marked unassessed, pass, fail, or inconclusive. Errors without trajectories provide no measured response, and earlier dynamic evidence is invalidated after a build change.

    For an unmet requirement, feedback combines the discrepancy or missing evidence with the related mechanisms, realized entities, and bindings obtained through Γᵥ. Given remaining allowances bᵥ, the agent proposes

    oᵥ∼π(I,ℝᵥ,Eᵥ,bᵥ), Xᵥ₊₁=Apply(Xᵥ,oᵥ),(5)
    ℝᵥ₊₁=Reconcile(ℝᵥ,oᵥ,Xᵥ₊₁;M₀).

    Correspondences localize inspection but do not guarantee a causal diagnosis: failures may arise from partitions, frames, supports, controls, material assumptions, bindings, or observation definitions. Reconciliation records the actual export and keeps unresolved discrepancies; accepted requirements remain traceable across revisions, so a reduced motion range cannot silently satisfy a full-closure requirement.

    A declared policy bounds construction and validation and preserves prior candidates when revisions fail. The system returns the best eligible candidate under a fixed evidence-based selection rule, together with its interactive preview and unresolved requirements. A preview may be useful without a valid simulation trajectory, while its dynamics remain unverified. Appendix A gives the implementation budgets, checks, and selection policy.

    4  Experiments

    4.1  Experimental Settings

    We evaluate single-image interactive generation on real photographs and external benchmarks, and ablate bounded refinement and source-surface preservation. Implementation and scoring details appear in Appendices A and B.

    Common protocol.

    All comparisons fix input lists, method versions, and inference configurations; image-conditioned methods receive the same source image. We record auxiliary conditioning, output support, and computational cost. Candidate selection uses only within-run evidence, without benchmark annotations or final evaluation scores. Refinement permits at most two Builder repairs after initial construction and returns the best available candidate. All attempted inputs remain in the outcome accounting. Static assets are evaluated for input consistency; missing or invalid interaction videos count as failures within the fixed action denominator.

    Qualitative development examples.

    Figure 1 shows separate development examples: mixer and compass articulation, approximate compliant ear pads, and telescope poses specified by joint parameters without dynamic validation.

    4.2  Single-Image Interactive Generation in the Wild

    Benchmark and comparisons.

    Our benchmark contains more than 200 real-object photographs; evaluation uses a fixed subset of 50 objects with 110 predefined semantic actions, spanning rigid, compliant, and mixed objects. Development cases are identified separately, and method-specific preprocessing is documented. We compare PhysAg3D with Particulate, PhysX-Omni, PAct, ArtiCraft, and aDSL [(Li et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)]. Additional qualitative comparisons appear in Appendix C.

    Evaluation metrics.

    For input-view consistency, a fixed spatial grid search selects the rendered camera view closest to the input; foreground IoU, PSNR, and CLIP similarity are computed on the aligned pair. Action Completion Rate (ACR) measures correct semantic completion. Strict Mis-Motion Rate (MMR) counts missing, incomplete, incorrectly related, structurally broken, or spuriously coupled actions. Video-based Range Achievement Rate (RAR) scores the maximum valid visible range in {0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1} after the ACR semantic gate. These three metrics are macro-averaged over objects. Function-and-Visible-Stability Pass (FVSP) is the fraction of objects completing all expected actions without video-visible instability. It assesses rendered video evidence, not simulator-log stability.

    PhysAg3D leads all reported input-consistency and interaction metrics in Table 1, reaching 91.3% ACR and 88.0% FVSP versus 66.8% and 42.0% for aDSL, the strongest baseline on these two measures. Figure 3 compares appearance and visible interaction states under consistent rendering conditions.

    4.3  Evaluation on External Benchmarks

    Reference-based evaluation.

    PhysXVerse and PhysX-Mobility provide reference assets for appearance, geometry, and attribute evaluation, with the dataset split reported by PhysX-Omni [(Cao et al., 2026)]. In Table 2, PhysAg3D achieves the best reported score in every column on both datasets, improving PSNR over the strongest baseline by 2.74 and 2.76 dB, respectively.

    Reference-free evaluation.

    PhysX-Bench evaluates generated assets using image and behavior evidence [(Cao et al., 2026)]. We use its released evidence-generation and scoring pipeline with fixed judge configuration and prompts. In Table 3, PhysAg3D ties MonoArt on CLIP, ranks second on RQS and MCS, and leads DQS, APS, KPS, MPS, and DCS. These results show strong attribute scores alongside competitive visual quality. The articulation score uses joint playback and does not establish dynamic contact stability.

    Qualitative comparison on PhysXVerse.

    Figure 4 compares five selected inputs with PAct, Particulate, ArtiCraft, and aDSL [(Liu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)]. PhysAg3D preserves patterned headphones during earcup rotation, camera housing during lens extension, and ornate cart surfaces during wheel rotation; the microscope and butterfly show localized mechanism and wing motion. ArtiCraft and aDSL simplify fine geometry or patterns, while some PAct and Particulate outputs show fragmented surfaces, misplaced parts, or implausible motion.

    4.4  Human Perceptual Evaluation

    We evaluate six methods for input-image consistency and motion plausibility. First, second, third, and last place receive 5, 4, 3, and 1 points; unranked methods receive 2. First and last place are required, whereas second and third are optional. A separate multi-select question records visible motion collapse.

    Across 102 valid evaluations (Table 4), PhysAg3D leads in mean input-consistency (4.63 versus 2.98) and motion-plausibility scores (4.38 versus 2.84), and first-place selections. Collapse is flagged 7 times versus 11–47 for baselines. These judgments measure perceived fidelity and motion plausibility, not calibrated dynamics or contact stability.

    4.5  Ablation Study

    Ablation settings.

    The three settings share PhysX-Bench inputs, cached TRELLIS.2 reconstructions, image priors, model and decoding settings, construction tools, and final scoring. Full pipeline preserves useful source geometry, UVs, and materials while allowing evidence-guided edits and up to two Builder repairs using visual and physical feedback. One-shot construction returns the same initial build without repair, but still undergoes final evaluation. w/o surface preservation removes the construction-time geometry, UV, and material preservation constraints while retaining the initial reconstruction, physical-to-visible bindings, repair budget, and candidate-selection rule.

    Results.

    Table 5 shows that Full pipeline improves KPS and MPS over One-shot by 19.68 and 17.26 points. Removing surface preservation reduces CLIP by 0.16 and RQS by 17.68. These results support bounded refinement and source preservation; failed and inconclusive runs remain in the evaluation.

    5  Conclusion

    We presented PhysAg3D for generating interactive 3D assets from a single image. Its hierarchical representation connects interaction requirements, physical mechanisms, and visible surfaces to guide construction and feedback-based refinement. Experiments support appearance preservation and plausible interactions, with ablations indicating benefits from refinement and surface preservation. Recovering hidden structure and material properties remains a limitation.

    Acknowledgments

    This research was financially supported by the Open Research Fund from Guangdong Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy (SZ), under Grant No. GML-KF-26-29.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Supplementary Material

    This supplement provides implementation details, evaluation protocols, and an extended qualitative comparison accompanying the main paper.

    Appendix A Method and Implementation Details

    A.1  Interaction Representation

    The representation in Section 3.2 separates interaction intent, mechanism design, and concrete assets. The semantic level S identifies the target region, action, expected response, and observation frame. The mechanism level K specifies bodies or compliant domains, connections, degrees of freedom, supports, and parameter assumptions. The realization level X identifies the meshes, materials, scene entities, controls, and exported bindings. The relations Γ connect these levels; ρ records the origin and modification of source surfaces; and E associates observations with the candidate that produced them. These correspondences link interaction requirements to mechanisms, realized entities, and surface bindings for construction and feedback-guided revision, as defined in Section 3.2. The following subsections detail the associated construction and validation procedures.

    For example, a lid-opening requirement refers to the lid region and measures its motion relative to the base. Its mechanism identifies the hinge axis and permitted range, while its realization identifies the moving body and the visible lid faces assigned to it. This correspondence allows the hinge configuration and visible-surface assignment to be inspected separately; it localizes the relevant entities without by itself establishing the cause of a failure. For a padded region, the corresponding records identify the load, support, physical discretization, and visible skin. These examples explain the representation without assuming that hidden mechanisms or material parameters are uniquely recoverable from the input image.

    A.2  Geometry, Materials, and Surface Binding

    The initial TRELLIS.2 reconstruction supplies the detailed visible geometry and materials. Geometric refinement uses rendered views and measurements to identify actionable regions: mesh connectivity alone does not determine which parts should move, and a texture boundary need not be a mechanical boundary. Bounded edits preserve useful source faces, UV coordinates, and material assignments. When topology changes, source correspondence must be updated rather than inherited from obsolete face indices.

    For rigid articulation, visible vertices follow the transform of their assigned body. Correct body ownership, local transforms, parent–child relationships, joint frames, and limits are all needed to produce the intended visible motion. Collision geometry can differ from the detailed render mesh, but motion of a collision proxy alone does not verify motion of the visible part.

    For compliant regions, the physical discretization and visible skin may also differ. The displacement binding in Eq. 4 transfers physical-node displacements to visible vertices in a common frame. Its node identities, dimensions, weights, and rest geometry are checked against the exported asset. Supports and loading conditions are specified separately from the skin binding. A local deformation observation removes common rigid motion before assessing shape change; otherwise, movement of the entire object could be mistaken for local compliance. The ear-pad example uses an approximate compliance model rather than a material calibration recovered from the image.

    A.3  Feedback and Candidate Records

    Rendered observations assess appearance, part separation, and visible response. Execution observations assess the requested action, achieved range, contacts, supports, and applicable deformation or recovery. Each record identifies the requirement, candidate, target region and entities, action, initial state, runtime and assessment configurations, and assessment outcome. The four outcomes are unassessed, pass, fail, and inconclusive. An execution error supplies no measured trajectory, and a changed build requires renewed dynamic evidence.

    Feedback associates a discrepancy with the relevant mechanism, realized entity, or binding. Local repairs can address motion range, tracking, surface assignment, or assembly; structural replanning addresses topology, ownership, joint-axis, or material contradictions. Previous candidates remain available when a revision fails. The budgets and selection procedure below bound this loop.

    A.4  Runtime Configuration and Budgets

    Table 6 summarizes the documented v0.2.0 runtime configuration. Blender handles geometry and material editing; MuJoCo executes supported physical models. The reasoning model is accessed through the local Codex interface. The configured generator seed identifies the initialization setting, without implying deterministic agent execution.

    Invalid returned messages consume their role-response allowance. Host validation attempts are reserved before execution, so an interrupted simulation also consumes an attempt. Candidate history and cumulative counters persist across continuations; selecting an earlier candidate does not reset them. Simulator calls made inside construction tools are not covered by the host-attempt limit. These counts therefore describe distinct resources rather than an aggregate computation budget. The initial construction and at most two repairs constitute the Builder budget in Section 4.1; structural replanning does not reset this budget. As in Section 3.4, a modified build requires new dynamic evidence, and a preview does not turn an unverified simulation status into a pass.

    A.5  Motion-Range Adaptation and Physical Checks

    For a hinge or slide with original interval [ℓ₀,h₀] and neutral coordinate q₀, the documented range helper tests

    ℓₙ=q₀+(ℓ₀-q₀)(2/3)ⁿ, hₙ=q₀+(h₀-q₀)(2/3)ⁿ, n∈{0,1,2}.

    		(6)

    The original interval remains the reference across repairs. The retained span must be at least 0.2(h₀-ℓ₀) and, for a hinge, at least 10^∘. A reduced interval is considered only after a completed failed sweep with a valid rest pose. The checks include rest and both motion directions where applicable. A colliding rest pose, missing clearance information, incomplete sweep, or execution error terminates this search. The achieved range is retained explicitly; reducing travel does not satisfy an unchanged full-closure requirement.

    Let D be the positive asset diagonal in meters. The documented acceptance profile uses a contact-proxy penetration tolerance of 0.005D, an angular endpoint tolerance of 5^∘, and a translational endpoint tolerance of 0.005D. Additional checks cover finite states, solver warnings, joint limits, measured interaction, and applicable compliant-region requirements. Geometric sweep checks apply to sampled configurations and do not replace dynamic execution.

    For a declared compliant region, a least-squares rigid alignment removes common motion from the simulation nodes. Let d_\max be the maximum residual over recorded samples and phase endpoints. The response criterion requires d_\max≥0.001D together with a pairwise-distance-change check. When recovery is required, the residual after unloading must not exceed \max(0.001D,0.35d_\max). These criteria are deformation heuristics on simulation nodes; exported-surface response is assessed separately through the binding and visible observations.

    A.6  Output Selection

    Selection excludes unloadable, empty, nonfinite, externally dependent assets and detected source-identity conflicts. In autonomous runs, eligible candidates are ranked by appearance evidence, native retention, semantic evidence, absence of unsupported additions, display checks, declared bodies, supported physics acceptance, and recency, in that order. Native retention includes source identity, face accounting, geometry, and UV/material checks. As specified in Section 4.5, Full pipeline and w/o surface preservation use the same selection rule. In the latter, source-geometry, UV, and material preservation constraints are removed from construction, while the shared ranking criteria and physical-to-visible bindings remain. This intervention therefore tests the construction constraints under a fixed output-selection policy. Supported physics acceptance requires a passing report, at least three trajectory states, and matching asset and trajectory identities. A preview can be returned without a valid dynamic trajectory, with that status kept distinct. If no refined candidate is eligible, the native reconstruction can serve as a static fallback. Such a fallback is not evidence that the requested interaction or dynamic validation succeeded; failed and inconclusive attempts remain in the outcome accounting.

    Appendix B Evaluation and Comparison Details

    B.1  Evaluation Scope and Aggregation

    The in-the-wild collection contains more than 200 photographs; the fixed evaluation subset contains 50 objects and 110 predefined semantic actions. Following Section 4.2, ACR, MMR, and RAR are macro-averaged over objects. For normalized object-level scores sᵢ⁽ᵐ⁾, metric m is reported as 100N⁻¹∑ᵢ₌₁^Nsᵢ⁽ᵐ⁾, with N=50. Thus, each object contributes equally, regardless of its number of rendered frames.

    ACR measures correct semantic action completion. Strict MMR counts missing, incomplete, incorrectly related, structurally broken, or spuriously coupled actions. RAR scores the maximum valid visible range in {0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1} after the ACR semantic gate. FVSP is the percentage of objects that complete every expected action without video-visible instability. It is a joint functional-and-visible-stability criterion based on rendered videos, not simulator logs.

    Support marks indicate declared or evaluated capabilities, not successful outputs. Static assets remain evaluable for input consistency; missing or invalid interaction videos count as failures within the fixed action denominator. Failed and inconclusive attempts remain in the outcome accounting, with unsupported output types distinguished in the records. Development examples remain separate from the benchmark comparison.

    B.2  Inputs, Baselines, and Scoring

    Section 4.1 specifies the common comparison protocol. Image-conditioned methods receive the same photograph; mesh-conditioned methods require an identified reconstruction and any auxiliary conditioning. Format and coordinate conversions are distinguished from geometry repair or inference of missing physical parameters, which would change the evaluated method. PhysXGen denotes the framework introduced in PhysX-3D [(Cao et al., 2025a)]. aDSL reports image-to-shape generation and articulated creation as a downstream application, motivating its inclusion in the single-image comparison.

    Reference-based comparisons use compatible alignment, pose, sampling, distance normalization, and scoring settings. Shape normalization must preserve the separately assessed absolute-scale error. Table 2 follows the PhysXVerse/PhysX-Mobility split reported by PhysX-Omni; its kinematic score is not a dynamics success rate. Missing scores, marked by a dash or NR, are unreported entries rather than measured zeros.

    PhysX-Bench uses fixed evidence generation, evaluator configuration, and prompts across methods. Joint playback supplies articulation evidence, while material response and static appearance are separate observations; playback does not establish dynamic contact stability. The selected states in Figure 4 likewise demonstrate visible articulation and surface appearance. Table 7 summarizes the evaluation settings.

    B.3  Ablation Configuration

    The three variants in Section 4.5 share inputs, cached reconstructions, initial priors, model and decoding settings, construction tools, and final scoring. Full pipeline and w/o surface preservation share the two-repair limit and candidate-selection rule. One-shot returns the initial candidate and receives final scoring without feeding it back for repair. All attempted inputs, including failed and inconclusive runs, remain in the outcome accounting.

    The source-preservation ablation removes construction-time geometry, UV, and material constraints while retaining the initial reconstruction and physical-to-visible bindings. It keeps output selection fixed, including the native-retention ranking criterion. The One-shot comparison measures refinement as a whole, including additional repair and candidate-selection opportunities; it does not isolate an individual feedback signal.

    Appendix C Additional Qualitative Comparisons

    Figure 5 extends Figure 3 with additional cases and methods, showing geometry, materials, and texture continuity alongside input-image agreement in proportions, parts, colors, and patterns. No additional aggregate score is introduced.

item.title: CAD 生成别只学着输出命令：CAD-WAM 把「命令」和「它造出的几何」一起建模，多步生成才不走偏 ｜ CAD-WAM: Anticipating Geometry for Text-to-CAD Generation
item.description:
一句话：一步错、步步错，是因为只监督命令不监督几何；借 world-action model 的思路联合预测状态。

要点：

  • 问题定位：从文本生成可编辑 CAD 需要选择「能对当前几何产生预期改变」的操作，一步选错就会毁掉后续步骤，多步生成因此不可靠
  • 现有基于 LLM 的方法主要学习预测命令，**没有对那些命令应当产生的几何状态做显式监督**——这正是误差累积的根源
  • CAD-WAM 借鉴 world-action model（世界动作模型）的思路，联合建模「动作（命令）」与「状态（几何）」，让模型在执行前先预判几何会变成什么样

为什么值得看：「AI 造资产」的失败常常不是画不出来，而是操作序列在第三、四步崩掉。把每一步的几何结果纳入监督，是程序化资产生成走向可用的关键；同样的思路可以直接搬到关卡/材质/动画的脚本化编辑上。

中文摘要：从文本生成可编辑 CAD 模型，需要在每一步选择「能对已有几何产生预期改变」的操作；一步选错就会影响后续步骤，因此多步生成很难可靠。现有基于大模型的方法主要学习预测命令序列，却没有对那些命令本应产生的几何状态做显式监督，这正是误差累积的原因。CAD-WAM 借用 world-action model（世界动作模型）的思路，把动作（命令）与状态（几何）联合建模，让模型在执行前先预判几何结果，从而在多步生成中保持方向。对程序化资产生成来说，这条把「监督信号放在结果上」的做法，比继续堆命令语料更接近工程可用。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-11-01

CAD-WAM: Anticipating Geometry for Text-to-CAD Generation

Abstract

Generating editable computer-aided design (CAD) models from text requires selecting operations that produce the intended changes to the geometry constructed so far. An incorrect operation can compromise subsequent steps, making reliable multi-step generation challenging. Existing methods based on large language models (LLMs) primarily learn to predict commands, without explicit supervision of the geometric states those commands should produce. Inspired by world-action models, we introduce CAD-WAM, which couples geometry-conditioned action generation with next-state prediction. We define complete modeling operations as actions in a CAD domain-specific language (DSL) and encode surface point clouds of intermediate solids into compact latent states using a pretrained variational autoencoder. An LLM backbone generates the next action from the target description and current geometric state, while an auxiliary head on the same backbone predicts the next state to provide geometric supervision during training. We construct step-wise training trajectories from parametric CAD models in the DeepCAD dataset, pairing each trajectory with an expert-level textual description. At inference, each generated action is executed by a CAD kernel, and the resulting solid is re-encoded to inform the next decision. On the DeepCAD test set, CAD-WAM outperforms the task-specific baselines in geometric accuracy and output validity, with larger gains on models requiring more operations, and produces more accurate geometry than general-purpose LLMs prompted with the same DSL. Ablations further show that next-state supervision reduces mean Chamfer distance by 13.2% relative to an otherwise identical model trained only to predict actions. Code is available at https://github.com/Lzy-1037/CAD-WAM.

1 Introduction

Parametric computer-aided design (CAD) represents a model through a sequence of editable geometric operations rather than only its final shape. Generating such models from natural language can reduce the manual effort required for CAD modeling. Existing approaches generate parametric command sequences [(Khan et al., 2024)] or fine-tune large language models (LLMs) to produce executable programs in CAD scripting languages such as CadQuery and FeatureScript [(Guan et al., 2025; Pyatov et al., 2026; Kolodiazhnyi et al., 2026)].

Reliable multi-step CAD generation requires more than producing executable commands: each operation must also realize the intended change to the geometry constructed so far. An incorrect operation can alter the solid on which subsequent operations act, causing further deviations from the target. Our experiments also reveal an uneven error distribution: several baselines achieve low median geometric error, yet some outputs deviate substantially from the target (Figure 4). Existing methods incorporate geometric information through reinforcement learning with geometric rewards [(Guan et al., 2025; Kolodiazhnyi et al., 2026)] or step-wise generation conditioned on the current boundary representation (B-rep) [(Qi et al., 2026)]. These approaches use geometry to evaluate generated programs or inform the next decision, but do not explicitly supervise predictions of the next geometric state. This motivates learning each modeling step through both its symbolic action and its intended geometric outcome, connecting operation generation with the evolving shape of the CAD model.

World-action models provide a natural perspective on this formulation by coupling action learning with prediction of future observations [(Tian et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025)].
