We likewise share stochastic computation, but retain continuation dependencies in a dynamically built DAG supporting weighted attachment, progressive refinement, and coverage-preserving compression without fixed probes or discretized interfaces.

    Adaptive Sampling and Interactive Updates.

    Learned directional and variance-aware path guiding in rendering [(Müller et al., 2017; Rath et al., 2020)] motivates steering WoS, despite unstable likelihood ratios. Differential WoS estimates geometry/boundary sensitivities [(Miller et al., 2024)]; WoDS updates affected local operators [(Jambon et al., 2026)]; and WoS-based cage cutting reuses cut-unaffected paths to update harmonic weights [(Saeed et al., 2026)]. Beyond per-query guiding or cutting-specific reuse, our bounded-weight attachment and variance-guided refinement maintain transport for repeated boundary solves, local geometry repair, and low-rank regional edits.

    3. Reusable WoS Skeleton Construction

    Let Ω⊂ℝ³ be the domain with Dirichlet boundary data g. For the source-free problem, the solution is represented by u(x)=𝔼[g(X_τ)|X₀=x], where X_τ is the boundary arrival of Brownian motion started at x, and τ its first exit time, allowing WoS to estimate this expectation via sampled walks. Independent queries repeatedly explore similar regions and recompute their continuations. The Markov property motivates retaining these continuations since once a spatial state is fixed, its remaining evolution does not depend on the prefix that reaches it. We therefore retain sampled WoS trajectories as directed chains, with multiple trajectories forming outgoing branches. When a new walk reaches a state p, it may reuse the completed continuations of an existing node q by connecting to its downstream branches rather than generating new walks termed path attachment. Such shared dependencies form a transport directed acyclic graph (DAG), dubbed skeleton.

    Skeleton Data-structure. Each DAG node p stores a position xₚ consisting of these types: query nodes are the locations where the solution is requested, boundary nodes supply terminal data, and the remaining states are internal nodes that a certain WoS path passes by. An edge p→q means that the estimate at p depends on the continuation at q and let ℂ(p) denote these outgoing dependencies. To support reuse, the skeleton also retains how each outgoing branch was sampled. For a completed node i, let S(i) denote its sampling groups. Each group s records the original sphere Bₛ=B(cₛ,Rₛ)⊂Ω, its surface-area proposal density rₛ, and the downstream nodes ℂₛ(i) sampled on ∂Bₛ, so that ℂ(i)=\bigcup_s∈S(i)ℂₛ(i). A node may contain groups from different spheres because attachments inherit the sampling records of reused branches. These records allow the same sampled continuations to be reweighted for new starting positions. For a fixed skeleton, internal nodes ûₚ and boundary nodes û_b are given by

    ûₚ=∑_q∈ℂ(p)w_pqû_q, û_b=g(x_b),

    where b denotes a boundary node and edge weight w_pq includes averaging and importance corrections. Boundary contributions propagate toward queries in reverse topological order, evaluating each shared continuation once. Since the graph retains boundary positions, changing boundary data supplies new leaf values without retracing the walks, enabling us to estimate queried values via a cheap traversal on the DAG.

    The main challenge of path attachment is that the current state and the reused node generally occupy different positions. Directly inheriting the latter’s sampled continuations introduces bias, while restricting attachment to nearly identical states limits opportunities for reuse. More aggressive attachment like directional guiding may improve reuse but may produce unstable importance weights as further analyzed in Appendix A. We first introduce a change-of-measure attachment rule with bounded importance weights in Section 3.1 motivated by [(Czekanski et al., 2026)] to address this tradeoff, and then describe efficient evaluation of the resulting DAG in Section 3.2, followed by progressive refinement of uncertain continuations for skeleton nodes with high variances in Section 3.3. Finally, Section 3.4 extends the skeleton construction to Poisson equations with source terms.

    3.1. Path Attachment

    Path attachment enables a walk at p to terminate early by reusing the completed continuations of an existing skeleton node q. Rather than treating p as q, we connect it to the downstream branches ℂ(q), avoiding new walks along these continuations. This raises three questions: how to reuse samples generated from a different starting position, when such reuse is sufficiently stable, and how to reach reusable regions efficiently.

    Reweighting. The sampled continuations of q cannot be directly reused at p, since their Brownian exit distributions differ. We account for this difference through a change of measure on each recorded sampling sphere. Attachment requires p∈Bₛ for every s∈S(q). For a branch j∈ℂₛ(q), its weight becomes

    (1)

    wₚⱼ=(K_Bₛ(p,xⱼ))/(K_Bₛ(q,xⱼ))w_qj,

    where K_Bₛ(x,z) is the exit density with respect to surface area on ∂Bₛ for a walk started at x, and xⱼ is the position of node j. The existing weight w_qj includes the averaging factor and original proposal correction, so the complete importance factor of the new connection is

    (2)

    ℓ_p,s(z)=(K_Bₛ(p,z))/(K_Bₛ(q,z))(K_Bₛ(q,z))/(rₛ(z))=(K_Bₛ(p,z))/(rₛ(z)).

    Admissibility and candidate search. Although reweighting corrects the exit distribution, large importance factors can increase estimator variance. Moreover, checking every completed node for attachment would undermine the efficiency gained from reuse. We address both issues by defining admissible regions that can be spatially indexed. A connection to q is admissible only if p lies inside every recorded sampling sphere and

    (3)

    Γ_q(p):=\max_s∈S(q)\sup_z∈∂Bₛℓ_p,s(z)≤Λ_attach,

    where Λ_attach is the prescribed attachment limit. These conditions define a reusable region for each completed node. We spatially index these regions and select the admissible candidate with the smallest Γ_q(p). Upon acceptance, p is connected to ℂ(q) using Eq. 1, and its walk terminates. If no admissible candidate exists, the walk continues. Since all reused subgraphs are already completed, these connections preserve acyclicity.

    Directional guiding. Even with efficient candidate search, uniform WoS walks may rarely enter reusable regions, especially those that are difficult to reach or sparsely covered by the skeleton. Guiding steers exploration toward these hard-to-reach regions in the form of a prescribed point or a selected object surface. Specifically, we sample directions from a mixture of the uniform distribution and a von Mises–Fisher distribution directed toward the target on each WoS sphere. In implementation, the step weight is multiplied by (4πQ(ω))⁻¹ for the resulting density of the unit direction ω.

    3.2. Graph Evaluation

    Once constructed, the skeleton can be evaluated for new boundary data without tracing additional WoS paths. Since each edge i→j represents a dependency on the continuation at j, terminal values û_b=g(x_b) propagate toward queries in reverse topological order. This follows a standard parallel DAG traversal, where nodes are evaluated once all their dependencies are resolved, as summarized in Algorithm 1. Each node is evaluated once and each edge contributes one weighted accumulation, yielding O(|V|+|E|) work.

    Topology-based scheduling.

    To reduce the scheduling overhead of frontier-based evaluation, particularly along single-dependency chains, we exploit the fixed skeleton topology to precompute an execution schedule. One scheduling variant fuses maximal single-dependency runs and assigns levels only to the remaining scheduled vertices. Let ℂ̄(i) denote the first scheduled descendants reached from i after skipping fused vertices. Set ℓ(i)=0 if ℂ̄(i)=∅, and otherwise ℓ(i)=1+\max_j∈ℂ̄(i)ℓ(j). Increasing levels respect the dependency order. A worker dispatched at a scheduled vertex evaluates its owned run of single-dependency predecessors locally, omitting those vertices from separate frontiers. This variant reduces intermediate queue operations while preserving the weighted DAG.

    3.3. Progressive Refinement

    Beyond reusing existing paths, the skeleton also enables more targeted allocation of additional samples. Rather than repeatedly launching new walks from query points, we can refine selected internal nodes by adding new continuations and propagating their updated estimates through the DAG. This allows additional sampling effort to improve multiple queries sharing the same downstream dependencies, without resampling their existing paths.

    Let Nᵢ=|ℂ(i)| count the existing outgoing contributions of node i, including inherited attachment contributions. If bᵢ new paths are added, let X̂_i,r be the value returned by the rth independent vanilla WoS continuation from xᵢ, run to boundary termination without attachment. We locally update the dependencies of node i by the following to ensure each sample weighs equally:

    (4)

    ûᵢ←Nᵢ/Nᵢ+bᵢûᵢ+1/Nᵢ+bᵢ∑ᵣ₌₁^bᵢX̂_i,r.

    Selecting refinement nodes.

    For a target query q, candidates are the internal nodes reachable along its outgoing dependencies. Their influences aᵢ=(∂û_q)/(∂ûᵢ) measure how changes in a node value affect the query and are obtained by forward propagation from q toward the boundary. To identify which nodes would benefit most from additional sampling, we also need their continuation variances. Rather than estimating these independently at every node, we partition the domain into subdomains and share a vanilla WoS estimate of single-continuation variance among nodes within each subdomain. Let σ̂ᵢ² denote the estimate assigned to node i. Using the local variance surrogate aᵢ²σ̂ᵢ²/Nᵢ, we rank candidates by the predicted reduction from one additional continuation as Eq. (5) and retain up to K highest-scoring candidates as a fixed set S.

    (5)

    Δᵢ=aᵢ²σ̂ᵢ²(1/Nᵢ-1/Nᵢ+1)=(aᵢ²σ̂ᵢ²)/(Nᵢ(Nᵢ+1)).

    Budget allocation.

    The preceding selection identifies promising refinement nodes, but does not determine how many additional continuations each should receive. Given a total budget C, we allocate bᵢ continuations to each selected node i∈S to minimize the estimated residual variance. Extending the local variance surrogate used for candidate selection gives

    (6)

    \min_{bᵢ≥0}∑_i∈S(aᵢ²σ̂ᵢ²)/(Nᵢ+bᵢ), s.t. ∑_i∈Sbᵢ=C.

    The continuous solution is bᵢ=\max(0,t|aᵢ|σ̂ᵢ-Nᵢ), where t is chosen to satisfy the budget constraint. Consequently, we round the allocations to integers while preserving the total budget C.

    3.4. Source Terms as an Additive DAG Structure

    For the Poisson equation Δu=f, a WoS step must account for the source field f inside its sampling ball as well as the continuation on the ball’s surface. With the Dirichlet Green function defined by -ΔG_B=δ with respect to the Dirac distribution δ, a point x∈B satisfies

    (7)

    u(x)=∫_∂BK_B(x,z)u(z) dσ(z)-∫_BG_B(x,y)f(y) dy.

    The two integrals become separate sets of weighted dependencies in the skeleton.

    Source sampling and graph representation.

    For a newly generated step on Bₛ=B(cₛ,Rₛ), draw a uniform surface exit X and L independent volumetric samples Yₖ with density ρₛ(y)=G_Bₛ(cₛ,y)/Zₛ, where Zₛ=∫_BₛG_Bₛ(cₛ,y) dy=Rₛ²/6 in ℝ³. The local estimator is

    (8)

    û(cₛ)=û(X)-Rₛ²/6L∑ₖ₌₁^Lf(Yₖ),

    where û(X) is the continuation estimate at the sampled exit. Thus each step adds one continuation and L source leaves with local weight -Rₛ²/6L. Retaining source locations gives a node q the additive estimator

    (9)

    û_q=∑ⱼw^K_qjûⱼ+∑ₖw^G_qkf(yₖ),

    where xⱼ and yₖ are its continuation and source locations, while weights w^K_qj and w^G_qk include the corresponding sampling and averaging factors. Source leaves supply f(yₖ) and do not continue walking or serve as spatial attachment targets.

    Attachment and reusable evaluation.

    Each source sample retains its original sampling-group record. To reuse a group of q from another point p∈Bₛ, keep the sampled locations and proposal fixed, and replace the Green kernel’s starting point through

    (10)

    w^Gₚₖ=(G_Bₛ(p,yₖ))/(G_Bₛ(q,yₖ))w^G_qk.

    The continuation edges use the Poisson ratio from Eq. 1, so attachment reuses both surface and volume contributions without resampling the target group. And the surface admissibility condition still follows Section 3.1 governs acceptance. For fixed geometry, the sampled positions and transport weights are independent of the values of g and f. Changing either field therefore requires only new terminal values: boundary leaves receive g(x_b) and source leaves receive f(yₖ). Algorithm 1 then evaluates the same DAG without new walks.

    3.5. Spatially Aware Graph Compression

    A completed skeleton may contain many intermediate states along WoS trajectories, increasing storage and evaluation cost without necessarily improving reuse. Consecutive single-dependency states can be eliminated exactly, but their removal also discards spatial entry points for future attachment and refinement. We therefore compress the graph while retaining selected states that provide useful spatial coverage or serve as important roles in the skeleton such as queries, terminals, branching and merging vertices. Any remaining chain S=(v₀,…,vₖ) whose interior vertices have one incoming and one outgoing edge can be replaced by a single edge with weight w_S=∏ᵣ₌₀ᵏ⁻¹w_vᵣvᵣ₊₁. This contraction preserves the linear map from terminal values to retained nodes, including all query estimates, while reducing the number of stored vertices and edges. However, eliminated states can no longer serve as aforementioned attachment or following refinement locations. We therefore preserve selected spatial anchors, together with their direct sampled-exit children, associated edges, and sampling records, while contracting the remaining eligible chains.

    Coverage-preserving anchor selection.

    An anchor set A is selected to provide at least m≥1 attachment choices over a target fraction ρ_target of the domain. With ℝᵥ denoting the reusable region of candidate v and ℙ a fixed set of uniform probes, coverage is measured by c_A(p)=∑_v∈A1_p∈ℝᵥ and ρₘ(A)=|{p∈ℙ:c_A(p)≥m}|/|ℙ|, subject to ρₘ(A)≥ρ_target. Selection follows the greedy criterion v^⋆=\arg\max_v∉AΔ_A(v), where Δ_A(v)=∑_p∈ℙ∩ℝᵥ1_c_A(p)

    Since anchors along one trajectory share downstream samples, coverage can be extended to distinct trajectory origins to reduce correlation in subsequent attachment. With b(v) identifying the trajectory that created v and B_A(p)={b(v):v∈A, p∈ℝᵥ} denoting the origins available at p, the count becomes c_A(p)=|B_A(p)| and the greedy score becomes Δ_A(v)=∑_p∈ℙ∩ℝᵥ1_c_A(p)

    4. Adaptive Transport Reuse for Interactive Scenes

    A reusable transport skeleton must support more than repeated evaluation on fixed geometry. In interactive scenes, new queries may appear in poorly covered regions, objects may move or be inserted, and users may wish to edit transport between selected regions. Rebuilding the skeleton after every change would discard much of its reusable computation. We therefore develop local graph updates that adapt the retained transport without reconstructing it globally: path refinement expands spatial attachment opportunities, hub-based reuse shares continuations across dense queries, geometry repair updates transitions affected by scene changes, and regional transport editing provides direct control over selected interactions.

    4.1. Path Refinement for New Queries

    The attachment bound in Section 3.1 limits the region from which a retained sampling sphere can be reused to avoid variance explosion, while path refinement comes to rescue by exposing intermediate positions within retained WoS steps, providing additional attachment locations for new queries. Path refinement also paves way for both building hub-sphere for intra-skeleton trajectories reuse (Section 4.2), and skeleton repairing and tiny-object capturing in dynamic scenarios (Section 4.3).

    Consider an ordinary WoS step p→q with sampling ball B=B(p,R), where the recorded exit q was sampled uniformly on ∂B. Starting at p₀=p, one can generate intermediate positions conditioned on that exit as Figure 2. For a local ball Bₖ=B(pₖ,Rₖ)⊂B, the next position s∈∂Bₖ is sampled with surface-area density

    (11)

    fₖ(s|q)=(1)/(|∂Bₖ|)(K_B(s,q))/(K_B(pₖ,q)).

    This Doob h-transform, with h(x)=K_B(x,q), recovers Brownian transitions conditioned on exiting B at q. We choose Rₖ=(R-∥pₖ-p∥)/2, half the remaining distance to the original sphere. This leaves each local ball strictly inside B while advancing the path and exposing intermediate positions. Appendix B.4 shows that it requires at most two draws per step on average in rejection sampling for this radius choice.

    The original edge p→q can coexists with the newly generated positions pₖ, 1≤k≤N-1, as a node with a unit-weight edge pₖ→q. To see why direct connections suffice, consider a chain p₁→⋯→pₘ→q with unit weights, which makes every node in this chain evaluate to the retained estimate U_q at q. In practice, one can replace an ordinary retained edge p→q of coefficient w by a chain p→p₁→⋯→pₘ→q uses w_p→p₁=w/N,w_pⱼ→pⱼ₊₁=1,w_pₘ→q=1. Connecting each node directly to q therefore preserves its value while reducing propagation depth. Notably, though these pₖ’s can be sampled sequentially, their values can still simply share a direct reference to the same continuation. Such conditional construction ensures that each new node z has the correct continuation law on its own sphere, making it a valid attachment target (Appendix B.1).

    As a conditioned path approaches q, shrinking local balls provide diminishing spatial coverage. We therefore limit each refinement path to L steps or terminate earlier when the sphere clearance falls below a prescribed tolerance, allocating further samples to fresh conditioned paths starting from p.

    4.2. Shared Query Evaluation in a Hub

    Path attachment and refinement allow individual queries to reuse existing continuations, but densely distributed queries may still incur repeated costs in searching for and connecting to the skeleton. To share these connections, we introduce a hub ball H=B(p₀,R_H)⊂Ω containing a group of queries. Rather than attaching each query separately, we construct a common pool of interface samples on ∂H, each referencing an existing downstream continuation. Queries inside H then reuse this pool through the Poisson kernel K_H, with only their query-dependent weights evaluated separately.

    These interfaces can be obtained either by conditionally refining retained paths to their crossings with ∂H or by sampling directly on portions of ∂H supported by retained sampling spheres. In the conditional construction (Figure 2), a retained step q₀→q₁ supported by a ball S is refined within S∩H, conditioned on q₁. If the path reaches ∂H before ∂S, its first crossing z∈∂H provides an interface referencing q₁ with unit weight, avoiding additional spatial importance ratios. While this construction reuses existing paths without reweighting their reconstructed crossings, direct sampling provides explicit control over the interface distribution, allowing contributions from different sampling groups to be combined across ∂H. We therefore develop the direct-sampling estimator below and leave the conditional construction and its probabilistic justification to Appendix C.

    For L retained sampling groups, indexed by j=1,…,L, let Sⱼ be the supporting ball of group j and let U_Qⱼ denote the retained continuation estimate at its exit Qⱼ. Each group contributes over a supported hub patch Γⱼ=∂H∩Sⱼ, which covers the entire ∂H if Sⱼ contains H. Then independently of its retained exit Qⱼ∼rⱼ, sample Z∼gⱼ(z)=1_Γⱼ(z)/|Γⱼ| on Γⱼ, where gⱼ is an area density, extended by zero outside the patch. The interface continuation is given by Eq. (12) where the weight converts the retained proposal density rⱼ to the Poisson kernel at Z.

    (12)

    Ûⱼ(Z)=(K_Sⱼ(Z,Qⱼ))/(rⱼ(Qⱼ))U_Qⱼ.

    Since individual sampling groups cover only portions of ∂H, their contributions must be combined without double-counting overlapping patches. We therefore sample a group J=j with probability βⱼ, followed by an interface Z∼gⱼ, giving the marginal density m(z)=∑ⱼ₌₀^Lβⱼgⱼ(z) with ∑ⱼβⱼ=1. As the retained groups may not cover the entire hub surface, we include a full-support fallback group with g₀(z)=1/|∂H| and β₀>0, whose continuation Û₀(Z) is generated by vanilla WoS and retained in the skeleton. This ensures m(z)>0 throughout ∂H, allowing the hub estimator to use N shared interface samples whose unbiasedness is validated by Proposition 4.1:

    (13)

    û_H(x)=1/N∑ₙ₌₁^N(K_H(x,Zₙ))/(m(Zₙ))Û_Jₙ(Zₙ).

    Proposition 4.1 (Unbiased hub reuse).

    If the retained downstream estimators are conditionally unbiased and interface sampling is independent of the retained continuations, then 𝔼[Ûⱼ(Z)|Z=z]=u(z) and 𝔼[û_H(x)]=u(x) for every x∈H.

    Proof sketch.

    The ratio in Eq. (12) recovers the Poisson representation at Z, while the mixture density m cancels the joint sampling density over ∂H. See Appendix B.6. ∎

    To represent the hub estimator in the skeleton, sampling groups and mixture probabilities are chosen independently of the retained exit and continuation samples. Each interface Zₙ generated from group j introduces edges with weights

    (14)

    w_x→Zₙ=(K_H(x,Zₙ))/(N m(Zₙ)), w_Zₙ→Qⱼ=(K_Sⱼ(Zₙ,Qⱼ))/(rⱼ(Qⱼ)).

    The first weight accounts for hub sampling and averaging, while the second reweights the retained continuation. Interface positions, mixture densities, and continuation references are stored once per hub, with queries evaluating their own weights against this shared pool. For M queries and N interfaces, this reduces explicit connection storage from O(MN) to O(M+N), although exact evaluation still requires O(MN) kernel contributions.

    4.3. Transport Adaptation for Dynamic Objects

    As Figure 3, dynamic geometry changes can invalidate previously sampled WoS transitions, but their downstream continuations may remain reusable. When a new object intersects a retained sampling ball, the recorded exit alone cannot determine whether the underlying Brownian path would have encountered the object first. Rather than discarding the entire continuation, we use conditional path refinement to reconstruct the transition and redirect it to the new boundary only when necessary. This enables local adaptation of the skeleton while preserving unaffected transport. We consider an object inserted into the domain, with the remaining geometry and boundary data fixed.

    We spatially index the sampling balls to identify transitions affected by the inserted object. For an affected edge p→q supported by a ball S, we reconstruct its path conditioned on the recorded exit q, using Eq. 11, with local sampling balls contained in S and outside the inserted object. If the reconstructed path hits the object, the edge is redirected to the new boundary; otherwise, it reconnects to q upon approaching ∂S within a prescribed tolerance, provided q remains outside the object. In both cases, the original edge coefficient is preserved, since the conditional sampling law accounts for the retained exit. To preserve shared transport, repair follows the affected dependencies from queries toward their continuations, replacing only invalidated references, while unaffected downstream subgraphs are retained and only those modified nodes with their ancestors are reevaluated. This confines both reconstruction and reevaluation to the affected transport.

    Conditional repair may suffer from high variance when small inserted objects with significant boundary contributions are rarely hit. Our framework is also compatible with bidirectional WoS (Bi-WoS) [(Qi et al., 2022)], whose reverse Green-function estimates can provide shared local corrections to affected sampling balls, accounting for both retained continuations and new boundary contributions. The integration and stopping criteria are detailed in Appendix D.

    4.4. Application: Regional Transport Editing

    The retained skeleton exposes transport dependencies between spatial regions, enabling artist-controlled amplification or attenuation of selected interactions. Rather than rebuilding the solver, we approximate the requested region-to-region transport as a low-rank patch applied to the original DAG.

    Eliminating internal states yields an effective transport operator on retained anchors. For retained states A and eliminated states I, û_I=W_IIû_I+W_IAû_A, giving T=W_AA+W_AI(I-W_II)⁻¹W_IA. Acyclicity allows T and Tᵀ to be applied through graph traversals without explicitly forming either matrix.

    For selected source and target clusters σ and τ, let P_σ inject source values and R_τ restrict target values, defining T_τ←σ=R_τTP_σ. We approximate this block using randomized range finding with target rank r and p oversampling vectors. Draw Ω∈ℝ^|σ|×(r+p) and compute Y=T_τ←σΩ, Q=orth(Y) by forward traversal, followed by Z=T_τ←σᵀQ by reverse traversal. This gives T_τ←σ≈QZᵀ. Only r+p batched forward probes and corresponding reverse propagation are needed, and forward probes can be shared across target clusters with the same source.

    To scale the selected interaction by γ, a low-rank correction is applied by û_τ←û_τ+(γ-1)QZᵀû_σ. The original solver is recovered at γ=1; other values deliberately modify the represented transport rather than the underlying PDE. However, the source and target clusters may interleave in topological order, so the correction must exclude backward dependencies to preserve the DAG. Let t(v) satisfy t(i)t(i)Zⱼûⱼ, giving Δûᵢ=(γ-1)Qᵢᵀsᵢ for i∈τ. When crossing source node j, update s←s+Zⱼûⱼ.

    Remark 1 (Edit Complexity).

    Each causal patch costs O(r(|σ|+|τ|)) per evaluation, without dense blocks or changes to the DAG. Regional edits can be applied as separate low-rank patches.

    5. Experiments and Results

    5.1. Experimental Setup

    We evaluate accuracy, solve time, and the amortization of construction cost, together with refinement, compression, and interactive reuse. Unless stated otherwise, experiments use the multi-object mesh domain shown in Figure 4 : irregular obstacles lie inside an enclosing sphere, with spatially varying scalar Dirichlet data on their surfaces. Specialized domains are introduced in the corresponding experiments.

    A typical construction procedure begins by tracing independent WoS trajectories from a set of initial queries to form an initial skeleton. We then introduce additional queries, whose walks reuse completed continuations through path attachment, producing an attached skeleton. For comparison, an independent-path skeleton traces independent WoS trajectories from all queries without attachment.

    Accuracy is measured by MSE=1/M∑ᵢ₌₁^M(û(xᵢ)-u_ref(xᵢ))², where M is the total number of queries, xᵢ is a query position, û is the estimated solution, and u_ref is an independent Monte Carlo reference using 10⁵ WoS trajectories. Each configuration was repeated for 5-10 runs, and the mean value was reported.

    All timed methods run serially on the CPU. Skeleton solve time measures weighted DAG evaluation (Section 3.2).Construction and solver preparation are included only in the amortization experiment; dynamic-update timings include repair and reevaluation. The attachment limit in Eq. 3 is set to 4 unless varied explicitly, as recommended by the accuracy–efficiency trade-off observed in Section 5.5.

    5.2. Skeleton Accuracy and Solve Time

    Can reuse support a more accurate estimate with a shorter solve time? We compare an independent-path skeleton, an attached skeleton that reuses an initial skeleton through path attachment, and Vanilla WoS. Varying their trajectories per query traces the accuracy–solve-time curves in Figure 5.

    Both skeletons have substantially lower solve time than Vanilla WoS. For example, the attached skeleton with 64 trajectories per query reduces MSE by 62% while solving about 275× faster than 16-trajectory Vanilla WoS. Reusing the skeleton removes repeated geometric traversal from the solve, allowing a larger construction budget to improve accuracy at low solve time.

    The skeleton detail separates this benefit from attachment’s contribution. At moderate budgets, attachment offers a better accuracy–solve-time trade-off than the independent-path skeleton: its 96-trajectory configuration has both lower error and lower solve time than the independent-path 64-trajectory skeleton. At larger budgets the attached curve flattens while the independent-path skeleton continues to improve. This behavior is consistent with shared continuations limiting the benefit of additional trajectories.

    5.3. Construction-Cost Amortization

    To measure when construction pays for itself, we build an independent-path skeleton, then solve successively for different boundary field. Cumulative skeleton time includes construction and solver preparation once, followed by skeleton evaluation for each field; Vanilla WoS generates fresh trajectories for each solve. Figure 6 compares the mean across skeleton builds with one measured Vanilla WoS solve sequence.

    Construction costs roughly one Vanilla WoS solve, while subsequent skeleton evaluations add little to the total. The skeleton amortizes its initial cost by the second solve and is 8.1× faster cumulatively at eight solves. Thus, even without attachment, retaining transport separates the cost of changing boundary data from the cost of exploring the geometry.

    5.4. Sample Budget Allocation

    To investigate how to allocate sampling budget between initial and additional queries to minimize their combined estimation error, we divide a fixed trajectory budget between equal-sized batches of initial and additional queries, varying the fraction allocated to attachment. Figure 7 reports mean error across matched trials.

    The error curve favors a balanced allocation. Spending too little on initial construction weakens the transport available for reuse, while spending too little on attachment undersamples the additional queries.

    5.5. Attachment Limit Sensitivity

    In Eq. 3, a smaller attachment limit favors higher accuracy at the cost of reduced attachment efficiency. To explore this trade-off, we vary this limit while holding the initial skeleton fixed. Table 1 reports MSE, the fraction of additional-query walks ending by attachment, and the mean WoS step count over all additional-query walks.

    Relaxing the limit initially removes most exploration work, at the cost of increased error. Beyond 4, attachment is already frequent: further relaxation buys little additional reuse while allowing larger importance factors and higher MSE. We therefore use 4 as the default compromise between accuracy and exploration cost.

    5.6. Poisson Problems with Source Terms

    We next test whether the additive source structure in Section 3.4 retains the accuracy–solve-time benefit for Poisson problems. Both methods use two source samples per WoS step.

    Figure 8 shows that the solve-time advantage extends to source terms. With 192 trajectories per query, the attached skeleton achieves 34% lower MSE than 96-trajectory Vanilla WoS while solving about 126× faster. Storing volume contributions alongside boundary transport avoids repeating geometry traversal and source sampling during evaluation. Increasing the skeleton budget from 192 to 256 does not further reduce mean error, whereas Vanilla WoS continues to improve. Thus, additional construction trajectories offer diminishing accuracy gains in this range despite the low evaluation cost.

    5.7. Variance-Guided Query Refinement

    Query refinement can be useful in a domain with localized regions of high variance, for example, surrounding cups with rapidly varying boundary data on a few of their interiors, as shown in Figure 9. Holding the base skeleton fixed, we compare our method with adding the continuation directly at the queries with the same budgets. Table 2 reports the average error before and after these updates.

    Refinement reduces mean error by 75.8% from the initial estimate and by 42.0% relative to adding WoS samples directly at the queries. Targeting high-variance internal contributions with strong query influence concentrates the new samples where they can most improve the estimate. Moreover, improving a shared continuation can benefit several queries, rather than only the query that receives additional samples. This makes local refinement useful when uncertainty is spatially concentrated within an otherwise reusable skeleton.

    5.8. Coverage-Preserving Compression

    To evaluate whether coverage preservation maintains attachment opportunities for new queries, we compare coverage-preserving compression with path-chain elimination on the same skeleton. The required multiplicity in Section 3.5 is set to m=1.

    After compression, both graphs add a same batch of queries and perform path attachment with the same sampling budgets. Then we measure the fraction of all graph nodes removed, attachment success rate, and mean WoS steps over all new trajectories. Table 3 summarizes the trade-off between node reduction and subsequent attachment.

    Preserving access costs only 0.76% of the original node count, yet reduces subsequent exploration by 21.7%. Aggressively contracting every eligible chain removes few additional nodes at the expense of useful spatial access points. Spatial anchors therefore preserve much of the compression benefit while making the retained transport easier for new queries to reach.

    5.9. Spatial Coverage from Path Refinement

    To evaluate how path refinement in Section 4.1 expands the region satisfying the attachment bound, we apply it to a single sampling ball and vary the number of refinement paths. Coverage is measured as the fraction of the ball’s volume satisfying the bound.

    Within a retained sampling ball, path refinement can substantially expands the attachable region, as shown in Table 4.

    With eight refinement paths, coverage increases from 6.56% to 34.69%, reaching approximately 5.3 times the original coverage. With 32 paths, coverage reaches 48.15%, approximately 7.3 times the original coverage.

    5.10. Dense Queries through a Hub

    To assess the memory savings of hub evaluation for dense queries, we compare it with ordinary path attachment on the same base skeleton. Queries are added within a hub inside an irregular domain (Figure 11). Figure 12 reports the additional persistent memory as the query count increases.

    The shared pool makes hub memory nearly independent of the number of added queries over the tested range. Its fixed interface cost is amortized across more queries, so the storage advantage increases with query density.

    Despite substantial memory savings, approaching ordinary attachment’s accuracy requires a larger sample ammount. In the trials, an average of 3893 shared interfaces gives a mean MSE of 1.224×10⁻³, compared with 1.094×10⁻³ for ordinary attachment using 32 trajectories per query. The hub thus needs more interface samples to compensate for shared downstream information.

    5.11. Local Repair of Dynamic Transport

    To test whether local repair preserves important continuations after a geometry change, we construct a dumbbell-shaped domain with two spherical chambers connected by a passage (Figure 13(a)). An initial skeleton is built and refined in the chamber with rapidly varying boundary data, referred to as the remote chamber. Target queries are then added in the other chamber. A small fraction of their walks traverse the passage and attach to the well-explored skeleton in the remote chamber. Finally, the obstacle shown in Figure 13(b) moves to the passage entrance, invalidating sampling balls along these connecting paths.

    We then compare conditional repair with suffix resampling, which replaces each affected continuation with a fresh WoS walk from its starting node. Both methods update the solution by reevaluating the affected ancestors. Among the reachable remote nodes, we measure the fraction that remain reachable afterward. This gives the retention rate of the existing downstream skeleton. Update time includes repair and ancestor reevaluation, excluding the shared initial construction. Table 5 reports mean results. Target-query MSE isolates the queries that rely on the remote structure.

    Conditional repair retains access to much of the existing remote transport, rather than replacing it when an earlier sampling ball becomes invalid. This reduces target-query MSE by 53.5% for an 8.0% increase in update time.

    5.12. Bidirectional Support for Local Repair

    We next consider a small obstacle with rapidly varying boundary values and a large contribution relative to its low-valued surroundings, as shown in Figure 14. Its spiked geometry is chosen to invalidate many sampling balls while remaining difficult for walks to hit. Conditional repair is augmented with Bi-WoS to better resolve the obstacle’s influence while retaining access to old continuations. Table 6 compares this extension with conditional repair alone and suffix resampling, using the same initial skeleton and query positions in matched trials.

    Adding Bi-WoS reduces mean MSE by 57.9% relative to conditional repair alone and by 44.4% relative to suffix resampling. The conditional-only result shows that preserving old transport does not by itself resolve a newly introduced contribution that is rarely encountered by forward paths. Reverse sampling complements this structural reuse: the repair can retain useful old continuations while better resolving the influence of a small, important boundary component.

    Together, the two experiments demonstrate local editing that preserves existing transport, with bidirectional support improving its accuracy in a difficult sampling regime.

    5.13. Regional Transport Editing

    We demonstrate selective transport editing by amplifying the influence of the volcano island’s boundary on queries around the village island. Figure 15 compares the original solution with three settings of the interaction scaling factorγ. All four panels use the same skeleton, query positions, and regional low-rank patch.

    Increasing γ strengthens the volcano’s contribution at the village queries, while query values in the other regions remain exactly unchanged. Once the regional patch has been extracted, changing γ requires neither new trajectories nor reconstruction of the skeleton. The retained graph thus serves as an editable transport operator, allowing independent control of a selected regional influence while preserving the remaining interactions.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Analysis of Guided Neighborhood Attachment

    We analyze a repeated-attempt model of guided neighborhood attachment to separate reaching a retained node from controlling the accumulated importance weights.

    A.1. Repeated-Attempt Model

    Consider successive attachment attempts with uniform target density P(ω)=1/4π and proposal

    Qₙ(ω)=α/4π+(1-α)(κe^κμₙ^⊤ω)/(4π\sinhκ), 0<α<1, κ>0.

    Here ω∈S² is a unit direction, densities are with respect to surface area on the unit sphere, α is the uniform mixture fraction, and κ is the von Mises–Fisher concentration. The unit guiding axis μₙ and success cap Aₙ={ω:μₙ^⊤ω≥1-2hₙ} are determined by the preceding history. Here hₙ=P(Aₙ); for a target on a valid sphere of radius Rₙ, an ε-neighborhood gives hₙ=ε²/4Rₙ². Let T denote the first successful attempt and Fₙ₋₁ the history before attempt n.

    A.2. Attachment-Time Tail

    Proposition A.1 (Attachment-time tail).

    If hₙ≥h₋>0 before attachment, then ℙ_Q(T>N)≤(1-s₋)^N≤e^-Ns₋ and 𝔼_Q[T]≤s₋⁻¹, where s₋=αh₋+(1-α)(1-e^-2κh₋)/(1-e^-2κ).

    Proof.

    Conditioned on the history before attempt n, the guiding axis μₙ and cap

    Aₙ={ω:μₙ^⊤ω≥1-2hₙ}

    are fixed. Since P(Aₙ)=hₙ, the uniform component of Qₙ contributes αhₙ to the success probability.

    For the von Mises–Fisher component, write t=μₙ^⊤ω. Under the rotationally symmetric surface measure on S², integration over the cap gives

    (15)∫_Aₙ(κe^κμₙ^⊤ω)/(4π\sinhκ) dω=(κ)/(2\sinhκ)∫_1-2hₙ¹e^κt dt
    (16)=e^κ-e^κ(1-2hₙ)/e^κ-e^-κ
    (17)=1-e^-2κhₙ/1-e^-2κ.

    Therefore the conditional success probability is

    s(hₙ)=αhₙ+(1-α)1-e^-2κhₙ/1-e^-2κ.

    The function s(h) is increasing in h, so hₙ≥h₋ implies

    ℚ(T=n|T≥n,Fₙ₋₁)=s(hₙ)≥s₋,

    where

    s₋=αh₋+(1-α)(1-e^-2κh₋)/(1-e^-2κ).

    Hence

    ℚ(T>n|T>n-1,Fₙ₋₁)≤1-s₋.

    Iterating conditional expectations gives

    ℚ(T>N)≤(1-s₋)^N≤e^-Ns₋.

    Finally, for a positive integer-valued stopping time,

    𝔼_Q[T]=∑_N=0^∞ℚ(T>N)≤∑_N=0^∞(1-s₋)^N=(1)/(s₋).

    ∎

    A.3. Stopped-Weight Divergence

    An exponential attachment-time tail does not guarantee a finite second moment of the accumulated likelihood ratio.

    Proposition A.2 (Stopped-weight divergence).

    Define ℓₙ=P(ωₙ)/Qₙ(ωₙ) and Wₙ=∏ⱼ₌₁ⁿℓⱼ. If 0A.1.

    Proof.

    Condition on the history Fₙ₋₁ before attempt n, so that μₙ, hₙ, and Aₙ are fixed. Write t=μₙ^⊤ω. Relative to the uniform target density P, the proposal satisfies

    Qₙ(ω)/P(ω)=D_κ(t):=α+(1-α)(κe^κt)/(\sinhκ),

    and therefore

    ℓₙ(ω)=P(ω)/Qₙ(ω)=D_κ(t)⁻¹.

    Since t is uniform on [-1,1] with density 1/2 under P, for any measurable set C depending only on t,

    𝔼_Q[ℓₙ²1_C|Fₙ₋₁]=∫_CP(ω)²/Qₙ(ω) dω=1/2∫_C(dt)/(D_κ(t)).

item.title: 单图生成整片城市街区：CityLift 把「整体布局」和「单栋建筑」拆成两级，都产出可编辑网格 ｜ CityLift: Compositional 3D Urban Generation from a Single Image
item.description:
一句话：遮挡与透视让单图推不全街区；先学摆放再逐栋合成，输出带贴图的独立建筑网格。

要点：

  • 难点说清楚了：从单张城市图生成可编辑 3D 场景，需要完整的建筑几何加上一致的相对尺度与位置，而遮挡与透视歧义让这两件事都难
  • CityLift 把两端拆开：场景级空间建模负责建筑的形状与摆放联合学习，建筑级合成负责逐栋生成带贴图的网格
  • 输出是「独立的建筑网格」，因此可编辑、可替换，而不是一整块不可拆的场景

为什么值得看：场景生成最容易翻车的地方是「一整块mesh，改不动」。这条把资产粒度定在「单栋建筑」——正好对齐引擎的关卡拼装与 LOD 流程：能单独替换、能单独优化。做开放世界或城市级资产管线的团队值得对照。

中文摘要：从单张图像生成可编辑的 3D 城市场景，需要细致且空间一致的建筑资产；遮挡与透视歧义使「推断完整建筑几何」与「保持相对尺度位置一致」都变得困难。CityLift 把问题拆成两级：先在场景层面联合学习建筑的形状与摆放，再在建筑层面逐栋合成带贴图的网格，最终输出的是独立、可编辑的建筑资产而非不可拆的整块场景。这种「资产粒度与引擎关卡拼装对齐」的做法，对开放世界城市、数字孪生与需要逐栋 LOD 的管线都有直接参考价值。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-11-01

CityLift: Compositional 3D Urban Generation from a Single Image

Abstract

Generating editable 3D urban scenes from a single image requires detailed building assets with a coherent spatial arrangement. Occlusion and perspective ambiguity make it difficult to infer complete building geometry together with consistent relative scales and positions. We present CityLift, a framework that generates individual textured building meshes from an urban image by coupling scene-level spatial modeling with building-level synthesis. CityLift first learns building shape and placement jointly through coupled scene and instance streams, producing coarse sparse structures in a common coordinate system. We then introduce generative spatial inheritance, which maps each building’s coarse occupancy and scene-conditioned 3D feature field into a local volume to guide a flow model that generates finer structure. The same coordinate mapping places the generated meshes back into the scene, preserving their spatial relationship to the scaffold. To address the scarcity of urban data pairing scene images with individual 3D buildings, we construct CityLift-5K, comprising 4,997 synthetic scenes with instance masks, building meshes, and placement annotations. Experiments on CityLift-5K and scene blocks from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding demonstrate improved building geometry and scene composition. The project page is available at https://ranhaogong.github.io/CityLift/.

1 Introduction

3D urban generation supports embodied intelligence, urban simulation, and urban world modeling [32, 23, 6]. Existing approaches employ neural scene representations [47, 48], asset retrieval and language-guided planning [5, 32, 13], or satellite-conditioned mesh generation [10, 11]. Neural representations do not directly yield complete building meshes, while unified city meshes require further decomposition to obtain independently editable assets. Retrieval constrains geometric diversity to the available library, and iterative planning and refinement incur additional inference costs.

Scalable data engines for urban world models and embodied intelligence require generators that produce explicit, textured building assets, support instance-level manipulation, and generalize to unseen buildings and layouts with efficient inference [32, 40]. These requirements motivate us to investigate single-image compositional urban generation, using an oblique urban image as a joint specification of architectural appearance and spatial composition. Given this image and building instance masks, the task generates a complete textured mesh for each building in a shared scene coordinate system. The resulting assets remain independently editable, with relative positions, orientations, scales, and heights consistent with the input image.

Compositional image-to-scene methods [12, 28, 53] demonstrate the potential of generating multiple assets from one image. In urban blocks, however, three key challenges arise. (1) Scene consistency. Generated buildings must maintain coherent relative positions, orientations, scales, and heights. Occlusion and height variation make these quantities ambiguous, leaving scene assembly sensitive to errors in explicit pose prediction [31] or estimated geometric anchors [53, 35]. (2) Geometric fidelity across scales. Joint generation in a shared scene frame models geometry and placement together [20], but a fixed-resolution grid covering an entire block restricts the geometric detail available to individual buildings [54]. Increasing instance resolution therefore requires preserving spatial correspondence between local geometry and the scene. (3) Limited urban supervision. Established scene datasets emphasize indoor compositions [7], while recent urban resources provide individual building assets [14, 41] or imagery paired with regional scene meshes [11]. Learning urban composition and building completion jointly requires supervision that combines these levels, pairing oblique block images with complete building instances and their spatial arrangement.

To address these challenges, we introduce CityLift, a generative framework that models urban composition in a shared scene space and synthesizes detailed buildings in dedicated local spaces. This design reconciles the need for joint spatial reasoning across buildings with the resolution required for individual architectural detail. A jointly generated urban scaffold connects these scales, providing the spatial reference and contextual conditions for local building generation.

Specifically, Urban Scaffold Generation jointly generates coarse building geometry and layout through coupled scene and instance streams, encoding placement directly in scene-space geometry without a separate pose-regression stage. To retain this spatial organization during local generation, Generative Spatial Inheritance maps scaffold occupancy and scene-conditioned features into aligned building volumes. Within these volumes, Conditioned Building Regeneration synthesizes finer sparse structures for textured mesh generation. A shared coordinate mapping governs local conditioning, supervision, and assembly, concentrating geometric resolution on individual buildings while maintaining their correspondence to the scene scaffold.

Training this framework requires paired supervision for scene composition and complete building geometry. We therefore curate building assets for geometric completeness and texture quality through vision-language-model-assisted filtering and manual screening, and construct CityLift-5K. The dataset comprises 4,997 synthetic multi-building scenes with paired oblique images, instance masks, complete building meshes, and placement annotations, providing supervision at both scene and building levels.

Trained on CityLift-5K, CityLift achieves state-of-the-art geometric performance on its held-out test split and two external datasets. On the CityLift-5K test split, it reduces building- and scene-level Chamfer distances by 60.3% and 58.4%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline at each level. Further evaluation on synthetic scenes from UrbanScene3D and real-world scenes from InstanceBuilding yields the best scene-level geometric results on both datasets, demonstrating strong generalization capability.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We present CityLift, a framework for compositional urban generation from a single oblique image and building instance masks. Its Urban Scaffold Generation jointly models coarse building geometry and layout, establishing shared spatial support for the synthesis and assembly of complete, independently editable textured building meshes.

  • •

    We introduce Generative Spatial Inheritance to align coarse occupancy and scene-conditioned hidden features with building-specific local volumes, and Conditioned Building Regeneration to synthesize finer sparse structures under these inherited conditions.

  • •

    We construct CityLift-5K, a dataset of 4,997 synthetic urban scenes. CityLift achieves state-of-the-art scene-level geometric performance on CityLift-5K, UrbanScene3D, and real-world scenes from InstanceBuilding.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 3D urban generation

    Urban generation methods differ in how they specify city structure and construct its constituent buildings. Program-generating methods [56, 25] construct editable cities through rules and executable programs, with architectural variation governed by the available procedural operations. Layout-conditioned generators [17, 47, 48, 27] synthesize urban appearance from spatial controls, but their neural representations do not directly provide complete building meshes for independent editing and reuse. Asset retrieval [5] provides explicit building meshes, with geometric diversity constrained by the asset library. Generative asset pipelines [32, 13, 40] support editable scene construction through map- or language-guided planning, requiring scene structure to be established through layouts or geospatial information. Satellite-conditioned methods introduce image-based scene control. Sat2City and its extension [10, 11] generate scene-level meshes, which require additional instance decomposition for building-level manipulation. CitySculpt [52] refines building geometry initialized from estimated height maps, while Sat2RealCity [41] uses OSM constraints to spatially organize generated buildings. These building-level approaches derive scene structure from overhead geometric estimates or geographic priors.

    CityLift introduces single-image compositional urban generation, jointly generating complete textured building meshes and their spatial arrangement from an oblique urban image and building instance masks. This task combines image-based control over building appearance and block composition with independently editable assets, enabling buildings to be replaced, rearranged, and reused in downstream environments.

    2.2 Single-image 3D object generation

    Object generators provide priors for completing geometry beyond the visible surface, with different mechanisms for incorporating image evidence. Optimization-based methods distill image diffusion priors into a 3D representation [38, 34], while view-synthesis approaches generate additional observations to constrain reconstruction [22, 33, 24, 26]. Feed-forward reconstruction models amortize this inference, mapping an input image or synthesized views to meshes, radiance fields, or Gaussians [9, 39, 37, 42, 49]. Native 3D generators model shape distributions directly in learned latent spaces [55, 43, 16, 57]; TRELLIS and TRELLIS.2 organize geometry and appearance through structured spatial latents [46, 45]. Beyond isolated assets, SAM 3D generates masked objects from natural images while also estimating layout variables [31]. Through large-scale pretraining, these models learn rich shape and appearance priors that provide a foundation for building synthesis with limited paired urban data. CityLift draws on these priors through the SLAT generation and mesh decoding stages of SAM 3D Objects for textured building synthesis.

    2.3 3D scene generation

    Scene generation requires coupling object geometry with a shared spatial arrangement. Indoor layout generators predict object attributes or plan asset placement before assembling a scene [30, 36, 50]. For single-image input, compositional generators couple objects or parts during denoising [12, 19], while other architectures represent spatial information through explicit position prediction [28] or pixel-aligned 3D feature volumes [15]. An alternative separates asset synthesis from scene assembly, using geometric correspondences or layout optimization to establish object placement [1, 8, 51, 35]. Mira-Scene aligns canonical object coordinates with a predicted scene point cloud to recover object transformations. Structure-conditioned refinement places greater emphasis on coarse geometric support: HIVE-3D extracts and hierarchically refines components from a generated scene [54], whereas 3D-Fixer completes objects in place using estimated visible geometry, without separate pose alignment [53]. CityLift shares the coarse-to-fine organization of component refinement, with a focus on the coupled placement, height, and geometric detail of urban buildings. Its link between stages is the joint transport of generated occupancy and hidden 3D features into building-specific volumes. Building arrangement is learned in scene coordinates, while local regeneration allocates resolution to each instance.

    3 Method

    3.1 Problem Definition

    Given a single oblique urban image I and building instance masks {Mᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, our goal is to generate a scene S={Mᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N comprising textured building meshes in a common normalized domain Ωₛ=[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]³. Each mesh Mᵢ corresponds to mask Mᵢ and remains independently editable. The task requires generating plausible building geometry and appearance while inferring placement, orientation, and relative dimensions, including height and footprint size, consistent with the input image.

    3.2 Overview of CityLift Pipeline

    Our design separates the spatial extent allocated to an instance from the geometry synthesized within it. The scene generator establishes coarse support Cᵢ and a hidden feature field Fᵢ under image context. These define a generative scaffold: an explicit geometric summary paired with a learned representation indexed by the same scene coordinates. A building-specific map Tᵢ transports the scaffold into a local volume, where a conditional flow generates refined structure Ŷᵢ:

    \begingathered(Cᵢ,Fᵢ)∼G_φ(I,Mᵢ,Mₛ), Aᵢ=ℙ_Tᵢ(Cᵢ,Fᵢ), Ŷᵢ∼p_θ(Y|eᵢ,Aᵢ).\endgathered

    		(1)

    Here Mₛ is the union of building masks, eᵢ contains the local building-image tokens and ℙ_Tᵢ is the spatial transport operator. The map Tᵢ is computed from the predicted support. It is reused to construct the local training target and to assemble the generated mesh, connecting all three operations to the same scene-space reference. Figure 2 summarizes this interface.

    3.3 Urban Scaffold Generation

    Local building generation requires a spatial reference that specifies each instance’s location and extent within the block. We obtain this reference by generating building occupancy directly in Ωₛ, where shape, placement, and relative scale are encoded by the same occupied cells. To infer these properties from partially occluded observations, the generator couples the target building’s appearance with an evolving representation of the surrounding building ensemble.

    Scene guidance.

    A scene stream and an instance stream share the parameters of a sparse-structure DiT. Their image conditions are obtained from I⊙Mₛ and I⊙Mᵢ, respectively, where Mₛ=\bigveeⱼ₌₁^NMⱼ. Both conditions use the same crop and resize, preserving the target’s projected position and size within the block. A frozen image encoder maps them to tokens eₛᵍ and eᵢᵍ.

    The two streams process independently noised SS latents at a common flow time. At selected transformer blocks, scene guidance extends the instance stream’s attention to the scene representation. For each attention head, the instance update is

    Lᵢᵣ=QᵢKᵣᵀ/√dₕ, r∈{i,s},(2)
    Uᵢ=softmax ([Lᵢᵢ,Lᵢₛ])\beginbmatrixVᵢ Vₛ\endbmatrix,

    where Qᵢ, Kᵣ, and Vᵣ are the projected attention tensors and dₕ is the head dimension. This joint normalization lets instance queries aggregate information from both their own structure and the scene. The scene stream attends within itself. Each stream then applies image cross-attention with its corresponding image tokens and a feed-forward layer. Other blocks retain within-stream self-attention.

    Learning the scaffold.

    We jointly train both streams with flow matching using scene-coordinate occupancy targets. The instance target Cᵢ^⋆ retains the building’s placement, while Cₛ^⋆=\bigveeⱼ₌₁^NCⱼ^⋆ represents the ensemble. Their shared normalization makes spatial arrangement part of the geometry supervision. At inference, the SS decoder produces coarse occupancies Cᵢ and Cₛ at resolution Rₛ=64. We retain Cᵢ together with the instance stream’s hidden 3D feature field Fᵢ before the output projection. This pair forms the urban scaffold. The occupancy determines the building’s spatial support, while the features retain scene-conditioned information at corresponding 3D locations for subsequent spatial inheritance.

    3.4 Generative Spatial Inheritance

    The scene grid distributes its resolution across multiple buildings. To allocate greater geometric capacity to each instance, we transfer its scaffold into a dedicated local volume. A deterministic coordinate map preserves the correspondence with Ωₛ, allowing local generation to retain the spatial reference established by the scaffold.

    Inherited local frame.

    For each nonempty Cᵢ, we construct a padded, axis-aligned cube enclosing its occupied cells. Let cᵢ be its center in scene coordinates and sᵢ its side length measured in scene-grid cells. The local domain Ωᵢ=[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]³ maps to the scene as

    Tᵢ(u)=cᵢ+αᵢu, αᵢ=sᵢ/Rₛ.

    		(3)

    This map preserves the scene axes. An Rₗ³ local grid, with Rₗ=64, assigns each building a dedicated voxel budget while retaining its scale through αᵢ.

    Aligned scaffold transfer.

    We use Tᵢ to sample occupancy and hidden features at corresponding 3D locations. Features are interpolated at local token centers. Occupancy is resampled on the local voxel grid and max-pooled to the same token resolution, yielding C̄ᵢ. The resulting condition is

    F̃ᵢ(u)=TriInterp (Fᵢ,Tᵢ(u)),(4)
    Aᵢ(u)=[LN (F̃ᵢ(u)),C̄ᵢ(u)].

    Each local token therefore receives both geometric support and scene-conditioned features for the region it will generate.

    The inherited frame also defines supervision for the subsequent building generator. We transform the ground-truth mesh Mᵢ^⋆ by Tᵢ⁻¹ and voxelize it to obtain the local target Yᵢ^⋆. Generated local meshes are returned to the scene using Tᵢ, so conditioning, supervision, and assembly share the same coordinate reference.

    3.5 Conditioned Building Regeneration

    To recover geometry beyond the coarse scaffold, we regenerate local structure from noise, conditioned on the inherited representation Aᵢ and image tokens eᵢ extracted from a tight building crop.

    Spatially aligned conditioning.

    We adapt the pretrained sparse-structure flow model of TRELLIS [46] by injecting the inherited condition after each transformer block,

    Hᵢ^ℓ+1(u)=B_ℓ(Hᵢ^ℓ,t,eᵢ)(u)(5)
    +W_ℓAᵢ(u)+b_ℓ,

    where B_ℓ combines self-attention, image cross-attention, and feed-forward operations. Shared spatial indexing supplies each token with the inherited occupancy and features of its corresponding local region. The projections are zero-initialized to preserve the pretrained computation at initialization. Repeated injection keeps this spatial condition available throughout the network and along the sampling trajectory.

    Training objective.

    The frozen SS encoder maps Yᵢ^⋆ to the target latent. We train the conditional velocity field using the flow-matching loss L_FM. To directly supervise decoded geometry, we additionally recover the estimated clean latent for low-noise samples and pass it through the frozen SS decoder to obtain occupancy probabilities Pᵢ. Our geometric objective combines soft Dice overlap with centroid and axial-distribution constraints,

    L_geo,i=\underbrace1-(2⟨Pᵢ,Yᵢ^⋆⟩+δ)/(∥Pᵢ∥₁+∥Yᵢ^⋆∥₁+δ)_L_Dice,i(6)
    +λ_c∥μ(Pᵢ)-μ(Yᵢ^⋆)∥₂²
    +MAE (m(Pᵢ),m(Yᵢ^⋆)),

    where δ is a smoothing constant, μ(X) denotes the occupancy-weighted centroid in voxel-index coordinates, and m(X) concatenates the unit-mass occupancy marginals along the three axes. These terms constrain occupied support, centroid position, and axial geometry distribution within the inherited frame. The total objective is L_local=L_FM+λ_gL_geo, where L_geo is averaged over the selected low-noise samples. The flow formulation and hyperparameters are provided in the appendix.

    Mesh realization and scene assembly.

    We adopt the pretrained structured-latent (SLAT) generator and mesh decoder of SAM 3D Objects [31]. The regenerated sparse structure Ŷᵢ defines the spatial support for image-conditioned SLAT generation, followed by mesh decoding. After converting the resulting mesh to the inherited local frame, we place it in the scene through Mᵢ=Tᵢ(M̂ᵢ). The assembled scene S={Mᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N retains individually editable building instances.

    4 CityLift-5K Dataset

    To address the scarcity of urban scene data pairing images with complete building-level geometry, we construct CityLift-5K, comprising 4,997 synthetic urban blocks and 36,338 building instances. Each scene provides a rendered image, instance masks, and individually accessible building meshes in a shared coordinate frame, supporting supervision of both building geometry and spatial arrangement.

    Asset preparation.

    We curate CityLift-Asset, a library of 42,339 building meshes from SAT-SKYLINES [14], CityCraft [5], UrbanVerse [21], and subsets of TRELLIS-500K [46, 4]. We apply multiview screening with Qwen3-VL [2], followed by further manual filtering, to exclude non-building content, disconnected building groups, and assets with incomplete geometry. The retained assets receive textual descriptions and annotations of function, architectural style, floor count, and estimated dimensions. These attributes guide asset selection and provide scale priors for scene construction.

    Scene construction and annotations.

    We combine MLLM-assisted layout planning with procedural parcel placement to assemble urban blocks on a planar ground. The scenes cover residential, office, commercial, civic, and industrial settings, with 2–12 buildings per scene. Buildings are selected according to their annotated function and size, then scaled and positioned within the planned layout.

    We render each scene with Blender’s Eevee engine, producing one 1024×1024 RGB image and a pixel-aligned instance segmentation map. An orthographic camera captures an oblique view with an off-nadir angle sampled between 30^∘ and 40^∘. Camera framing accounts for the block extent and maximum building height, while sun direction and intensity vary across scenes. Each sample retains individual meshes, placement transforms, camera parameters, and instance identifiers. The dataset contains 4,497 training, 250 validation, and 250 test scenes. Further construction details and statistics are provided in the appendix.

    5 Experiments

    We compare CityLift with representative baselines in terms of building-level geometric fidelity and scene-level spatial consistency. Experiments cover the held-out CityLift-5K test split and scene blocks constructed from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding. We report geometric metrics at both building and scene levels, complemented by a MLLM-as-a-judge visual evaluation.

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    The test split of CityLift-5K contains 250 scenes, averaging 7.8 buildings per scene. Both the scenes and their constituent building assets are disjoint from the training split, ensuring evaluation on unseen scenes and buildings. For external evaluation, we use the synthetic Shenzhen city scene from UrbanScene3D [18], extracting its scene mesh and individual building meshes from Unreal Engine. We also evaluate on Scene3 of InstanceBuilding [3], a real, densely built town scene reconstructed from UAV imagery. Both scenes are partitioned into blocks and rendered into RGB images and instance masks using the CityLift data preparation pipeline. These tests cover synthetic and photogrammetrically reconstructed building geometry.

    Baselines.

    We compare with TRELLIS.2 [44], SAM 3D [31], Pixal3D [15], 3D-Fixer [53], and SceneGen [28]. TRELLIS.2 is applied to the entire scene image and produces a single scene mesh, so we report its scene-level metrics. The other baselines produce building instances that can be assembled into a scene. We additionally report SceneGen-SFT, fine-tuned on the CityLift training data, in the CityLift-5K comparison. This separates the released SceneGen model from its adaptation to the target domain.

    Geometric evaluation.

    We evaluate geometry at both the building and scene levels using Chamfer distance (CD), accuracy (Acc), completeness (Comp), and F-scores at thresholds of one and two grid cells (F@1 and F@2). Lower distance errors and higher F-scores indicate better performance. Detailed evaluation protocols are provided in the appendix.

    Implementation details.

    Both generation modules are trained on CityLift-5K using 64³ voxel grids. Training is performed on two NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each with 80 GB of memory. We use DINOv2 [29] as the image feature extractor. We first train the scaffold generator using AdamW with a learning rate of 3.5×10⁻⁵ and a global batch size of 16. We then freeze the scaffold generator and train the building regeneration module, initialized from TRELLIS [46], for 18,000 iterations with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵. At inference, pretrained SAM 3D converts the generated sparse structures into textured meshes. Further implementation details are provided in the appendix.

    5.2 Comparison on CityLift-5K

    CityLift achieves the best geometric results at both building and scene levels (Table 1). Building-level CD decreases from 2.547 for Pixal3D to 1.011 cells, a reduction of 60.3%. Scene-level CD decreases from 2.595 for SAM 3D to 1.079 cells, a reduction of 58.4%, while scene F@2 improves from 0.597 to 0.855. CityLift requires approximately 115 s per scene, faster than SceneGen, 3D-Fixer, and Pixal3D.

    Figure 3 reveals differences in building proportions and spatial arrangement. TRELLIS.2 produces incorrect building heights, altering the relative height relationships within a block. SAM 3D generates recognizable individual buildings but introduces errors in their relative positions and orientations. Pixal3D exhibits flattened or fragmented geometry, while 3D-Fixer shows structural distortions and less coherent spatial arrangements. SceneGen produces pronounced scale inconsistencies and building overlaps. CityLift more faithfully preserves building proportions, relative orientations, and spacing, while retaining coherent roof structures and facade details.

    To assess whether dataset-specific fine-tuning can close the performance gap, we additionally fine-tune SceneGen on the CityLift-5K training split. SceneGen-SFT still yields higher building- and scene-level CDs of 3.843 and 3.422, compared with 1.011 and 1.079 for CityLift. These results suggest that adapting SceneGen to the same training data is insufficient to match CityLift’s performance.

    5.3 Evaluation on External Scene Sources

    UrbanScene3D.

    CityLift obtains the lowest building CD and leads all five scene-level metrics in Table 2. Its scene CD is 1.577 cells, compared with 2.067 for Pixal3D, and its scene F@2 is 0.750 compared with 0.693. These correspond to a 23.7% reduction in scene CD and a 5.7 percentage-point increase in F@2. The gain persists when the input arrangement comes from an extracted urban scene rather than the procedural layouts used to construct CityLift-5K.

    At the building level, Pixal3D achieves the lowest accuracy error and the highest F-scores, indicating closer prediction-to-reference surface agreement on average and stronger correspondence within the evaluated thresholds. This advantage is consistent with its pixel-aligned conditioning, which back-projects image features into 3D to establish explicit image–geometry correspondence [15]. CityLift achieves a lower completeness error of 1.128 cells, compared with 1.678 for Pixal3D, yielding a lower symmetric CD of 1.421 versus 1.490 cells. Since CD averages the two directional errors, the reduction in completeness error outweighs the increase in accuracy error. F-scores instead summarize surface precision and recall within fixed distance thresholds. CityLift thus provides better average reference-surface coverage, while Pixal3D retains an advantage in thresholded surface agreement for individual buildings.

    InstanceBuilding.

    CityLift also leads all five scene-level metrics on real-world scenes from InstanceBuilding (Table 3). Compared with Pixal3D, scene CD decreases from 2.012 to 1.531 cells, a reduction of 23.9%, and F@2 increases from 0.694 to 0.717, an improvement of 2.3 percentage points. The building-level results exhibit the same pattern. Pixal3D retains the best accuracy and F-scores, whereas CityLift reduces completeness error from 1.816 to 1.334 cells and CD from 1.768 to 1.625 cells. Across both external datasets, CityLift consistently improves average building-surface coverage and assembled-scene geometry, demonstrating generalization to both synthetic and real-world scene sources. Figure 4 presents the corresponding visual comparisons.

    5.4 Multi-view Visual Evaluation

    Surface distances describe geometric agreement with the reference, but do not measure texture quality or the visual quality of completed facades. We therefore render four views of each generated UrbanScene3D block and use ChatGPT 6 Astra as a visual assessor. For each method and block, the assessor inspects the conditioning image together with all four rendered views. It assigns scores to layout and completeness (L), shape and proportion (G), appearance and detail (A), and multi-view structural quality (M). The overall score is

    S=10(0.35L+0.30G+0.20A+0.15M).

    		(7)

    As shown in Table 4, CityLift achieves the highest scores across all four dimensions, with an overall score of 82.8 compared with 77.6 for TRELLIS.2.

    5.5 Ablation Studies

    We ablate scene guidance and replace local regeneration with direct coarse decoding (Table 5). Removing scene guidance causes the largest degradation, increasing scene-level CD from 1.079 to 2.590 and highlighting the importance of scene conditioning. Direct coarse decoding achieves a building-level CD of 1.150, but produces smoother, simplified surfaces with less distinct windows and other facade details (Fig. 5). Local regeneration reduces CD to 1.011 and recovers finer architectural details, complementing the overall building geometry captured by the scaffold.

    We further examine inherited conditioning by removing hidden-feature and occupancy injection separately and jointly, and replacing aligned hidden features with spatially pooled features. Removing both injection pathways increases building-level CD to 2.510, exceeding that of coarse decoding. Thus, local regeneration can degrade an initially useful scaffold without aligned conditioning. Removing hidden-feature injection and pooling hidden features yield similar scene-level CDs of 2.170 and 2.200, suggesting that their benefit depends strongly on preserving spatial variation. Occupancy injection provides a smaller additional gain, with its removal increasing scene-level CD to 1.260. Consistent with these findings, Fig. 5 shows fragmented building surfaces when aligned or hidden-feature injection is removed, or hidden features are pooled, whereas CityLift produces more complete facades and roofs.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented CityLift, a framework for compositional 3D urban generation from a single image and building instance masks. Urban scaffold generation captures scene layout and coarse building geometry, while generative spatial inheritance transfers geometric support and hidden features into local building frames. Conditioned building regeneration refines individual structures, which are converted into explicit, individually editable meshes and assembled using the inherited spatial transforms. We also introduced CityLift-5K to support training and evaluation of this task. Experiments on CityLift-5K, UrbanScene3D, and InstanceBuilding demonstrate improved scene-level geometric fidelity. These results support the effectiveness of combining scene-level spatial organization with local building generation for compositional urban content creation.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：遮挡与透视让单图推不全街区；先学摆放再逐栋合成，输出带贴图的独立建筑网格。

要点：

  • 难点说清楚了：从单张城市图生成可编辑 3D 场景，需要完整的建筑几何加上一致的相对尺度与位置，而遮挡与透视歧义让这两件事都难
  • CityLift 把两端拆开：场景级空间建模负责建筑的形状与摆放联合学习，建筑级合成负责逐栋生成带贴图的网格
  • 输出是「独立的建筑网格」，因此可编辑、可替换，而不是一整块不可拆的场景

为什么值得看：场景生成最容易翻车的地方是「一整块mesh，改不动」。这条把资产粒度定在「单栋建筑」——正好对齐引擎的关卡拼装与 LOD 流程：能单独替换、能单独优化。做开放世界或城市级资产管线的团队值得对照。

中文摘要：从单张图像生成可编辑的 3D 城市场景，需要细致且空间一致的建筑资产；遮挡与透视歧义使「推断完整建筑几何」与「保持相对尺度位置一致」都变得困难。CityLift 把问题拆成两级：先在场景层面联合学习建筑的形状与摆放，再在建筑层面逐栋合成带贴图的网格，最终输出的是独立、可编辑的建筑资产而非不可拆的整块场景。这种「资产粒度与引擎关卡拼装对齐」的做法，对开放世界城市、数字孪生与需要逐栋 LOD 的管线都有直接参考价值。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-23

本期推送：2026-11-01

CityLift: Compositional 3D Urban Generation from a Single Image

Abstract

Generating editable 3D urban scenes from a single image requires detailed building assets with a coherent spatial arrangement. Occlusion and perspective ambiguity make it difficult to infer complete building geometry together with consistent relative scales and positions. We present CityLift, a framework that generates individual textured building meshes from an urban image by coupling scene-level spatial modeling with building-level synthesis. CityLift first learns building shape and placement jointly through coupled scene and instance streams, producing coarse sparse structures in a common coordinate system. We then introduce generative spatial inheritance, which maps each building’s coarse occupancy and scene-conditioned 3D feature field into a local volume to guide a flow model that generates finer structure. The same coordinate mapping places the generated meshes back into the scene, preserving their spatial relationship to the scaffold. To address the scarcity of urban data pairing scene images with individual 3D buildings, we construct CityLift-5K, comprising 4,997 synthetic scenes with instance masks, building meshes, and placement annotations. Experiments on CityLift-5K and scene blocks from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding demonstrate improved building geometry and scene composition. The project page is available at https://ranhaogong.github.io/CityLift/.

1 Introduction

3D urban generation supports embodied intelligence, urban simulation, and urban world modeling [32, 23, 6]. Existing approaches employ neural scene representations [47, 48], asset retrieval and language-guided planning [5, 32, 13], or satellite-conditioned mesh generation [10, 11]. Neural representations do not directly yield complete building meshes, while unified city meshes require further decomposition to obtain independently editable assets. Retrieval constrains geometric diversity to the available library, and iterative planning and refinement incur additional inference costs.

Scalable data engines for urban world models and embodied intelligence require generators that produce explicit, textured building assets, support instance-level manipulation, and generalize to unseen buildings and layouts with efficient inference [32, 40]. These requirements motivate us to investigate single-image compositional urban generation, using an oblique urban image as a joint specification of architectural appearance and spatial composition. Given this image and building instance masks, the task generates a complete textured mesh for each building in a shared scene coordinate system. The resulting assets remain independently editable, with relative positions, orientations, scales, and heights consistent with the input image.

Compositional image-to-scene methods [12, 28, 53] demonstrate the potential of generating multiple assets from one image. In urban blocks, however, three key challenges arise. (1) Scene consistency. Generated buildings must maintain coherent relative positions, orientations, scales, and heights. Occlusion and height variation make these quantities ambiguous, leaving scene assembly sensitive to errors in explicit pose prediction [31] or estimated geometric anchors [53, 35]. (2) Geometric fidelity across scales. Joint generation in a shared scene frame models geometry and placement together [20], but a fixed-resolution grid covering an entire block restricts the geometric detail available to individual buildings [54]. Increasing instance resolution therefore requires preserving spatial correspondence between local geometry and the scene. (3) Limited urban supervision. Established scene datasets emphasize indoor compositions [7], while recent urban resources provide individual building assets [14, 41] or imagery paired with regional scene meshes [11]. Learning urban composition and building completion jointly requires supervision that combines these levels, pairing oblique block images with complete building instances and their spatial arrangement.

To address these challenges, we introduce CityLift, a generative framework that models urban composition in a shared scene space and synthesizes detailed buildings in dedicated local spaces. This design reconciles the need for joint spatial reasoning across buildings with the resolution required for individual architectural detail. A jointly generated urban scaffold connects these scales, providing the spatial reference and contextual conditions for local building generation.

Specifically, Urban Scaffold Generation jointly generates coarse building geometry and layout through coupled scene and instance streams, encoding placement directly in scene-space geometry without a separate pose-regression stage. To retain this spatial organization during local generation, Generative Spatial Inheritance maps scaffold occupancy and scene-conditioned features into aligned building volumes. Within these volumes, Conditioned Building Regeneration synthesizes finer sparse structures for textured mesh generation. A shared coordinate mapping governs local conditioning, supervision, and assembly, concentrating geometric resolution on individual buildings while maintaining their correspondence to the scene scaffold.
