Training this framework requires paired supervision for scene composition and complete building geometry. We therefore curate building assets for geometric completeness and texture quality through vision-language-model-assisted filtering and manual screening, and construct CityLift-5K. The dataset comprises 4,997 synthetic multi-building scenes with paired oblique images, instance masks, complete building meshes, and placement annotations, providing supervision at both scene and building levels.

Trained on CityLift-5K, CityLift achieves state-of-the-art geometric performance on its held-out test split and two external datasets. On the CityLift-5K test split, it reduces building- and scene-level Chamfer distances by 60.3% and 58.4%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline at each level. Further evaluation on synthetic scenes from UrbanScene3D and real-world scenes from InstanceBuilding yields the best scene-level geometric results on both datasets, demonstrating strong generalization capability.

Our main contributions are as follows.

  • •

    We present CityLift, a framework for compositional urban generation from a single oblique image and building instance masks. Its Urban Scaffold Generation jointly models coarse building geometry and layout, establishing shared spatial support for the synthesis and assembly of complete, independently editable textured building meshes.

  • •

    We introduce Generative Spatial Inheritance to align coarse occupancy and scene-conditioned hidden features with building-specific local volumes, and Conditioned Building Regeneration to synthesize finer sparse structures under these inherited conditions.

  • •

    We construct CityLift-5K, a dataset of 4,997 synthetic urban scenes. CityLift achieves state-of-the-art scene-level geometric performance on CityLift-5K, UrbanScene3D, and real-world scenes from InstanceBuilding.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 3D urban generation

    Urban generation methods differ in how they specify city structure and construct its constituent buildings. Program-generating methods [56, 25] construct editable cities through rules and executable programs, with architectural variation governed by the available procedural operations. Layout-conditioned generators [17, 47, 48, 27] synthesize urban appearance from spatial controls, but their neural representations do not directly provide complete building meshes for independent editing and reuse. Asset retrieval [5] provides explicit building meshes, with geometric diversity constrained by the asset library. Generative asset pipelines [32, 13, 40] support editable scene construction through map- or language-guided planning, requiring scene structure to be established through layouts or geospatial information. Satellite-conditioned methods introduce image-based scene control. Sat2City and its extension [10, 11] generate scene-level meshes, which require additional instance decomposition for building-level manipulation. CitySculpt [52] refines building geometry initialized from estimated height maps, while Sat2RealCity [41] uses OSM constraints to spatially organize generated buildings. These building-level approaches derive scene structure from overhead geometric estimates or geographic priors.

    CityLift introduces single-image compositional urban generation, jointly generating complete textured building meshes and their spatial arrangement from an oblique urban image and building instance masks. This task combines image-based control over building appearance and block composition with independently editable assets, enabling buildings to be replaced, rearranged, and reused in downstream environments.

    2.2 Single-image 3D object generation

    Object generators provide priors for completing geometry beyond the visible surface, with different mechanisms for incorporating image evidence. Optimization-based methods distill image diffusion priors into a 3D representation [38, 34], while view-synthesis approaches generate additional observations to constrain reconstruction [22, 33, 24, 26]. Feed-forward reconstruction models amortize this inference, mapping an input image or synthesized views to meshes, radiance fields, or Gaussians [9, 39, 37, 42, 49]. Native 3D generators model shape distributions directly in learned latent spaces [55, 43, 16, 57]; TRELLIS and TRELLIS.2 organize geometry and appearance through structured spatial latents [46, 45]. Beyond isolated assets, SAM 3D generates masked objects from natural images while also estimating layout variables [31]. Through large-scale pretraining, these models learn rich shape and appearance priors that provide a foundation for building synthesis with limited paired urban data. CityLift draws on these priors through the SLAT generation and mesh decoding stages of SAM 3D Objects for textured building synthesis.

    2.3 3D scene generation

    Scene generation requires coupling object geometry with a shared spatial arrangement. Indoor layout generators predict object attributes or plan asset placement before assembling a scene [30, 36, 50]. For single-image input, compositional generators couple objects or parts during denoising [12, 19], while other architectures represent spatial information through explicit position prediction [28] or pixel-aligned 3D feature volumes [15]. An alternative separates asset synthesis from scene assembly, using geometric correspondences or layout optimization to establish object placement [1, 8, 51, 35]. Mira-Scene aligns canonical object coordinates with a predicted scene point cloud to recover object transformations. Structure-conditioned refinement places greater emphasis on coarse geometric support: HIVE-3D extracts and hierarchically refines components from a generated scene [54], whereas 3D-Fixer completes objects in place using estimated visible geometry, without separate pose alignment [53]. CityLift shares the coarse-to-fine organization of component refinement, with a focus on the coupled placement, height, and geometric detail of urban buildings. Its link between stages is the joint transport of generated occupancy and hidden 3D features into building-specific volumes. Building arrangement is learned in scene coordinates, while local regeneration allocates resolution to each instance.

    3 Method

    3.1 Problem Definition

    Given a single oblique urban image I and building instance masks {Mᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N, our goal is to generate a scene S={Mᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N comprising textured building meshes in a common normalized domain Ωₛ=[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]³. Each mesh Mᵢ corresponds to mask Mᵢ and remains independently editable. The task requires generating plausible building geometry and appearance while inferring placement, orientation, and relative dimensions, including height and footprint size, consistent with the input image.

    3.2 Overview of CityLift Pipeline

    Our design separates the spatial extent allocated to an instance from the geometry synthesized within it. The scene generator establishes coarse support Cᵢ and a hidden feature field Fᵢ under image context. These define a generative scaffold: an explicit geometric summary paired with a learned representation indexed by the same scene coordinates. A building-specific map Tᵢ transports the scaffold into a local volume, where a conditional flow generates refined structure Ŷᵢ:

    \begingathered(Cᵢ,Fᵢ)∼G_φ(I,Mᵢ,Mₛ), Aᵢ=ℙ_Tᵢ(Cᵢ,Fᵢ), Ŷᵢ∼p_θ(Y|eᵢ,Aᵢ).\endgathered

    		(1)

    Here Mₛ is the union of building masks, eᵢ contains the local building-image tokens and ℙ_Tᵢ is the spatial transport operator. The map Tᵢ is computed from the predicted support. It is reused to construct the local training target and to assemble the generated mesh, connecting all three operations to the same scene-space reference. Figure 2 summarizes this interface.

    3.3 Urban Scaffold Generation

    Local building generation requires a spatial reference that specifies each instance’s location and extent within the block. We obtain this reference by generating building occupancy directly in Ωₛ, where shape, placement, and relative scale are encoded by the same occupied cells. To infer these properties from partially occluded observations, the generator couples the target building’s appearance with an evolving representation of the surrounding building ensemble.

    Scene guidance.

    A scene stream and an instance stream share the parameters of a sparse-structure DiT. Their image conditions are obtained from I⊙Mₛ and I⊙Mᵢ, respectively, where Mₛ=\bigveeⱼ₌₁^NMⱼ. Both conditions use the same crop and resize, preserving the target’s projected position and size within the block. A frozen image encoder maps them to tokens eₛᵍ and eᵢᵍ.

    The two streams process independently noised SS latents at a common flow time. At selected transformer blocks, scene guidance extends the instance stream’s attention to the scene representation. For each attention head, the instance update is

    Lᵢᵣ=QᵢKᵣᵀ/√dₕ, r∈{i,s},(2)
    Uᵢ=softmax ([Lᵢᵢ,Lᵢₛ])\beginbmatrixVᵢ Vₛ\endbmatrix,

    where Qᵢ, Kᵣ, and Vᵣ are the projected attention tensors and dₕ is the head dimension. This joint normalization lets instance queries aggregate information from both their own structure and the scene. The scene stream attends within itself. Each stream then applies image cross-attention with its corresponding image tokens and a feed-forward layer. Other blocks retain within-stream self-attention.

    Learning the scaffold.

    We jointly train both streams with flow matching using scene-coordinate occupancy targets. The instance target Cᵢ^⋆ retains the building’s placement, while Cₛ^⋆=\bigveeⱼ₌₁^NCⱼ^⋆ represents the ensemble. Their shared normalization makes spatial arrangement part of the geometry supervision. At inference, the SS decoder produces coarse occupancies Cᵢ and Cₛ at resolution Rₛ=64. We retain Cᵢ together with the instance stream’s hidden 3D feature field Fᵢ before the output projection. This pair forms the urban scaffold. The occupancy determines the building’s spatial support, while the features retain scene-conditioned information at corresponding 3D locations for subsequent spatial inheritance.

    3.4 Generative Spatial Inheritance

    The scene grid distributes its resolution across multiple buildings. To allocate greater geometric capacity to each instance, we transfer its scaffold into a dedicated local volume. A deterministic coordinate map preserves the correspondence with Ωₛ, allowing local generation to retain the spatial reference established by the scaffold.

    Inherited local frame.

    For each nonempty Cᵢ, we construct a padded, axis-aligned cube enclosing its occupied cells. Let cᵢ be its center in scene coordinates and sᵢ its side length measured in scene-grid cells. The local domain Ωᵢ=[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]³ maps to the scene as

    Tᵢ(u)=cᵢ+αᵢu, αᵢ=sᵢ/Rₛ.

    		(3)

    This map preserves the scene axes. An Rₗ³ local grid, with Rₗ=64, assigns each building a dedicated voxel budget while retaining its scale through αᵢ.

    Aligned scaffold transfer.

    We use Tᵢ to sample occupancy and hidden features at corresponding 3D locations. Features are interpolated at local token centers. Occupancy is resampled on the local voxel grid and max-pooled to the same token resolution, yielding C̄ᵢ. The resulting condition is

    F̃ᵢ(u)=TriInterp (Fᵢ,Tᵢ(u)),(4)
    Aᵢ(u)=[LN (F̃ᵢ(u)),C̄ᵢ(u)].

    Each local token therefore receives both geometric support and scene-conditioned features for the region it will generate.

    The inherited frame also defines supervision for the subsequent building generator. We transform the ground-truth mesh Mᵢ^⋆ by Tᵢ⁻¹ and voxelize it to obtain the local target Yᵢ^⋆. Generated local meshes are returned to the scene using Tᵢ, so conditioning, supervision, and assembly share the same coordinate reference.

    3.5 Conditioned Building Regeneration

    To recover geometry beyond the coarse scaffold, we regenerate local structure from noise, conditioned on the inherited representation Aᵢ and image tokens eᵢ extracted from a tight building crop.

    Spatially aligned conditioning.

    We adapt the pretrained sparse-structure flow model of TRELLIS [46] by injecting the inherited condition after each transformer block,

    Hᵢ^ℓ+1(u)=B_ℓ(Hᵢ^ℓ,t,eᵢ)(u)(5)
    +W_ℓAᵢ(u)+b_ℓ,

    where B_ℓ combines self-attention, image cross-attention, and feed-forward operations. Shared spatial indexing supplies each token with the inherited occupancy and features of its corresponding local region. The projections are zero-initialized to preserve the pretrained computation at initialization. Repeated injection keeps this spatial condition available throughout the network and along the sampling trajectory.

    Training objective.

    The frozen SS encoder maps Yᵢ^⋆ to the target latent. We train the conditional velocity field using the flow-matching loss L_FM. To directly supervise decoded geometry, we additionally recover the estimated clean latent for low-noise samples and pass it through the frozen SS decoder to obtain occupancy probabilities Pᵢ. Our geometric objective combines soft Dice overlap with centroid and axial-distribution constraints,

    L_geo,i=\underbrace1-(2⟨Pᵢ,Yᵢ^⋆⟩+δ)/(∥Pᵢ∥₁+∥Yᵢ^⋆∥₁+δ)_L_Dice,i(6)
    +λ_c∥μ(Pᵢ)-μ(Yᵢ^⋆)∥₂²
    +MAE (m(Pᵢ),m(Yᵢ^⋆)),

    where δ is a smoothing constant, μ(X) denotes the occupancy-weighted centroid in voxel-index coordinates, and m(X) concatenates the unit-mass occupancy marginals along the three axes. These terms constrain occupied support, centroid position, and axial geometry distribution within the inherited frame. The total objective is L_local=L_FM+λ_gL_geo, where L_geo is averaged over the selected low-noise samples. The flow formulation and hyperparameters are provided in the appendix.

    Mesh realization and scene assembly.

    We adopt the pretrained structured-latent (SLAT) generator and mesh decoder of SAM 3D Objects [31]. The regenerated sparse structure Ŷᵢ defines the spatial support for image-conditioned SLAT generation, followed by mesh decoding. After converting the resulting mesh to the inherited local frame, we place it in the scene through Mᵢ=Tᵢ(M̂ᵢ). The assembled scene S={Mᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N retains individually editable building instances.

    4 CityLift-5K Dataset

    To address the scarcity of urban scene data pairing images with complete building-level geometry, we construct CityLift-5K, comprising 4,997 synthetic urban blocks and 36,338 building instances. Each scene provides a rendered image, instance masks, and individually accessible building meshes in a shared coordinate frame, supporting supervision of both building geometry and spatial arrangement.

    Asset preparation.

    We curate CityLift-Asset, a library of 42,339 building meshes from SAT-SKYLINES [14], CityCraft [5], UrbanVerse [21], and subsets of TRELLIS-500K [46, 4]. We apply multiview screening with Qwen3-VL [2], followed by further manual filtering, to exclude non-building content, disconnected building groups, and assets with incomplete geometry. The retained assets receive textual descriptions and annotations of function, architectural style, floor count, and estimated dimensions. These attributes guide asset selection and provide scale priors for scene construction.

    Scene construction and annotations.

    We combine MLLM-assisted layout planning with procedural parcel placement to assemble urban blocks on a planar ground. The scenes cover residential, office, commercial, civic, and industrial settings, with 2–12 buildings per scene. Buildings are selected according to their annotated function and size, then scaled and positioned within the planned layout.

    We render each scene with Blender’s Eevee engine, producing one 1024×1024 RGB image and a pixel-aligned instance segmentation map. An orthographic camera captures an oblique view with an off-nadir angle sampled between 30^∘ and 40^∘. Camera framing accounts for the block extent and maximum building height, while sun direction and intensity vary across scenes. Each sample retains individual meshes, placement transforms, camera parameters, and instance identifiers. The dataset contains 4,497 training, 250 validation, and 250 test scenes. Further construction details and statistics are provided in the appendix.

    5 Experiments

    We compare CityLift with representative baselines in terms of building-level geometric fidelity and scene-level spatial consistency. Experiments cover the held-out CityLift-5K test split and scene blocks constructed from UrbanScene3D and InstanceBuilding. We report geometric metrics at both building and scene levels, complemented by a MLLM-as-a-judge visual evaluation.

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    The test split of CityLift-5K contains 250 scenes, averaging 7.8 buildings per scene. Both the scenes and their constituent building assets are disjoint from the training split, ensuring evaluation on unseen scenes and buildings. For external evaluation, we use the synthetic Shenzhen city scene from UrbanScene3D [18], extracting its scene mesh and individual building meshes from Unreal Engine. We also evaluate on Scene3 of InstanceBuilding [3], a real, densely built town scene reconstructed from UAV imagery. Both scenes are partitioned into blocks and rendered into RGB images and instance masks using the CityLift data preparation pipeline. These tests cover synthetic and photogrammetrically reconstructed building geometry.

    Baselines.

    We compare with TRELLIS.2 [44], SAM 3D [31], Pixal3D [15], 3D-Fixer [53], and SceneGen [28]. TRELLIS.2 is applied to the entire scene image and produces a single scene mesh, so we report its scene-level metrics. The other baselines produce building instances that can be assembled into a scene. We additionally report SceneGen-SFT, fine-tuned on the CityLift training data, in the CityLift-5K comparison. This separates the released SceneGen model from its adaptation to the target domain.

    Geometric evaluation.

    We evaluate geometry at both the building and scene levels using Chamfer distance (CD), accuracy (Acc), completeness (Comp), and F-scores at thresholds of one and two grid cells (F@1 and F@2). Lower distance errors and higher F-scores indicate better performance. Detailed evaluation protocols are provided in the appendix.

    Implementation details.

    Both generation modules are trained on CityLift-5K using 64³ voxel grids. Training is performed on two NVIDIA A100 GPUs, each with 80 GB of memory. We use DINOv2 [29] as the image feature extractor. We first train the scaffold generator using AdamW with a learning rate of 3.5×10⁻⁵ and a global batch size of 16. We then freeze the scaffold generator and train the building regeneration module, initialized from TRELLIS [46], for 18,000 iterations with a learning rate of 5×10⁻⁵. At inference, pretrained SAM 3D converts the generated sparse structures into textured meshes. Further implementation details are provided in the appendix.

    5.2 Comparison on CityLift-5K

    CityLift achieves the best geometric results at both building and scene levels (Table 1). Building-level CD decreases from 2.547 for Pixal3D to 1.011 cells, a reduction of 60.3%. Scene-level CD decreases from 2.595 for SAM 3D to 1.079 cells, a reduction of 58.4%, while scene F@2 improves from 0.597 to 0.855. CityLift requires approximately 115 s per scene, faster than SceneGen, 3D-Fixer, and Pixal3D.

    Figure 3 reveals differences in building proportions and spatial arrangement. TRELLIS.2 produces incorrect building heights, altering the relative height relationships within a block. SAM 3D generates recognizable individual buildings but introduces errors in their relative positions and orientations. Pixal3D exhibits flattened or fragmented geometry, while 3D-Fixer shows structural distortions and less coherent spatial arrangements. SceneGen produces pronounced scale inconsistencies and building overlaps. CityLift more faithfully preserves building proportions, relative orientations, and spacing, while retaining coherent roof structures and facade details.

    To assess whether dataset-specific fine-tuning can close the performance gap, we additionally fine-tune SceneGen on the CityLift-5K training split. SceneGen-SFT still yields higher building- and scene-level CDs of 3.843 and 3.422, compared with 1.011 and 1.079 for CityLift. These results suggest that adapting SceneGen to the same training data is insufficient to match CityLift’s performance.

    5.3 Evaluation on External Scene Sources

    UrbanScene3D.

    CityLift obtains the lowest building CD and leads all five scene-level metrics in Table 2. Its scene CD is 1.577 cells, compared with 2.067 for Pixal3D, and its scene F@2 is 0.750 compared with 0.693. These correspond to a 23.7% reduction in scene CD and a 5.7 percentage-point increase in F@2. The gain persists when the input arrangement comes from an extracted urban scene rather than the procedural layouts used to construct CityLift-5K.

    At the building level, Pixal3D achieves the lowest accuracy error and the highest F-scores, indicating closer prediction-to-reference surface agreement on average and stronger correspondence within the evaluated thresholds. This advantage is consistent with its pixel-aligned conditioning, which back-projects image features into 3D to establish explicit image–geometry correspondence [15]. CityLift achieves a lower completeness error of 1.128 cells, compared with 1.678 for Pixal3D, yielding a lower symmetric CD of 1.421 versus 1.490 cells. Since CD averages the two directional errors, the reduction in completeness error outweighs the increase in accuracy error. F-scores instead summarize surface precision and recall within fixed distance thresholds. CityLift thus provides better average reference-surface coverage, while Pixal3D retains an advantage in thresholded surface agreement for individual buildings.

    InstanceBuilding.

    CityLift also leads all five scene-level metrics on real-world scenes from InstanceBuilding (Table 3). Compared with Pixal3D, scene CD decreases from 2.012 to 1.531 cells, a reduction of 23.9%, and F@2 increases from 0.694 to 0.717, an improvement of 2.3 percentage points. The building-level results exhibit the same pattern. Pixal3D retains the best accuracy and F-scores, whereas CityLift reduces completeness error from 1.816 to 1.334 cells and CD from 1.768 to 1.625 cells. Across both external datasets, CityLift consistently improves average building-surface coverage and assembled-scene geometry, demonstrating generalization to both synthetic and real-world scene sources. Figure 4 presents the corresponding visual comparisons.

    5.4 Multi-view Visual Evaluation

    Surface distances describe geometric agreement with the reference, but do not measure texture quality or the visual quality of completed facades. We therefore render four views of each generated UrbanScene3D block and use ChatGPT 6 Astra as a visual assessor. For each method and block, the assessor inspects the conditioning image together with all four rendered views. It assigns scores to layout and completeness (L), shape and proportion (G), appearance and detail (A), and multi-view structural quality (M). The overall score is

    S=10(0.35L+0.30G+0.20A+0.15M).

    		(7)

    As shown in Table 4, CityLift achieves the highest scores across all four dimensions, with an overall score of 82.8 compared with 77.6 for TRELLIS.2.

    5.5 Ablation Studies

    We ablate scene guidance and replace local regeneration with direct coarse decoding (Table 5). Removing scene guidance causes the largest degradation, increasing scene-level CD from 1.079 to 2.590 and highlighting the importance of scene conditioning. Direct coarse decoding achieves a building-level CD of 1.150, but produces smoother, simplified surfaces with less distinct windows and other facade details (Fig. 5). Local regeneration reduces CD to 1.011 and recovers finer architectural details, complementing the overall building geometry captured by the scaffold.

    We further examine inherited conditioning by removing hidden-feature and occupancy injection separately and jointly, and replacing aligned hidden features with spatially pooled features. Removing both injection pathways increases building-level CD to 2.510, exceeding that of coarse decoding. Thus, local regeneration can degrade an initially useful scaffold without aligned conditioning. Removing hidden-feature injection and pooling hidden features yield similar scene-level CDs of 2.170 and 2.200, suggesting that their benefit depends strongly on preserving spatial variation. Occupancy injection provides a smaller additional gain, with its removal increasing scene-level CD to 1.260. Consistent with these findings, Fig. 5 shows fragmented building surfaces when aligned or hidden-feature injection is removed, or hidden features are pooled, whereas CityLift produces more complete facades and roofs.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented CityLift, a framework for compositional 3D urban generation from a single image and building instance masks. Urban scaffold generation captures scene layout and coarse building geometry, while generative spatial inheritance transfers geometric support and hidden features into local building frames. Conditioned building regeneration refines individual structures, which are converted into explicit, individually editable meshes and assembled using the inherited spatial transforms. We also introduced CityLift-5K to support training and evaluation of this task. Experiments on CityLift-5K, UrbanScene3D, and InstanceBuilding demonstrate improved scene-level geometric fidelity. These results support the effectiveness of combining scene-level spatial organization with local building generation for compositional urban content creation.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 重建与生成不该串起来用：Generative SfM 用原生 3D 扩散一次解出结构、相机与没拍到的部分 ｜ Generative Structure from Motion with Native 3D Diffusion
item.description:
一句话：SfM 只能还原拍到的、生成只能编；把两步串起来会级联误差，不如联合求解。

要点：

  • 问题拆得准：经典 SfM 能给出与输入一致的几何，但补不出未观测区域；生成方法能编出合理的 3D，却不保证忠于输入
  • 简单把两者串起来（先重建再生成）会让误差级联，得不到「既一致又完整」的 3D
  • Generative SfM 用原生 3D 扩散模型联合求解结构、相机运动与未观测部分，从少量未标定视图直接出结果

为什么值得看：「重建 + 补全」是摄影测量转资产的常见流水线，级联误差也是常态。这条主张联合求解，属于表示层的方法论修正；对做实景转资产、场景级 3DGS 之外的几何资产管线有参考价值。

中文摘要：从少量未标定视图同时恢复物体 3D 结构与相机运动是计算机视觉的基础问题。经典 Structure-from-Motion 能给出与输入图像一致的几何，但无法恢复未观测区域；原生生成方法能产出看似合理的 3D，却不一定忠于输入。把重建与生成简单串起来会让误差在两个阶段之间级联，得不到既一致又完整的 3D。Generative SfM 因此改用原生 3D 扩散模型，把结构、相机运动与未观测区域放在一起联合求解，从少数未标定视图直接产出结果。对把实拍转成可用资产的管线来说，这条的意义是：别在流程上打补丁，回到表示层一起解。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-11-01

Generative Structure from Motion
with Native 3D Diffusion

Abstract

Recovering an object’s 3D structure and camera motion from a few uncalibrated views is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Classical structure from motion methods recover 3D geometry consistent with the input images but cannot recover unseen regions; native generation methods produce plausible 3D objects which are related but not necessarily faithful to the input images. Methods simply concatenating reconstruction and generation allow error to cascade across the two stages, instead of producing a 3D object consistent with both the distribution and the input. We propose GenSfM, which integrates image-based 3D reconstruction with a native 3D diffusion model. In particular, we use a multi-modal diffusion transformer to jointly denoise the shape latent and per-view pose latents under shared self-attention, grounding generated geometry in the observed views while using object-level priors to infer unobserved regions. A compact 3D-native UV-volume tokenization keeps the joint sequence small as views are added, and a pose-aware stage refines geometry and texture by sampling per-voxel image features at the recovered camera poses. On Toys4k and GSO, for 4 uncalibrated views, GenSfM improves novel-view PSNR by 3.2–4.5 dB and reduces median Chamfer distance by 2.8–3.8× over a strong native-3D generation baseline, while recovering input-view poses over 96% Acc@5^∘ without any external pose-estimation backbone, post-hoc optimization, or known intrinsics. Project page: https://dotb1ue.github.io/GenSfm/.

1 Introduction

Recovering 3D structure and camera motion from images is a foundational problem in computer vision. Classical Structure-from-Motion and Multi-View Stereo pipelines [Schönberger and Frahm (2016); Schönberger et al. (2016); Furukawa and Ponce (2009)] estimate camera poses from multi-view correspondences and reconstruct geometry through photometric or geometric consistency, often regularized by hand-crafted priors. While effective when input views provide sufficient texture, overlap, and coverage, this geometric paradigm becomes brittle in sparse object-centric settings, where only a few uncalibrated views are available and large object regions go unrecovered.

Such settings are common in practice, from robotic manipulation to AR capture and content-creation pipelines, all of which need a holistic 3D representation to reason about occluded surfaces and contact regions. Sparse-view 3D object recovery therefore requires more than triangulating visible evidence: it must infer a complete 3D explanation that is both consistent with the input images and plausible as an object, jointly answering what the object is and where each view was taken from.

Recent learning-based methods relax the texture and overlap assumptions of classical pipelines by introducing large-scale data-driven priors. Feed-forward reconstructors [Wang et al. (2024); Leroy et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025)] predict camera parameters and pixel-aligned 3D representations jointly, while pose-centric works [Zhang et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2023); Sinha et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024a)] estimate relative camera motion under limited overlap and pose ambiguity. Both threads remain primarily observation-driven: they recover what the input views support but do not explicitly model the distribution of complete object shapes, leaving outputs incomplete in unobserved regions when input coverage is poor.

A complementary line of work introduces generative priors learned from large-scale 3D datasets [Deitke et al. (2023)] into sparse reconstruction. View-based generative SfM [Zhao et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2024b); Xu et al. (2024a); Zhao and Tulsiani (2024)] casts structure and motion as a generative problem in view space, while reconstruct-then-generate pipelines [Ardelean et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026); Chang et al. (2025); Team et al. (2025); Siddiqui et al. (2026)] pair feed-forward reconstructors with native 3D generators [Tochilkin et al. (2024); Xiang et al. (2025); Zhao et al. (2025b)]. The latter family in particular has shown that 3D generative priors can complete hidden geometry that observation-driven methods cannot. These systems remain cascaded: an external module predicts poses or image-aligned representations and the 3D generator only completes the result, propagating errors across stages and preventing joint optimization of a single 3D hypothesis that explains all input views.

In this paper, we invert this pipeline: instead of using a generative prior to complete the output of a feed-forward reconstructor, we treat the 3D generative prior itself as the primary reasoning mechanism for sparse-view reconstruction. We propose GenSfM, an end-to-end framework that formulates joint recovery of complete object structure and per-view camera motion as a single conditional inference problem in a native 3D diffusion model, as shown in Fig. 1. The diffusion prior operates directly on a native 3D representation throughout inference, simultaneously denoising shape and per-view pose under joint self-attention. This grounds the generated object in the observed views while using object-level regularities to infer unobserved geometry.

Realizing this formulation requires a single diffusion transformer that jointly denoises a shared 3D shape with a per-view pose latent bound to its input image, while keeping the per-view pose-token overhead small as views are added. We adopt CUPID’s [Huang et al. (2025)] 3D-native UV-volume pose tokenization, but compress each view’s pose latent to a compact token grid, since the dense volume over-parameterizes a low-DoF perspective projection. A learned view embedding tags each view’s pose latent and image tokens, binding pose to its source image. Since neither stream natively carries cross-view information, we prepend a small set of register tokens to the shape stream as a shared channel for all views to communicate through self-attention.

Instead of relying on back-projection to recover surface texture like feed-forward methods [(Wang et al., 2024)], we add a second stage of native 3D refinement and texturing [(Xiang et al., 2025)] so that hidden regions stay coherent with the observed views. We design a pose-aware fine stage that, using the cameras predicted in the coarse stage, projects every active voxel into the input views and conditions denoising on per-voxel semantic and texture features sampled and averaged across views.

On the Toys4k [Stojanov et al. (2021)] and GSO [Downs et al. (2022)] sparse-view object benchmarks under uncalibrated 4-view inputs, GenSfM improves novel-view PSNR by 3.2–4.5 dB, reduces median Chamfer distance by 2.8–3.8×, and lifts F@.01 from 0.56 to 0.83 on Toys4k over the strong native-3D generation baseline TRELLIS-M [Xiang et al. (2025)], while recovering input-view camera poses to over 96% Acc@5^∘ (a 5× rotation-error reduction over the strongest pose baseline VGGT [Wang et al. (2025)]) without requiring known intrinsics. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose GenSfM, a joint native-3D architecture that recasts a diffusion model from a post-hoc completion module into the primary inference mechanism for joint sparse-view structure and motion recovery, eliminating any external feed-forward reconstruction backbone.

  • •

    A 3D-native multi-view pose tokenization that places per-view UV-volume pose latents and the shape latent in a single multi-modal sequence, jointly denoised by a diffusion transformer under shared self-attention.

  • •

    A pose-aware fine stage that, with cameras recovered from the coarse stage, anchors semantic and texture features at every active voxel and averages them across views, sharpening surface detail beyond global, pose-agnostic conditioning.

    • 2 Related Work

    Sparse-view object reconstruction must jointly answer two coupled questions: what is the 3D object, and where was each view taken from? What requires both visible and hidden object structure, while where requires the camera motion relating the input views. Existing methods typically excel on one side or address the two with separate models stacked in series (Tab. 1).

    Feed-forward pose and 3D reconstruction.

    Pose-centric approaches [Zhang et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2023); Sinha et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024a)] target the where side, regressing relative camera motion under limited overlap and pose ambiguity, but leave what largely untouched. More general feed-forward reconstructors [Wang et al. (2024); Leroy et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025)] predict dense pointmaps, correspondences, and camera parameters jointly, addressing camera motion and visible geometry; hidden geometry, however, is recovered only indirectly through learned priors.

    Native 3D generation.

    Native 3D generators trained on large 3D corpora [Deitke et al. (2023)], such as TripoSR [Tochilkin et al. (2024)], TRELLIS[Xiang et al. (2025)], and Hunyuan3D [Zhao et al. (2025b)], are strong on what: complete object structure is modeled explicitly and hidden geometry is hallucinated from the prior. They do not target where: camera motion is typically assumed and only weakly encoded through cross-attention, so applied directly to uncalibrated sparse views they can produce plausible but misaligned geometry.

    View-based generative SfM.

    View-based generative SfM [Zhao et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2024b); Xu et al. (2024a); Zhao and Tulsiani (2024)] casts what and where as a joint generative problem in view space; DiffusionSfM, for instance, diffuses ray origins and endpoints to recover per-view geometry and camera motion jointly. Because diffusion operates over view-based quantities (rays, pointmaps, depths), hidden what is recovered only insofar as it can be back-projected from individual views.

    Reconstruction with 3D generative priors.

    Reconstruct-then-generate pipelines [Ardelean et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026); Chang et al. (2025); Team et al. (2025); Siddiqui et al. (2026); Yao et al. (2025)] couple feed-forward reconstruction with native 3D generators: e.g., ReconViaGen [Chang et al. (2025)] injects VGGT [Wang et al. (2025)] geometry tokens into a 3D generator. These pipelines recover hidden geometry through the generative prior while grounding camera motion and visible structure with feed-forward geometry, but solve what and where in separate stages, so errors from the reconstruction backbone propagate into a 3D hypothesis that need not remain coherent with all input views.

    3 Preliminaries

    Overview.

    Given N uncalibrated multi-view images I={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N of an object O, our goal is to recover the holistic 3D structure and per-view camera poses ℙ={Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N as a coarse-to-fine generative problem in a native 3D diffusion model. We build on two native 3D generators reviewed below: TRELLIS[Xiang et al. (2025)] provides the two-stage backbone and CFM objective we inherit, and CUPID[Huang et al. (2025)] contributes the 3D-native single-image pose tokenization we lift to multi-view.

    Coarse-to-fine 3D generation.

    Our backbone is TRELLIS[Xiang et al. (2025)], which generates a 3D object in two coarse-to-fine stages under a shared conditional flow matching [Lipman et al. (2022)] (CFM) objective. The first stage produces a sparse-structure (SS) latent zˢ on a 16³ grid, decoded to a 64³ occupancy grid whose active voxels define positions {xⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L. The second stage produces the structured-latent (SLat) set S={xⱼ,fⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L with per-voxel features fⱼ, which separate decoders [Shen et al. (2023); Kerbl et al. (2023)] map to 3D Gaussians, a radiance field, or a mesh. Both stages train with

    L_CFM(φ)=𝔼_t,z₀,ε∥v_φ(zₜ,I,t)-(ε-z₀)∥₂²,

    		(1)

    where zₜ=(1-t)z₀+t ε is the noisy latent at t∈[0,1] for clean target z₀ (zˢ for SS, {fⱼ} for SLat) and noise ε∼ℕ(0,I); v_φ is the DiT velocity prediction conditioned on I.

    3D-native pose representation.

    Our pose tokenization derives from CUPID[Huang et al. (2025)], which extends TRELLIS’s SS stage to jointly recover the camera pose for a single input image: the SS latent gains channels encoding per-voxel UV coordinates, decoded to a 64³ UV volume that gives each active voxel’s projection uⱼ∈[0,1]². The 3×4 projection matrix P is thus a dense 3D-2D field on the active voxels, recovered from the per-voxel correspondences {xⱼ,uⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L by Direct Linear Transform (DLT) least-squares [(Abdel-Aziz et al., 2015)]:

    P^*=\argmin_P∑ⱼ₌₁^L∥π(P,xⱼ)-uⱼ∥²,

    		(2)

    where π is the perspective projection. Finally, camera intrinsic K and extrinsic [R|t] are recovered from P^* via RQ decomposition.

    4 Method

    We frame this joint recovery as a coarse-to-fine generative problem in the latent space of a native 3D diffusion model (Fig. 2). Building on TRELLIS’s two-stage architecture and CUPID’s 3D-native pose representation (Sec. 3), Sec. 4.1 jointly generates 3D structure and multi-view poses with a multi-modal DiT over per-view pose tokens, and Sec. 4.2 refines geometry and appearance via per-voxel pose-sampled image conditioning.

    4.1 3D structure and pose recovery from multi-view images

    The coarse stage casts joint recovery of 3D structure and per-view camera poses as a single denoising problem: each camera is encoded as a per-view 3D-native pose token, and shape and pose are denoised jointly by a multi-modal DiT with joint self-attention over both streams.

    Tokenizing multi-view camera poses.

    For each view i, every active voxel xⱼ projects to u_j,i=π(Pᵢ,xⱼ), yielding a UV volume uᵢ∈[0,1]^2×64³. A shared pose VAE compresses each uᵢ into a latent grid zᵖᵢ∈ℝ^c×r×r×r with c=8,r=4. To represent multiple input views, we form a unified token sequence with the shape latent zˢ followed by the per-view pose latents {zᵖᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N — in contrast to CUPID[(Huang et al., 2025)], whose channel-wise concatenation of shape and pose into a single SS latent is restricted to one view. We choose r=4 (vs CUPID’s r=16), giving 64× fewer tokens per pose at negligible accuracy cost since the UV volume is heavily over-parameterized for a low-DoF projection. At inference, the pose VAE decodes each generated zᵖᵢ back to a UV volume, from which Pᵢ^* is recovered by solving Eq. 2. See App. A.3 for details.

    Multi-view conditioned shape-pose DiT.

    A shared transformer backbone denoises shape and pose jointly, with stream-specific projections and grid-aligned positional embeddings. Learnable register tokens zʳ are prepended to the shape stream to capture global context. We extend the CFM interpolation of Eq. 1 to a shape timestep tˢ∈[0,1] and per-view pose timesteps tᵖ∈[0,1]^N, giving z₀=[zˢ; zᵖ] and zₜ=[zₜˢ; zₜᵖ]. Stream-specific in-projections then lift each noisy latent to the shared transformer width, where positional and view embeddings are added in to form the layer-0 hidden state of the DiT:

    h₀=[ zʳ; Wᵢₙˢ zₜˢ+eˢ; Wᵢₙᵖ zₜᵖ+eᵖ+eᵛ ],

    		(3)

    where eˢ,eᵖ are absolute 3D PEs over the 16³ and 4³ grids that anchor each stream to its native voxel layout, and eᵛ is a per-view ID embedding shared between each pose latent and its source view’s image-condition tokens (Eq. 6), binding each pose to its view through cross-attention. We then stack L DiT blocks; each block injects the multi-view condition tokens z^I={z^Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N,

    hₗ₊₁=CrossAttn (Q(hₗ), K(z^I), V(z^I)),

    		(4)

    where Q,K,V are the query/key/value projections, applied jointly over all N views without per-view masking. Each block also runs a joint self-attention over the entire sequence and a feed-forward sub-layer, both modulated by per-modality AdaLN values conditioned on tˢ for shape tokens and on tᵖᵢ for view-i pose tokens. After the final block, stream-specific out-projections read out the velocities (register outputs are discarded), v_φ(zₜ,z^I,tˢ,tᵖ)=[ Wₒᵤₜˢ h_Lˢ; Wₒᵤₜᵖ h_Lᵖ ], and the whole network is trained with a stream-wise conditional flow matching loss:

    L_coarse(φ)=𝔼_tˢ, tᵖ, z₀, ε ∥v_φ(zₜ,z^I,tˢ,tᵖ)-(ε-z₀)∥₂².

    		(5)

    Multi-scale enhanced image condition.

    DINOv2 patch features capture rich semantics but are spatially coarse, providing limited cues for the fine appearance and accurate 2D-3D correspondences our coarse stage must recover. We therefore augment them with multi-scale local features extracted by a small convolutional pyramid on the same image: for each view i, the condition tokens are

    z^Iᵢ=(\textscDINOv2(Iᵢ) ⊕ Φˢ_cnn(Iᵢ))+eᵛ,

    		(6)

    where \textscDINOv2(Iᵢ) are the frozen patch tokens, Φˢ_cnn(Iᵢ) stacks features from a 4-level convolutional pyramid where each level patchified to the DINOv2 patch grid and channel-concatenated across levels, ⊕ denotes channel-wise concatenation per token, and eᵛ is the view-tag embedding from Eq. 3. The resulting z^I={z^Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N serves as the cross-attention key/value sequence in every DiT block. See App. A.4 for details.

    4.2 Pose-aware generation of fine geometry and appearance

    The fine stage generates geometry and appearance with pose-aware per-voxel image conditioning: each voxel receives a semantic feature from DINOv2 and a texture feature from a multi-scale CNN pyramid, with both features average-pooled over pose-aligned projections across views.

    Pose-aware per-voxel image conditioning.

    TRELLIS’s SLat stage conditions on the input image only through global cross-attention with DINOv2 patch tokens, leaving fine-appearance cues unanchored from any specific voxel and producing blurry surface detail. Once P^* is recovered by the coarse stage (Sec. 4.1), every active voxel xⱼ has a known image projection uⱼ=π(P^*,xⱼ), so image features can be sampled directly per voxel. At each xⱼ we form two complementary features: a semantic feature cˢᵉᵐⱼ from pose-sampled DINOv2 patches re-encoded through the frozen SLat encoder Enc_L (placing it on the same latent manifold as the SLat target fⱼ), and a texture feature cᵗᵉˣⱼ from a multi-scale CNN pyramid Φˡ_cnn that supplies the low-level cues that DINOv2 lacks:

    {cˢᵉᵐⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L=Enc_L({xⱼ, BilinearInterp(uⱼ, \textscDINOv2(I))}ⱼ₌₁^L),(7)
    cᵗᵉˣⱼ=BilinearInterp(uⱼ, Φˡ_cnn(I)).

    where BilinearInterp denotes bilinear interpolation. We channel-wise concatenate cˢᵉᵐⱼ and cᵗᵉˣⱼ with the noisy voxel feature fⱼᵗ (the SLat target fⱼ noised via Eq. 1) and linearly project to form the per-voxel layer-0 DiT token h₀(xⱼ)=Wˡᵢₙ[ fⱼᵗ ⊕ cˢᵉᵐⱼ ⊕ cᵗᵉˣⱼ ]; the remainder of the DiT follows TRELLIS. See App. A.4 for the visual pyramid architecture.

    Pooling per-voxel features across views.

    With N input views, every active voxel has N pose-aligned projections u_j,i=π(Pᵢ^*,xⱼ). We extend BilinearInterp to per-view sampling followed by averaging, BilinearInterp(uⱼ, Φ(I)):=\tfrac1N∑ᵢ₌₁^NBilinearInterp(u_j,i, Φ(Iᵢ)), so Eq. 7 applies unchanged with I replaced by I. The cross-attention condition is likewise the per-view mean of DINOv2 patch tokens. The mean operator itself is parameter-free and view-count-agnostic; the model in this work is trained with N=4.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    We train our model on four public 3D-asset datasets: Objaverse-XL [Deitke et al. (2023)] (GitHub and Sketchfab partitions), HSSD [Khanna et al. (2024)], 3D-FUTURE [Fu et al. (2021)], and ABO [Collins et al. (2022)]. After TRELLIS’s aesthetic filter (≥4.5), about 430K instances remain. Each is rendered following TRELLIS’s protocol, with 24 condition views at 1024×1024 from cameras uniformly sampled on the upper hemisphere. We evaluate on two held-out test sets, Toys4k [Stojanov et al. (2021)] (synthetic) and GSO [Downs et al. (2022)] (real-captured), neither overlapping the training corpus.

    Evaluation protocol.

    We assess photometric fidelity, 3D geometry, and camera-pose accuracy. Each test set uses its first 400 objects with two disjoint 4-view sets, {0,6,12,18} and {3,9,15,21}, yielding 800 object–viewset instances for aggregation. As baselines fall into three capability families, we apply the most suitable evaluation protocol to each: (i) least squares on predicted vs ground-truth input-view pointmaps for feed-forward reconstruction, tight only with accurate predicted geometry and poses; (ii) similarity ICP on sampled point clouds for 3D generation; and (iii) gauge-invariant pairwise relative-pose comparison on unordered input-view pairs for pose-predicting methods. GenSfM is reevaluated under each applicable protocol; comparisons are restricted to methods sharing a table and protocol. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [Zhang et al. (2018)] on 512×512 novel views at the 8 held-out condition-view indices {2,4,8,10,14,16,20,22}; bidirectional Chamfer Distance (CD; reported as the median across objects, since a few severe failures dominate the mean) and F-scores at τ∈{0.01, 0.05}; and Relative Rotation Error (RRE) with Acc@{5^∘,15^∘}, Relative Translation Error (RTE), and mean absolute FOV error (RFOV; only for methods that predict intrinsics). See App. A.1 for the full alignment protocol and App. A.2 for the pose metric definitions.

    Baseline methods.

    We compare against a representative set of multi-view image-to-3D baselines: (a) TRELLIS-S[Xiang et al. (2025)]: TRELLIS run as a single-image generator on each input view independently, with the mean over the four outputs reported; (b) TRELLIS-M[Xiang et al. (2025)]: TRELLIS with multi-view input in stochastic mode, where each denoising step is conditioned on one randomly chosen input view; (c) SAM 3D[Team et al. (2025)]: a single-image-to-3D generator run once per input view, with the mean over the four outputs reported; (d) FreeSplatter[Xu et al. (2024b)]: predicts per-view pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians together with input camera parameters in a pose-free setting; (e) LucidFusion[He et al. (2025)]: predicts per-view relative coordinate maps that are fused into a 3D Gaussian output; (f) ReconViaGen[Chang et al. (2025)]: combines feed-forward reconstruction with generative refinement, using VGGT-derived geometry tokens to condition a 3D generator; (g) VGGT[Wang et al. (2025)]: a transformer that jointly regresses per-view pointmaps and camera extrinsics/intrinsics from uncalibrated images. Our table appear in three families: 3D generation (a,b,c,f), feed-forward reconstruction (d,e,f), and pose prediction (d,f,g).

    5.2 Main Results

    Comparison with feed-forward reconstruction methods.

    Tab. 2 and Fig. 3 compare against feed-forward reconstruction baselines under input-view pointmap LSQ alignment. GenSfM outperforms every baseline on every metric and on both datasets, with the gap widening at the strict F@.01 threshold and qualitatively in the form of alignment artifacts and surface noise. Feed-forward methods compound any disagreement between their predicted geometry and predicted poses, while a generative 3D-native model refines it away.

    Comparison with 3D generation methods.

    Tab. 3 and Fig. 4 compare against 3D generation models that produce a canonical, pose-free output, under similarity-ICP alignment. GenSfM leads on every metric, with the largest margins on the strict-threshold geometry metrics (F@.01, CD-med). Pose-free baselines hallucinate plausible but mismatched detail on unseen sides; the two strong multi-view baselines (TRELLIS-M’s stochastic per-step view conditioning and ReconViaGen’s feed-forward reconstruction with generative refinement) still trail GenSfM by large margins, indicating the gain comes from joint shape–pose denoising rather than late-stage view sampling.

    Pose prediction accuracy.

    Tab. 4 reports camera-pose accuracy on baselines that predict input-view extrinsics. GenSfM achieves substantially lower rotation and translation errors, with Acc.@5^∘ saturating; baselines commonly fail on symmetric objects whose orientation depends on low-level visual cues. Our model also recovers intrinsics accurately (known-intrinsics row shown for reference); VGGT, not trained on varying-FOV synthetic data, incurs large RFOV despite strong extrinsics, whereas GenSfM keeps RFOV under 3^∘ on both datasets while saturating Acc.@5^∘. Thus, RFOV confirms reliable intrinsic recovery under varying FOV, but its margin over VGGT also reflects training-distribution coverage, not architecture alone.

    5.3 Ablation Study

    We ablate each design choice on Toys4k in Tab. 5, with rows added cumulatively. In Stage 1, full cross-attention enables cross-view information sharing and improves all metrics; visual feature conditioning sharpens photometric fidelity and pose accuracy with only marginal geometry gains, suggesting appearance cues primarily help rendering and pose grounding; shared register tokens aggregate global information and contribute most to pose accuracy and the strict F@.01 threshold. In Stage 2, a fine decoder trained natively on multi-view data sharpens photometric fidelity, while 3D geometry is already saturated. The decoder swap leaves raw coarse-stage cameras unchanged but shifts geometry-aligned pose metrics because their similarity fit depends on the final pointmap. Fig. 5 corroborates these trends qualitatively: surface details (e.g., the screwdriver cap, the snake’s head) sharpen left-to-right and the full model best matches GT.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented GenSfM, which recasts a native 3D diffusion model as the primary inference mechanism for sparse-view object reconstruction, jointly denoising shape and per-view camera poses in a single multi-modal diffusion transformer. Three choices keep the formulation tractable: a UV-volume pose latent compressed to a compact token grid, a unified multi-modal sequence that places shape and per-view pose tokens in a single self-attention, and a pose-aware fine stage that conditions each voxel on features sampled at its pose-aligned image projection. On Toys4k and GSO, GenSfM outperforms feed-forward, 3D-generation, and pose-prediction baselines on photometric, geometric, and pose metrics simultaneously, recovering both extrinsics and intrinsics to high accuracy without any external pose estimator or post-hoc optimization.

    Limitations and future work.

    Our results are restricted to object-centric inputs at N=4; extending to larger view counts, scene-level inputs, and in-the-wild captures with looser segmentation is a natural next step. Under distribution shift, large pose/calibration errors may misregister fine-stage image features, degrading local refinement while the coarse 3D prior preserves global completion. The model also inherits the object distribution and resolution limits of its TRELLIS backbone, so scaling the underlying generator should directly improve sparse-view recovery.

    Appendix A Technical appendices and supplementary material

    A.1 Alignment protocol

    Our baselines differ in what they natively output (input-view pointmaps, canonical pose-free 3D, or input-camera poses), so a single shared alignment would unfairly discard the structure each method already provides. We therefore align each prediction with the protocol best matched to its output family before evaluating, and GenSfM is evaluated under each applicable family using that family’s protocol so all comparisons within a table are like-for-like.

    Input-view pointmap least squares (Table 2).

    This protocol applies to feed-forward reconstruction methods (LucidFusion, FreeSplatter, ReconViaGen), which already place geometry in a noisy estimate of the input-camera frame. For each input view, we back-project the per-pixel predicted depth at the predicted camera into 3D, alpha-mask the result, randomly subsample to at most 50K points per view, and pair it with the GT pointmap obtained by back-projecting GT depth at the GT camera. Stacking the per-view pairs with equal aggregate weight per view yields one set of 3D-to-3D correspondences per object, which we fit with a closed-form Umeyama similarity [(Umeyama, 2002)]. The resulting transform is applied once to the full predicted 3D before all photometric and geometric evaluation; we log the per-object LSQ residual as an alignment-fidelity diagnostic. Note that this protocol exercises both halves of feed-forward reconstruction: the matched correspondences require the predicted geometry to align with the predicted cameras, so a method with weak geometry, weak pose recovery, or any mismatch between the two will produce noisy correspondences and a loose Umeyama fit, inflating all downstream metrics.

    Similarity ICP (Table 3).

    This protocol applies to 3D generation methods (TRELLIS-S, TRELLIS-M, SAM 3D), which output a canonical pose-free 3D, and to GenSfM when evaluated under the same family. To obtain the prediction-side point cloud uniformly across output formats (whether the prediction is a mesh or a set of 3D Gaussians), we render depth from a set of orbiting random views around the prediction and back-project the depth maps into 3D, which yields a well-covered surface point cloud without surface-sampling biases specific to the underlying representation. The GT-side cloud is sampled directly on the GT mesh surface. We initialize alignment by sweeping the 24 orientation-preserving signed axis permutations of the PCA-aligned bounding box and keep the candidate with the lowest post-ICP residual; we then refine with similarity ICP and use the resulting transform to map the prediction into the GT frame for evaluation.

    A.2 Pose metric protocol

    Pose metric definitions.

    Different pose-predicting baselines fix their world frame in different ways (some anchor to the first input view, some to an internal canonical frame, others through their own internal similarity fit), so absolute predicted extrinsics cannot be directly compared to GT extrinsics. To bypass this gauge ambiguity entirely, all metrics in Table 4 are computed on unordered pairs of input views: for each pair, the relative pose between the two views cancels any global rotation, translation, and scale that affects all views jointly, leaving only the camera geometry intrinsic to the pair. We adopt this pairwise form uniformly for both rotation and translation rather than anchoring to one reference view, which would entangle every error with the chosen anchor. For each object, we average each metric over the N(N-1)/2 unordered pairs and then average across objects. Relative Rotation Error (RRE) is the geodesic angle (in degrees) between the predicted and GT relative rotations of the pair; Acc.@5^∘ / Acc.@15^∘ is the fraction of pairs whose RRE falls below the corresponding threshold; Relative Translation Error (RTE) is the angular error (in degrees) between the predicted and GT relative-translation directions, an angular form chosen because absolute translation magnitude is itself gauge-dependent (a global similarity scale can be reabsorbed by any consistent rescaling of all camera centers); and Field-of-View Error (RFOV) is the mean absolute difference (in degrees) between predicted and GT FOV, computed directly on intrinsics without any pose alignment, since intrinsics are independent of the world frame. To score baselines with a coarse front/back chirality ambiguity on geometric correctness rather than chirality alone, all angular metrics (RRE, Acc.@{5^∘,15^∘}, RTE) are read off after collapsing R_predR_gt^⊤ under the diag(±1,±1,-1) sign-flip equivalence class. The same rule is applied uniformly to all methods, including ours, to compare geometric recovery under a shared front/back equivalence. Chirality remains relevant for camera-dependent applications, so we explicitly note that this metric does not assess that failure mode.

    A.3 Pose VAE

    Architecture and training.

    The pose VAE is a 3D-convolutional encoder–decoder over a 64³ voxel grid with a deliberately aggressive bottleneck: four 2× spatial downsamples compress the input into a 4³ token grid with 8 channels per token. This compression is feasible because each per-voxel target is a smooth function of voxel position and a low-DoF camera, so the latent does not need to absorb high-frequency content. Per voxel the encoder receives three input channels (a binary in-frustum indicator plus the two pixel coordinates obtained by projecting the voxel center under the input camera), and the decoder emits the same three channels through a classification head (visibility mask) and a regression head (pixel UV).

    We use a dice loss on the visibility classifier and an L1 loss on the UV regression, with a small KL weight (10⁻³) so the latent stays close to a standard Gaussian for the downstream diffusion stage. The training distribution matches inference: each minibatch sample takes a real camera pose from the multi-view renders of a sampled training object and projects it on the fly into the 64³ voxel grid. We optimize for 1M steps with AdamW (lr 3×10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻³) on a cosine schedule.

    Out-of-frame voxels.

    Voxel centers can project outside the input image. We handle this by clamping target UVs to [0,1]² rather than dropping out-of-frame voxels, keeping the decoder output well-defined everywhere. The visibility channel encodes the same in-/out-of-frame information as a binary indicator with a small 1% inset margin (0.01≤u,v≤0.99); the inference DLT solve uses this channel to restrict to in-frustum voxels, so saturated boundary UVs never contaminate the recovered pose. The UV reconstruction loss is applied uniformly to all voxels rather than only the in-frustum subset, keeping saturated-boundary regions consistent between encoder and decoder.

    Pose autoencoding accuracy.

    Table 6 reports the autoencoding fidelity of the trained pose VAE on the Toys4k held-out split, sweeping the latent spatial resolution. We encode each held-out 64³ ground-truth UV volume to the chosen latent grid, decode back, and recover camera pose via a DLT solve over in-frustum voxels. UV Dist. is the per-voxel L2 distance in normalized image coordinates; RRE, RTE, and RFOV are the standard rotation, translation-direction, and FOV errors in degrees. All three latent resolutions deliver near-identical pose accuracy (within a few hundredths of a degree on RRE/RTE/RFOV), and even the worst row stays an order of magnitude below the downstream pose-prediction residuals in Table 4, so the latent is not the bottleneck on overall pose accuracy. We adopt the 4³ latent in the main paper as the most compute-efficient operating point, since the larger grids carry 8× and 64× more tokens at no measurable pose gain.

    A.4 Image conditioning across stages

    Coarse stage: dual-stream encoder and token fusion.

    Each view is encoded by two complementary streams that fuse into a single per-view token sequence for the coarse DiT to cross-attend to. A frozen DINOv2-L/14 with registers at 518×518 produces 1374 tokens per view (CLS + 4 registers + a 37×37 patch grid) at 1024 channels, supplying object-level semantics. In parallel, a lightweight 4-level CNN at 296×296 (5×5 convolutions, strides {1,2,2,2}, output channels [6,6,6,8]) is patchified down to the same 37×37 grid, with per-token contributions [384,96,24,8] channel-concatenating into a 512-dim local-texture feature. We append the 512 local channels onto the 1024 semantic channels at every patch token (non-patch tokens zero-pad on the local side), giving a uniform per-token width of 1536 and a cross-attention key/value of length N×1374. The two streams are deliberately complementary: semantic anchors pose to image content, while local texture restores the pixel-faithful appearance cues the semantic encoder has discarded, letting cross-attention recover accurate cameras without polluting the joint self-attention with raw image tokens.

    Fine stage: visual pyramid and per-voxel projection.

    The fine stage refines up to L≤32,768 active voxels at 64³ under the cameras already recovered by the coarse stage. Cross-attending every voxel to thousands of image tokens per view is intractable, so we replace cross-attention with per-voxel pixel-aligned feature sampling: each voxel projects to u_j,i in view i under the predicted camera, and visual features are bilinearly sampled at that pixel. The visual encoder is a ConvNeXt-style pyramid run once per view at 256×256: four stages, each one ConvNeXt block with a 7×7 depthwise kernel at internal width 32, with a 2× downsample between stages. Each stage exposes a 4-channel tap (LayerNorm + 1×1 Conv); the four taps sampled at u_j,i and channel-concatenated yield a 16-channel multi-scale texture feature cᵗᵉˣⱼ. We pair it with an 8-channel semantic feature cˢᵉᵐⱼ: the coarse-stage DINOv2 patch tokens (reused, no extra DINOv2 pass) are bilinearly sampled at the same per-voxel projection and re-encoded through the frozen SLat encoder, placing them on the SLat target’s latent manifold and giving a compact 24-channel per-voxel conditioning vector. This keeps fine-stage cost proportional to active voxels rather than view tokens, while the multi-scale taps let each voxel combine coarse contour cues with fine local texture without inflating the per-voxel width.

    A.5 Implementation details

    Pose VAE training.

    The pose VAE of App. A.3 is trained for 1M steps on 8 H200 GPUs with batch size 4 per GPU, using AdamW (lr 3×10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻³) under a cosine schedule with 1000 warmup steps decaying to 10⁻⁵, EMA 0.9999, and FP16 mixed precision. The same recipe trains the 4³, 8³, and 16³ latent variants of Tab. 6.

    Coarse-stage shape-pose DiT training.

    The coarse stage is fine-tuned for 1M steps on 8 H200 GPUs at global batch size 64 (8 per GPU, split into two gradient-accumulation microbatches), initialized from a prior single-view coarse-stage checkpoint of ours (itself from the pretrained TRELLIS-image-large SS DiT). Each instance contributes N=4 random condition views uniformly sampled from the 24 rendered views of the object; each input image is crop-resized at a 1.2× tightness ratio around the alpha-mask bounding box and bilinearly resampled to 518×518 for the frozen DINOv2 ViT-L/14-with-registers encoder. The DiT operates on 4096 shape, 256 pose, and 128 shared register tokens, with cross-attention over N×1374=5496 image-condition tokens augmented by the convolutional pyramid of Eq. 6. We use AdamW (lr 10⁻⁴, no weight decay), CFG dropout 0.1, the same cosine schedule and EMA as above, and timesteps drawn from a logit-normal distribution with mean 1.0 and std 1.0 (σ_\min=10⁻⁵). At each step we randomly choose between two timestep-coupling modes: with probability 0.8, the shape stream and all pose streams share a single timestep; with probability 0.2, each stream draws an independent timestep. The shared mode dominates so the model stays well-calibrated to the synchronized inference schedule, while the per-pose mode supplies enough timestep diversity that the per-modality AdaLN modulation actually learns to handle independent noise levels.

    Fine-stage SLat DiT training.

    The fine stage is fine-tuned independently for 1M steps on 4 H200 GPUs at global batch size 32 (8 per GPU), initialized from TRELLIS’s pretrained SLat DiT checkpoint. It denoises up to L≤32,768 active voxels at 64³; ground-truth cameras and occupancy are used during training so the fine stage learns from clean projections. Each instance again contributes N=4 random condition views, with per-voxel features pooled across views by mean (16-channel ConvNeXt-pyramid texture and 8-channel SLat-encoded semantic) and the cross-attention condition the per-view mean of DINOv2 patches. We use AdamW (lr 10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻³), CFG dropout 0.1, and the same cosine schedule and logit-normal timestep distribution as the coarse stage.

    Inference.

    The coarse stage runs a 25-step flow-Euler sampler over the joint shape-pose sequence at classifier-free guidance strength 7.5, active on the noise interval t∈[0.5,1.0] with a guidance time-rescale factor of 3.0[Esser et al. (2024)]. We then decode each per-view pose latent through the pose VAE and recover Pᵢ^* by the DLT solve of Eq. 2. The fine stage runs a 25-step flow-Euler sampler with sequential multi-view fusion at CFG strength 3.0 on the same [0.5,1.0] interval and rescale factor, conditioned on the recovered cameras and on the per-voxel pose-sampled features of Eq. 7.

    A.6 Broader impacts

    GenSfM produces a 3D representation of an object from a few uncalibrated images, jointly recovering shape and camera. The most direct positive applications are in robotics (object-level scene understanding from a small number of viewpoints), augmented and virtual reality (capturing personal items as 3D assets for placement in virtual environments), and content creation (3D meshes from reference photos as a starting point for downstream editing). Joint recovery of camera intrinsics and extrinsics with shape removes the calibration friction that has limited deployment of feed-forward reconstruction methods in casually-captured settings.

    The negative considerations are those shared with image-conditioned 3D generation more broadly: the resulting 3D models could be used to fabricate convincing 3D content of real-world objects, including objects belonging to others, without their consent; coupled with downstream rendering pipelines, this could enable image-only digital reproduction at a scale that traditional photogrammetry has not previously allowed. The model is trained only on common, non-sensitive object categories from public 3D-asset datasets, and recovery quality degrades on out-of-distribution categories, which provides a partial natural mitigation. Released model checkpoints will carry an attribution requirement and an acceptable-use note as the safeguard accompanying our open release.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：SfM 只能还原拍到的、生成只能编；把两步串起来会级联误差，不如联合求解。

要点：

  • 问题拆得准：经典 SfM 能给出与输入一致的几何，但补不出未观测区域；生成方法能编出合理的 3D，却不保证忠于输入
  • 简单把两者串起来（先重建再生成）会让误差级联，得不到「既一致又完整」的 3D
  • Generative SfM 用原生 3D 扩散模型联合求解结构、相机运动与未观测部分，从少量未标定视图直接出结果

为什么值得看：「重建 + 补全」是摄影测量转资产的常见流水线，级联误差也是常态。这条主张联合求解，属于表示层的方法论修正；对做实景转资产、场景级 3DGS 之外的几何资产管线有参考价值。

中文摘要：从少量未标定视图同时恢复物体 3D 结构与相机运动是计算机视觉的基础问题。经典 Structure-from-Motion 能给出与输入图像一致的几何，但无法恢复未观测区域；原生生成方法能产出看似合理的 3D，却不一定忠于输入。把重建与生成简单串起来会让误差在两个阶段之间级联，得不到既一致又完整的 3D。Generative SfM 因此改用原生 3D 扩散模型，把结构、相机运动与未观测区域放在一起联合求解，从少数未标定视图直接产出结果。对把实拍转成可用资产的管线来说，这条的意义是：别在流程上打补丁，回到表示层一起解。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-26

本期推送：2026-11-01

Generative Structure from Motion
with Native 3D Diffusion

Abstract

Recovering an object’s 3D structure and camera motion from a few uncalibrated views is a fundamental problem in computer vision. Classical structure from motion methods recover 3D geometry consistent with the input images but cannot recover unseen regions; native generation methods produce plausible 3D objects which are related but not necessarily faithful to the input images. Methods simply concatenating reconstruction and generation allow error to cascade across the two stages, instead of producing a 3D object consistent with both the distribution and the input. We propose GenSfM, which integrates image-based 3D reconstruction with a native 3D diffusion model. In particular, we use a multi-modal diffusion transformer to jointly denoise the shape latent and per-view pose latents under shared self-attention, grounding generated geometry in the observed views while using object-level priors to infer unobserved regions. A compact 3D-native UV-volume tokenization keeps the joint sequence small as views are added, and a pose-aware stage refines geometry and texture by sampling per-voxel image features at the recovered camera poses. On Toys4k and GSO, for 4 uncalibrated views, GenSfM improves novel-view PSNR by 3.2–4.5 dB and reduces median Chamfer distance by 2.8–3.8× over a strong native-3D generation baseline, while recovering input-view poses over 96% Acc@5^∘ without any external pose-estimation backbone, post-hoc optimization, or known intrinsics. Project page: https://dotb1ue.github.io/GenSfm/.

1 Introduction

Recovering 3D structure and camera motion from images is a foundational problem in computer vision. Classical Structure-from-Motion and Multi-View Stereo pipelines [Schönberger and Frahm (2016); Schönberger et al. (2016); Furukawa and Ponce (2009)] estimate camera poses from multi-view correspondences and reconstruct geometry through photometric or geometric consistency, often regularized by hand-crafted priors. While effective when input views provide sufficient texture, overlap, and coverage, this geometric paradigm becomes brittle in sparse object-centric settings, where only a few uncalibrated views are available and large object regions go unrecovered.

Such settings are common in practice, from robotic manipulation to AR capture and content-creation pipelines, all of which need a holistic 3D representation to reason about occluded surfaces and contact regions. Sparse-view 3D object recovery therefore requires more than triangulating visible evidence: it must infer a complete 3D explanation that is both consistent with the input images and plausible as an object, jointly answering what the object is and where each view was taken from.

Recent learning-based methods relax the texture and overlap assumptions of classical pipelines by introducing large-scale data-driven priors. Feed-forward reconstructors [Wang et al. (2024); Leroy et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025)] predict camera parameters and pixel-aligned 3D representations jointly, while pose-centric works [Zhang et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2023); Sinha et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024a)] estimate relative camera motion under limited overlap and pose ambiguity. Both threads remain primarily observation-driven: they recover what the input views support but do not explicitly model the distribution of complete object shapes, leaving outputs incomplete in unobserved regions when input coverage is poor.

A complementary line of work introduces generative priors learned from large-scale 3D datasets [Deitke et al. (2023)] into sparse reconstruction. View-based generative SfM [Zhao et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2024b); Xu et al. (2024a); Zhao and Tulsiani (2024)] casts structure and motion as a generative problem in view space, while reconstruct-then-generate pipelines [Ardelean et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026); Chang et al. (2025); Team et al. (2025); Siddiqui et al. (2026)] pair feed-forward reconstructors with native 3D generators [Tochilkin et al. (2024); Xiang et al. (2025); Zhao et al. (2025b)]. The latter family in particular has shown that 3D generative priors can complete hidden geometry that observation-driven methods cannot. These systems remain cascaded: an external module predicts poses or image-aligned representations and the 3D generator only completes the result, propagating errors across stages and preventing joint optimization of a single 3D hypothesis that explains all input views.

In this paper, we invert this pipeline: instead of using a generative prior to complete the output of a feed-forward reconstructor, we treat the 3D generative prior itself as the primary reasoning mechanism for sparse-view reconstruction. We propose GenSfM, an end-to-end framework that formulates joint recovery of complete object structure and per-view camera motion as a single conditional inference problem in a native 3D diffusion model, as shown in Fig. 1. The diffusion prior operates directly on a native 3D representation throughout inference, simultaneously denoising shape and per-view pose under joint self-attention. This grounds the generated object in the observed views while using object-level regularities to infer unobserved geometry.

Realizing this formulation requires a single diffusion transformer that jointly denoises a shared 3D shape with a per-view pose latent bound to its input image, while keeping the per-view pose-token overhead small as views are added. We adopt CUPID’s [Huang et al. (2025)] 3D-native UV-volume pose tokenization, but compress each view’s pose latent to a compact token grid, since the dense volume over-parameterizes a low-DoF perspective projection. A learned view embedding tags each view’s pose latent and image tokens, binding pose to its source image. Since neither stream natively carries cross-view information, we prepend a small set of register tokens to the shape stream as a shared channel for all views to communicate through self-attention.

Instead of relying on back-projection to recover surface texture like feed-forward methods [(Wang et al., 2024)], we add a second stage of native 3D refinement and texturing [(Xiang et al., 2025)] so that hidden regions stay coherent with the observed views. We design a pose-aware fine stage that, using the cameras predicted in the coarse stage, projects every active voxel into the input views and conditions denoising on per-voxel semantic and texture features sampled and averaged across views.

On the Toys4k [Stojanov et al. (2021)] and GSO [Downs et al. (2022)] sparse-view object benchmarks under uncalibrated 4-view inputs, GenSfM improves novel-view PSNR by 3.2–4.5 dB, reduces median Chamfer distance by 2.8–3.8×, and lifts F@.01 from 0.56 to 0.83 on Toys4k over the strong native-3D generation baseline TRELLIS-M [Xiang et al. (2025)], while recovering input-view camera poses to over 96% Acc@5^∘ (a 5× rotation-error reduction over the strongest pose baseline VGGT [Wang et al. (2025)]) without requiring known intrinsics. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose GenSfM, a joint native-3D architecture that recasts a diffusion model from a post-hoc completion module into the primary inference mechanism for joint sparse-view structure and motion recovery, eliminating any external feed-forward reconstruction backbone.

  • •

    A 3D-native multi-view pose tokenization that places per-view UV-volume pose latents and the shape latent in a single multi-modal sequence, jointly denoised by a diffusion transformer under shared self-attention.

  • •

    A pose-aware fine stage that, with cameras recovered from the coarse stage, anchors semantic and texture features at every active voxel and averages them across views, sharpening surface detail beyond global, pose-agnostic conditioning.

    • 2 Related Work

    Sparse-view object reconstruction must jointly answer two coupled questions: what is the 3D object, and where was each view taken from? What requires both visible and hidden object structure, while where requires the camera motion relating the input views. Existing methods typically excel on one side or address the two with separate models stacked in series (Tab. 1).

    Feed-forward pose and 3D reconstruction.

    Pose-centric approaches [Zhang et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2023); Sinha et al. (2023); Zhang et al. (2024a)] target the where side, regressing relative camera motion under limited overlap and pose ambiguity, but leave what largely untouched. More general feed-forward reconstructors [Wang et al. (2024); Leroy et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025)] predict dense pointmaps, correspondences, and camera parameters jointly, addressing camera motion and visible geometry; hidden geometry, however, is recovered only indirectly through learned priors.

    Native 3D generation.

    Native 3D generators trained on large 3D corpora [Deitke et al. (2023)], such as TripoSR [Tochilkin et al. (2024)], TRELLIS[Xiang et al. (2025)], and Hunyuan3D [Zhao et al. (2025b)], are strong on what: complete object structure is modeled explicitly and hidden geometry is hallucinated from the prior. They do not target where: camera motion is typically assumed and only weakly encoded through cross-attention, so applied directly to uncalibrated sparse views they can produce plausible but misaligned geometry.

    View-based generative SfM.

    View-based generative SfM [Zhao et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2024b); Xu et al. (2024a); Zhao and Tulsiani (2024)] casts what and where as a joint generative problem in view space; DiffusionSfM, for instance, diffuses ray origins and endpoints to recover per-view geometry and camera motion jointly. Because diffusion operates over view-based quantities (rays, pointmaps, depths), hidden what is recovered only insofar as it can be back-projected from individual views.

    Reconstruction with 3D generative priors.

    Reconstruct-then-generate pipelines [Ardelean et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026); Chang et al. (2025); Team et al. (2025); Siddiqui et al. (2026); Yao et al. (2025)] couple feed-forward reconstruction with native 3D generators: e.g., ReconViaGen [Chang et al. (2025)] injects VGGT [Wang et al. (2025)] geometry tokens into a 3D generator. These pipelines recover hidden geometry through the generative prior while grounding camera motion and visible structure with feed-forward geometry, but solve what and where in separate stages, so errors from the reconstruction backbone propagate into a 3D hypothesis that need not remain coherent with all input views.

    3 Preliminaries

    Overview.
