    Given N uncalibrated multi-view images I={Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N of an object O, our goal is to recover the holistic 3D structure and per-view camera poses ℙ={Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N as a coarse-to-fine generative problem in a native 3D diffusion model. We build on two native 3D generators reviewed below: TRELLIS[Xiang et al. (2025)] provides the two-stage backbone and CFM objective we inherit, and CUPID[Huang et al. (2025)] contributes the 3D-native single-image pose tokenization we lift to multi-view.

    Coarse-to-fine 3D generation.

    Our backbone is TRELLIS[Xiang et al. (2025)], which generates a 3D object in two coarse-to-fine stages under a shared conditional flow matching [Lipman et al. (2022)] (CFM) objective. The first stage produces a sparse-structure (SS) latent zˢ on a 16³ grid, decoded to a 64³ occupancy grid whose active voxels define positions {xⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L. The second stage produces the structured-latent (SLat) set S={xⱼ,fⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L with per-voxel features fⱼ, which separate decoders [Shen et al. (2023); Kerbl et al. (2023)] map to 3D Gaussians, a radiance field, or a mesh. Both stages train with

    L_CFM(φ)=𝔼_t,z₀,ε∥v_φ(zₜ,I,t)-(ε-z₀)∥₂²,

    		(1)

    where zₜ=(1-t)z₀+t ε is the noisy latent at t∈[0,1] for clean target z₀ (zˢ for SS, {fⱼ} for SLat) and noise ε∼ℕ(0,I); v_φ is the DiT velocity prediction conditioned on I.

    3D-native pose representation.

    Our pose tokenization derives from CUPID[Huang et al. (2025)], which extends TRELLIS’s SS stage to jointly recover the camera pose for a single input image: the SS latent gains channels encoding per-voxel UV coordinates, decoded to a 64³ UV volume that gives each active voxel’s projection uⱼ∈[0,1]². The 3×4 projection matrix P is thus a dense 3D-2D field on the active voxels, recovered from the per-voxel correspondences {xⱼ,uⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L by Direct Linear Transform (DLT) least-squares [(Abdel-Aziz et al., 2015)]:

    P^*=\argmin_P∑ⱼ₌₁^L∥π(P,xⱼ)-uⱼ∥²,

    		(2)

    where π is the perspective projection. Finally, camera intrinsic K and extrinsic [R|t] are recovered from P^* via RQ decomposition.

    4 Method

    We frame this joint recovery as a coarse-to-fine generative problem in the latent space of a native 3D diffusion model (Fig. 2). Building on TRELLIS’s two-stage architecture and CUPID’s 3D-native pose representation (Sec. 3), Sec. 4.1 jointly generates 3D structure and multi-view poses with a multi-modal DiT over per-view pose tokens, and Sec. 4.2 refines geometry and appearance via per-voxel pose-sampled image conditioning.

    4.1 3D structure and pose recovery from multi-view images

    The coarse stage casts joint recovery of 3D structure and per-view camera poses as a single denoising problem: each camera is encoded as a per-view 3D-native pose token, and shape and pose are denoised jointly by a multi-modal DiT with joint self-attention over both streams.

    Tokenizing multi-view camera poses.

    For each view i, every active voxel xⱼ projects to u_j,i=π(Pᵢ,xⱼ), yielding a UV volume uᵢ∈[0,1]^2×64³. A shared pose VAE compresses each uᵢ into a latent grid zᵖᵢ∈ℝ^c×r×r×r with c=8,r=4. To represent multiple input views, we form a unified token sequence with the shape latent zˢ followed by the per-view pose latents {zᵖᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N — in contrast to CUPID[(Huang et al., 2025)], whose channel-wise concatenation of shape and pose into a single SS latent is restricted to one view. We choose r=4 (vs CUPID’s r=16), giving 64× fewer tokens per pose at negligible accuracy cost since the UV volume is heavily over-parameterized for a low-DoF projection. At inference, the pose VAE decodes each generated zᵖᵢ back to a UV volume, from which Pᵢ^* is recovered by solving Eq. 2. See App. A.3 for details.

    Multi-view conditioned shape-pose DiT.

    A shared transformer backbone denoises shape and pose jointly, with stream-specific projections and grid-aligned positional embeddings. Learnable register tokens zʳ are prepended to the shape stream to capture global context. We extend the CFM interpolation of Eq. 1 to a shape timestep tˢ∈[0,1] and per-view pose timesteps tᵖ∈[0,1]^N, giving z₀=[zˢ; zᵖ] and zₜ=[zₜˢ; zₜᵖ]. Stream-specific in-projections then lift each noisy latent to the shared transformer width, where positional and view embeddings are added in to form the layer-0 hidden state of the DiT:

    h₀=[ zʳ; Wᵢₙˢ zₜˢ+eˢ; Wᵢₙᵖ zₜᵖ+eᵖ+eᵛ ],

    		(3)

    where eˢ,eᵖ are absolute 3D PEs over the 16³ and 4³ grids that anchor each stream to its native voxel layout, and eᵛ is a per-view ID embedding shared between each pose latent and its source view’s image-condition tokens (Eq. 6), binding each pose to its view through cross-attention. We then stack L DiT blocks; each block injects the multi-view condition tokens z^I={z^Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N,

    hₗ₊₁=CrossAttn (Q(hₗ), K(z^I), V(z^I)),

    		(4)

    where Q,K,V are the query/key/value projections, applied jointly over all N views without per-view masking. Each block also runs a joint self-attention over the entire sequence and a feed-forward sub-layer, both modulated by per-modality AdaLN values conditioned on tˢ for shape tokens and on tᵖᵢ for view-i pose tokens. After the final block, stream-specific out-projections read out the velocities (register outputs are discarded), v_φ(zₜ,z^I,tˢ,tᵖ)=[ Wₒᵤₜˢ h_Lˢ; Wₒᵤₜᵖ h_Lᵖ ], and the whole network is trained with a stream-wise conditional flow matching loss:

    L_coarse(φ)=𝔼_tˢ, tᵖ, z₀, ε ∥v_φ(zₜ,z^I,tˢ,tᵖ)-(ε-z₀)∥₂².

    		(5)

    Multi-scale enhanced image condition.

    DINOv2 patch features capture rich semantics but are spatially coarse, providing limited cues for the fine appearance and accurate 2D-3D correspondences our coarse stage must recover. We therefore augment them with multi-scale local features extracted by a small convolutional pyramid on the same image: for each view i, the condition tokens are

    z^Iᵢ=(\textscDINOv2(Iᵢ) ⊕ Φˢ_cnn(Iᵢ))+eᵛ,

    		(6)

    where \textscDINOv2(Iᵢ) are the frozen patch tokens, Φˢ_cnn(Iᵢ) stacks features from a 4-level convolutional pyramid where each level patchified to the DINOv2 patch grid and channel-concatenated across levels, ⊕ denotes channel-wise concatenation per token, and eᵛ is the view-tag embedding from Eq. 3. The resulting z^I={z^Iᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N serves as the cross-attention key/value sequence in every DiT block. See App. A.4 for details.

    4.2 Pose-aware generation of fine geometry and appearance

    The fine stage generates geometry and appearance with pose-aware per-voxel image conditioning: each voxel receives a semantic feature from DINOv2 and a texture feature from a multi-scale CNN pyramid, with both features average-pooled over pose-aligned projections across views.

    Pose-aware per-voxel image conditioning.

    TRELLIS’s SLat stage conditions on the input image only through global cross-attention with DINOv2 patch tokens, leaving fine-appearance cues unanchored from any specific voxel and producing blurry surface detail. Once P^* is recovered by the coarse stage (Sec. 4.1), every active voxel xⱼ has a known image projection uⱼ=π(P^*,xⱼ), so image features can be sampled directly per voxel. At each xⱼ we form two complementary features: a semantic feature cˢᵉᵐⱼ from pose-sampled DINOv2 patches re-encoded through the frozen SLat encoder Enc_L (placing it on the same latent manifold as the SLat target fⱼ), and a texture feature cᵗᵉˣⱼ from a multi-scale CNN pyramid Φˡ_cnn that supplies the low-level cues that DINOv2 lacks:

    {cˢᵉᵐⱼ}ⱼ₌₁^L=Enc_L({xⱼ, BilinearInterp(uⱼ, \textscDINOv2(I))}ⱼ₌₁^L),(7)
    cᵗᵉˣⱼ=BilinearInterp(uⱼ, Φˡ_cnn(I)).

    where BilinearInterp denotes bilinear interpolation. We channel-wise concatenate cˢᵉᵐⱼ and cᵗᵉˣⱼ with the noisy voxel feature fⱼᵗ (the SLat target fⱼ noised via Eq. 1) and linearly project to form the per-voxel layer-0 DiT token h₀(xⱼ)=Wˡᵢₙ[ fⱼᵗ ⊕ cˢᵉᵐⱼ ⊕ cᵗᵉˣⱼ ]; the remainder of the DiT follows TRELLIS. See App. A.4 for the visual pyramid architecture.

    Pooling per-voxel features across views.

    With N input views, every active voxel has N pose-aligned projections u_j,i=π(Pᵢ^*,xⱼ). We extend BilinearInterp to per-view sampling followed by averaging, BilinearInterp(uⱼ, Φ(I)):=\tfrac1N∑ᵢ₌₁^NBilinearInterp(u_j,i, Φ(Iᵢ)), so Eq. 7 applies unchanged with I replaced by I. The cross-attention condition is likewise the per-view mean of DINOv2 patch tokens. The mean operator itself is parameter-free and view-count-agnostic; the model in this work is trained with N=4.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Experimental Setup

    Datasets.

    We train our model on four public 3D-asset datasets: Objaverse-XL [Deitke et al. (2023)] (GitHub and Sketchfab partitions), HSSD [Khanna et al. (2024)], 3D-FUTURE [Fu et al. (2021)], and ABO [Collins et al. (2022)]. After TRELLIS’s aesthetic filter (≥4.5), about 430K instances remain. Each is rendered following TRELLIS’s protocol, with 24 condition views at 1024×1024 from cameras uniformly sampled on the upper hemisphere. We evaluate on two held-out test sets, Toys4k [Stojanov et al. (2021)] (synthetic) and GSO [Downs et al. (2022)] (real-captured), neither overlapping the training corpus.

    Evaluation protocol.

    We assess photometric fidelity, 3D geometry, and camera-pose accuracy. Each test set uses its first 400 objects with two disjoint 4-view sets, {0,6,12,18} and {3,9,15,21}, yielding 800 object–viewset instances for aggregation. As baselines fall into three capability families, we apply the most suitable evaluation protocol to each: (i) least squares on predicted vs ground-truth input-view pointmaps for feed-forward reconstruction, tight only with accurate predicted geometry and poses; (ii) similarity ICP on sampled point clouds for 3D generation; and (iii) gauge-invariant pairwise relative-pose comparison on unordered input-view pairs for pose-predicting methods. GenSfM is reevaluated under each applicable protocol; comparisons are restricted to methods sharing a table and protocol. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [Zhang et al. (2018)] on 512×512 novel views at the 8 held-out condition-view indices {2,4,8,10,14,16,20,22}; bidirectional Chamfer Distance (CD; reported as the median across objects, since a few severe failures dominate the mean) and F-scores at τ∈{0.01, 0.05}; and Relative Rotation Error (RRE) with Acc@{5^∘,15^∘}, Relative Translation Error (RTE), and mean absolute FOV error (RFOV; only for methods that predict intrinsics). See App. A.1 for the full alignment protocol and App. A.2 for the pose metric definitions.

    Baseline methods.

    We compare against a representative set of multi-view image-to-3D baselines: (a) TRELLIS-S[Xiang et al. (2025)]: TRELLIS run as a single-image generator on each input view independently, with the mean over the four outputs reported; (b) TRELLIS-M[Xiang et al. (2025)]: TRELLIS with multi-view input in stochastic mode, where each denoising step is conditioned on one randomly chosen input view; (c) SAM 3D[Team et al. (2025)]: a single-image-to-3D generator run once per input view, with the mean over the four outputs reported; (d) FreeSplatter[Xu et al. (2024b)]: predicts per-view pixel-aligned 3D Gaussians together with input camera parameters in a pose-free setting; (e) LucidFusion[He et al. (2025)]: predicts per-view relative coordinate maps that are fused into a 3D Gaussian output; (f) ReconViaGen[Chang et al. (2025)]: combines feed-forward reconstruction with generative refinement, using VGGT-derived geometry tokens to condition a 3D generator; (g) VGGT[Wang et al. (2025)]: a transformer that jointly regresses per-view pointmaps and camera extrinsics/intrinsics from uncalibrated images. Our table appear in three families: 3D generation (a,b,c,f), feed-forward reconstruction (d,e,f), and pose prediction (d,f,g).

    5.2 Main Results

    Comparison with feed-forward reconstruction methods.

    Tab. 2 and Fig. 3 compare against feed-forward reconstruction baselines under input-view pointmap LSQ alignment. GenSfM outperforms every baseline on every metric and on both datasets, with the gap widening at the strict F@.01 threshold and qualitatively in the form of alignment artifacts and surface noise. Feed-forward methods compound any disagreement between their predicted geometry and predicted poses, while a generative 3D-native model refines it away.

    Comparison with 3D generation methods.

    Tab. 3 and Fig. 4 compare against 3D generation models that produce a canonical, pose-free output, under similarity-ICP alignment. GenSfM leads on every metric, with the largest margins on the strict-threshold geometry metrics (F@.01, CD-med). Pose-free baselines hallucinate plausible but mismatched detail on unseen sides; the two strong multi-view baselines (TRELLIS-M’s stochastic per-step view conditioning and ReconViaGen’s feed-forward reconstruction with generative refinement) still trail GenSfM by large margins, indicating the gain comes from joint shape–pose denoising rather than late-stage view sampling.

    Pose prediction accuracy.

    Tab. 4 reports camera-pose accuracy on baselines that predict input-view extrinsics. GenSfM achieves substantially lower rotation and translation errors, with Acc.@5^∘ saturating; baselines commonly fail on symmetric objects whose orientation depends on low-level visual cues. Our model also recovers intrinsics accurately (known-intrinsics row shown for reference); VGGT, not trained on varying-FOV synthetic data, incurs large RFOV despite strong extrinsics, whereas GenSfM keeps RFOV under 3^∘ on both datasets while saturating Acc.@5^∘. Thus, RFOV confirms reliable intrinsic recovery under varying FOV, but its margin over VGGT also reflects training-distribution coverage, not architecture alone.

    5.3 Ablation Study

    We ablate each design choice on Toys4k in Tab. 5, with rows added cumulatively. In Stage 1, full cross-attention enables cross-view information sharing and improves all metrics; visual feature conditioning sharpens photometric fidelity and pose accuracy with only marginal geometry gains, suggesting appearance cues primarily help rendering and pose grounding; shared register tokens aggregate global information and contribute most to pose accuracy and the strict F@.01 threshold. In Stage 2, a fine decoder trained natively on multi-view data sharpens photometric fidelity, while 3D geometry is already saturated. The decoder swap leaves raw coarse-stage cameras unchanged but shifts geometry-aligned pose metrics because their similarity fit depends on the final pointmap. Fig. 5 corroborates these trends qualitatively: surface details (e.g., the screwdriver cap, the snake’s head) sharpen left-to-right and the full model best matches GT.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented GenSfM, which recasts a native 3D diffusion model as the primary inference mechanism for sparse-view object reconstruction, jointly denoising shape and per-view camera poses in a single multi-modal diffusion transformer. Three choices keep the formulation tractable: a UV-volume pose latent compressed to a compact token grid, a unified multi-modal sequence that places shape and per-view pose tokens in a single self-attention, and a pose-aware fine stage that conditions each voxel on features sampled at its pose-aligned image projection. On Toys4k and GSO, GenSfM outperforms feed-forward, 3D-generation, and pose-prediction baselines on photometric, geometric, and pose metrics simultaneously, recovering both extrinsics and intrinsics to high accuracy without any external pose estimator or post-hoc optimization.

    Limitations and future work.

    Our results are restricted to object-centric inputs at N=4; extending to larger view counts, scene-level inputs, and in-the-wild captures with looser segmentation is a natural next step. Under distribution shift, large pose/calibration errors may misregister fine-stage image features, degrading local refinement while the coarse 3D prior preserves global completion. The model also inherits the object distribution and resolution limits of its TRELLIS backbone, so scaling the underlying generator should directly improve sparse-view recovery.

    Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding

    This work is partially supported by funding and computing resources provided by the HKU-Shanghai Intelligent Computing Research Center. This work was supported by the General Research Fund of the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong under Grant No. 17200725 and the JC STEM Lab funded by The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Technical appendices and supplementary material

    A.1 Alignment protocol

    Our baselines differ in what they natively output (input-view pointmaps, canonical pose-free 3D, or input-camera poses), so a single shared alignment would unfairly discard the structure each method already provides. We therefore align each prediction with the protocol best matched to its output family before evaluating, and GenSfM is evaluated under each applicable family using that family’s protocol so all comparisons within a table are like-for-like.

    Input-view pointmap least squares (Table 2).

    This protocol applies to feed-forward reconstruction methods (LucidFusion, FreeSplatter, ReconViaGen), which already place geometry in a noisy estimate of the input-camera frame. For each input view, we back-project the per-pixel predicted depth at the predicted camera into 3D, alpha-mask the result, randomly subsample to at most 50K points per view, and pair it with the GT pointmap obtained by back-projecting GT depth at the GT camera. Stacking the per-view pairs with equal aggregate weight per view yields one set of 3D-to-3D correspondences per object, which we fit with a closed-form Umeyama similarity [(Umeyama, 2002)]. The resulting transform is applied once to the full predicted 3D before all photometric and geometric evaluation; we log the per-object LSQ residual as an alignment-fidelity diagnostic. Note that this protocol exercises both halves of feed-forward reconstruction: the matched correspondences require the predicted geometry to align with the predicted cameras, so a method with weak geometry, weak pose recovery, or any mismatch between the two will produce noisy correspondences and a loose Umeyama fit, inflating all downstream metrics.

    Similarity ICP (Table 3).

    This protocol applies to 3D generation methods (TRELLIS-S, TRELLIS-M, SAM 3D), which output a canonical pose-free 3D, and to GenSfM when evaluated under the same family. To obtain the prediction-side point cloud uniformly across output formats (whether the prediction is a mesh or a set of 3D Gaussians), we render depth from a set of orbiting random views around the prediction and back-project the depth maps into 3D, which yields a well-covered surface point cloud without surface-sampling biases specific to the underlying representation. The GT-side cloud is sampled directly on the GT mesh surface. We initialize alignment by sweeping the 24 orientation-preserving signed axis permutations of the PCA-aligned bounding box and keep the candidate with the lowest post-ICP residual; we then refine with similarity ICP and use the resulting transform to map the prediction into the GT frame for evaluation.

    A.2 Pose metric protocol

    Pose metric definitions.

    Different pose-predicting baselines fix their world frame in different ways (some anchor to the first input view, some to an internal canonical frame, others through their own internal similarity fit), so absolute predicted extrinsics cannot be directly compared to GT extrinsics. To bypass this gauge ambiguity entirely, all metrics in Table 4 are computed on unordered pairs of input views: for each pair, the relative pose between the two views cancels any global rotation, translation, and scale that affects all views jointly, leaving only the camera geometry intrinsic to the pair. We adopt this pairwise form uniformly for both rotation and translation rather than anchoring to one reference view, which would entangle every error with the chosen anchor. For each object, we average each metric over the N(N-1)/2 unordered pairs and then average across objects. Relative Rotation Error (RRE) is the geodesic angle (in degrees) between the predicted and GT relative rotations of the pair; Acc.@5^∘ / Acc.@15^∘ is the fraction of pairs whose RRE falls below the corresponding threshold; Relative Translation Error (RTE) is the angular error (in degrees) between the predicted and GT relative-translation directions, an angular form chosen because absolute translation magnitude is itself gauge-dependent (a global similarity scale can be reabsorbed by any consistent rescaling of all camera centers); and Field-of-View Error (RFOV) is the mean absolute difference (in degrees) between predicted and GT FOV, computed directly on intrinsics without any pose alignment, since intrinsics are independent of the world frame. To score baselines with a coarse front/back chirality ambiguity on geometric correctness rather than chirality alone, all angular metrics (RRE, Acc.@{5^∘,15^∘}, RTE) are read off after collapsing R_predR_gt^⊤ under the diag(±1,±1,-1) sign-flip equivalence class. The same rule is applied uniformly to all methods, including ours, to compare geometric recovery under a shared front/back equivalence. Chirality remains relevant for camera-dependent applications, so we explicitly note that this metric does not assess that failure mode.

    A.3 Pose VAE

    Architecture and training.

    The pose VAE is a 3D-convolutional encoder–decoder over a 64³ voxel grid with a deliberately aggressive bottleneck: four 2× spatial downsamples compress the input into a 4³ token grid with 8 channels per token. This compression is feasible because each per-voxel target is a smooth function of voxel position and a low-DoF camera, so the latent does not need to absorb high-frequency content. Per voxel the encoder receives three input channels (a binary in-frustum indicator plus the two pixel coordinates obtained by projecting the voxel center under the input camera), and the decoder emits the same three channels through a classification head (visibility mask) and a regression head (pixel UV).

    We use a dice loss on the visibility classifier and an L1 loss on the UV regression, with a small KL weight (10⁻³) so the latent stays close to a standard Gaussian for the downstream diffusion stage. The training distribution matches inference: each minibatch sample takes a real camera pose from the multi-view renders of a sampled training object and projects it on the fly into the 64³ voxel grid. We optimize for 1M steps with AdamW (lr 3×10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻³) on a cosine schedule.

    Out-of-frame voxels.

    Voxel centers can project outside the input image. We handle this by clamping target UVs to [0,1]² rather than dropping out-of-frame voxels, keeping the decoder output well-defined everywhere. The visibility channel encodes the same in-/out-of-frame information as a binary indicator with a small 1% inset margin (0.01≤u,v≤0.99); the inference DLT solve uses this channel to restrict to in-frustum voxels, so saturated boundary UVs never contaminate the recovered pose. The UV reconstruction loss is applied uniformly to all voxels rather than only the in-frustum subset, keeping saturated-boundary regions consistent between encoder and decoder.

    Pose autoencoding accuracy.

    Table 6 reports the autoencoding fidelity of the trained pose VAE on the Toys4k held-out split, sweeping the latent spatial resolution. We encode each held-out 64³ ground-truth UV volume to the chosen latent grid, decode back, and recover camera pose via a DLT solve over in-frustum voxels. UV Dist. is the per-voxel L2 distance in normalized image coordinates; RRE, RTE, and RFOV are the standard rotation, translation-direction, and FOV errors in degrees. All three latent resolutions deliver near-identical pose accuracy (within a few hundredths of a degree on RRE/RTE/RFOV), and even the worst row stays an order of magnitude below the downstream pose-prediction residuals in Table 4, so the latent is not the bottleneck on overall pose accuracy. We adopt the 4³ latent in the main paper as the most compute-efficient operating point, since the larger grids carry 8× and 64× more tokens at no measurable pose gain.

    A.4 Image conditioning across stages

    Coarse stage: dual-stream encoder and token fusion.

    Each view is encoded by two complementary streams that fuse into a single per-view token sequence for the coarse DiT to cross-attend to. A frozen DINOv2-L/14 with registers at 518×518 produces 1374 tokens per view (CLS + 4 registers + a 37×37 patch grid) at 1024 channels, supplying object-level semantics. In parallel, a lightweight 4-level CNN at 296×296 (5×5 convolutions, strides {1,2,2,2}, output channels [6,6,6,8]) is patchified down to the same 37×37 grid, with per-token contributions [384,96,24,8] channel-concatenating into a 512-dim local-texture feature. We append the 512 local channels onto the 1024 semantic channels at every patch token (non-patch tokens zero-pad on the local side), giving a uniform per-token width of 1536 and a cross-attention key/value of length N×1374. The two streams are deliberately complementary: semantic anchors pose to image content, while local texture restores the pixel-faithful appearance cues the semantic encoder has discarded, letting cross-attention recover accurate cameras without polluting the joint self-attention with raw image tokens.

    Fine stage: visual pyramid and per-voxel projection.

    The fine stage refines up to L≤32,768 active voxels at 64³ under the cameras already recovered by the coarse stage. Cross-attending every voxel to thousands of image tokens per view is intractable, so we replace cross-attention with per-voxel pixel-aligned feature sampling: each voxel projects to u_j,i in view i under the predicted camera, and visual features are bilinearly sampled at that pixel. The visual encoder is a ConvNeXt-style pyramid run once per view at 256×256: four stages, each one ConvNeXt block with a 7×7 depthwise kernel at internal width 32, with a 2× downsample between stages. Each stage exposes a 4-channel tap (LayerNorm + 1×1 Conv); the four taps sampled at u_j,i and channel-concatenated yield a 16-channel multi-scale texture feature cᵗᵉˣⱼ. We pair it with an 8-channel semantic feature cˢᵉᵐⱼ: the coarse-stage DINOv2 patch tokens (reused, no extra DINOv2 pass) are bilinearly sampled at the same per-voxel projection and re-encoded through the frozen SLat encoder, placing them on the SLat target’s latent manifold and giving a compact 24-channel per-voxel conditioning vector. This keeps fine-stage cost proportional to active voxels rather than view tokens, while the multi-scale taps let each voxel combine coarse contour cues with fine local texture without inflating the per-voxel width.

    A.5 Implementation details

    Pose VAE training.

    The pose VAE of App. A.3 is trained for 1M steps on 8 H200 GPUs with batch size 4 per GPU, using AdamW (lr 3×10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻³) under a cosine schedule with 1000 warmup steps decaying to 10⁻⁵, EMA 0.9999, and FP16 mixed precision. The same recipe trains the 4³, 8³, and 16³ latent variants of Tab. 6.

    Coarse-stage shape-pose DiT training.

    The coarse stage is fine-tuned for 1M steps on 8 H200 GPUs at global batch size 64 (8 per GPU, split into two gradient-accumulation microbatches), initialized from a prior single-view coarse-stage checkpoint of ours (itself from the pretrained TRELLIS-image-large SS DiT). Each instance contributes N=4 random condition views uniformly sampled from the 24 rendered views of the object; each input image is crop-resized at a 1.2× tightness ratio around the alpha-mask bounding box and bilinearly resampled to 518×518 for the frozen DINOv2 ViT-L/14-with-registers encoder. The DiT operates on 4096 shape, 256 pose, and 128 shared register tokens, with cross-attention over N×1374=5496 image-condition tokens augmented by the convolutional pyramid of Eq. 6. We use AdamW (lr 10⁻⁴, no weight decay), CFG dropout 0.1, the same cosine schedule and EMA as above, and timesteps drawn from a logit-normal distribution with mean 1.0 and std 1.0 (σ_\min=10⁻⁵). At each step we randomly choose between two timestep-coupling modes: with probability 0.8, the shape stream and all pose streams share a single timestep; with probability 0.2, each stream draws an independent timestep. The shared mode dominates so the model stays well-calibrated to the synchronized inference schedule, while the per-pose mode supplies enough timestep diversity that the per-modality AdaLN modulation actually learns to handle independent noise levels.

    Fine-stage SLat DiT training.

    The fine stage is fine-tuned independently for 1M steps on 4 H200 GPUs at global batch size 32 (8 per GPU), initialized from TRELLIS’s pretrained SLat DiT checkpoint. It denoises up to L≤32,768 active voxels at 64³; ground-truth cameras and occupancy are used during training so the fine stage learns from clean projections. Each instance again contributes N=4 random condition views, with per-voxel features pooled across views by mean (16-channel ConvNeXt-pyramid texture and 8-channel SLat-encoded semantic) and the cross-attention condition the per-view mean of DINOv2 patches. We use AdamW (lr 10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻³), CFG dropout 0.1, and the same cosine schedule and logit-normal timestep distribution as the coarse stage.

    Inference.

    The coarse stage runs a 25-step flow-Euler sampler over the joint shape-pose sequence at classifier-free guidance strength 7.5, active on the noise interval t∈[0.5,1.0] with a guidance time-rescale factor of 3.0[Esser et al. (2024)]. We then decode each per-view pose latent through the pose VAE and recover Pᵢ^* by the DLT solve of Eq. 2. The fine stage runs a 25-step flow-Euler sampler with sequential multi-view fusion at CFG strength 3.0 on the same [0.5,1.0] interval and rescale factor, conditioned on the recovered cameras and on the per-voxel pose-sampled features of Eq. 7.

    A.6 Broader impacts

    GenSfM produces a 3D representation of an object from a few uncalibrated images, jointly recovering shape and camera. The most direct positive applications are in robotics (object-level scene understanding from a small number of viewpoints), augmented and virtual reality (capturing personal items as 3D assets for placement in virtual environments), and content creation (3D meshes from reference photos as a starting point for downstream editing). Joint recovery of camera intrinsics and extrinsics with shape removes the calibration friction that has limited deployment of feed-forward reconstruction methods in casually-captured settings.

    The negative considerations are those shared with image-conditioned 3D generation more broadly: the resulting 3D models could be used to fabricate convincing 3D content of real-world objects, including objects belonging to others, without their consent; coupled with downstream rendering pipelines, this could enable image-only digital reproduction at a scale that traditional photogrammetry has not previously allowed. The model is trained only on common, non-sensitive object categories from public 3D-asset datasets, and recovery quality degrades on out-of-distribution categories, which provides a partial natural mitigation. Released model checkpoints will carry an attribution requirement and an acceptable-use note as the safeguard accompanying our open release.

item.title: 3D 风格化别把颜色和纹理一起搬：DiDE 把两者解耦，可以只换配色、保留材质细节 ｜ DiDE: Direct Injection with Color-Texture DEcoupling for 3D Stylization
item.description:
一句话：现有「全有或全无」的迁移方式没法单独调色；解耦后按风格需求分别注入。

要点：

  • 背景：基于 rectified flow 的图生 3D 模型已经能生成高质量资产，随之出现一批「训练无关」的风格化方法，把参考图的视觉属性迁移到生成资产上
  • 现有方法的通病是「全有或全无」：颜色与纹理被联合迁移，没有任何机制能分别控制——作者把这个限制形式化为 Disentangled 3D Stylization 问题
  • DiDE 用「直接注入 + 颜色/纹理解耦」来解决：颜色与纹理作为两条可控通道分别作用到 3D 资产上

为什么值得看：关卡与角色经常需要「同一套模型、换一套配色」——美术叫它调色板复用。如果风格迁移能把颜色与纹理拆开，就等于让 AI 生成也支持这种最常用的资产复用方式，而不是每次都重生成。

中文摘要：基于 rectified flow 的图像生成 3D 模型已经能产出高保真资产，随之出现一类「训练无关」的风格化做法：把参考图的视觉属性迁移到生成好的 3D 资产上。但现有方法采取的是全有或全无的策略——颜色与纹理被联合迁移，没有机制能独立控制二者，作者把这个限制形式化为 Disentangled 3D Stylization 问题。DiDE 用「直接注入 + 颜色纹理解耦」来应对：颜色与纹理作为两条可分别控制的通道作用于 3D 资产，从而支持「只换配色、保留材质细节」或反之。对需要调色板复用与批量变体的资产管线，这是最贴近美术工作方式的控制粒度。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-11-01

DiDE:Direct Injection with Color-Texture DEcoupling for 3D Stylization

Abstract

Recent advances in rectified flow-based image-to-3D generative models have enabled high-fidelity 3D asset generation. Building on this, a growing line of work has exploited these strong 3D priors for training-free stylization, transferring visual attributes from a reference image onto a generated 3D asset. However, existing methods enforce an all-or-nothing paradigm: color and texture are transferred jointly, with no mechanism to control them independently — a limitation we formalize as Disentangled 3D Stylization (Disen3D). To address this, we propose DiDE, the first training-free framework for Disen3D. Key to our approach is the observation that the structured latent space of image-to-3D models is overcomplete with respect to texture: texture information occupies only a small subset of the style-significant channels, leaving a free subspace available for independent color encoding. DiDE exploits this via a channel partition mechanism that processes a content image, a texture reference, and a color reference through dedicated branches and composes both style signals interference-free at every self-attention layer, preserving content geometry throughout. Experiments on Disen3D-Bench, our newly collected multi-reference benchmark, show that DiDE consistently outperforms 2D and 3D stylization baselines in color fidelity, texture transfer, and content preservation.

1 Introduction

Generative models for 3D asset creation have witnessed significant advancements  [Team (2024); Team (2025a); Xiang et al. (2025a)], facilitating their widespread adoption across diverse domains, including entertainment [Xu et al. (2024)], robotics [Ke et al. (2024)] and healthcare [Khader et al. (2023)]. In particular, recent rectified flow-based approaches [Lipman et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023); Team (2025b)], exemplified by TRELLIS [Xiang et al. (2025a); Xiang et al. (2025b)], have demonstrated the ability to generate high-fidelity 3D objects by jointly modeling sparse structural representations and appearance features within a unified latent space, while explicitly disentangling geometric structures from appearance attributes. Beyond 3D asset generation, a growing line of work has extended generative models to support 3D stylization[Hu et al. (2026); Qu et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026)] — the task of transferring stylistic attributes from a reference image onto a generated 3D asset. By conditioning generation on a style reference, these methods allow the produced asset to inherit visual properties such as surface material, color palette, and structural texture, while remaining semantically aligned with a content image. This capability carries significant practical value: a single base geometry can be re-stylized for different artistic contexts, production pipelines, or brand identities without requiring manual re-authoring. Although existing stylized 3D generation methods [Qu et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026)] have achieved promising results, they still exhibit a critical limitation: style attributes (such as texture and color) cannot be controlled independently, which severely restricts artistic freedom in practice.

In practice, content creators rarely want to adopt a single reference style. Instead, they often wish to selectively borrow specific components while preserving the core of their own artistic vision [Epstein et al. (2023); Hertzmann (2022)]. Color palettes play an essential role in this process: they are carefully designed to convey specific emotions or maintain brand consistency, and a creator may wish to preserve their own color scheme while borrowing surface texture from a reference. Equally, one might want to adopt the rough, weathered texture of aged stone from one reference while keeping the warm tones of an entirely different palette. These two attributes — color and texture — are visually and semantically distinct, yet current 3D stylization approaches [Hu et al. (2026); Qu et al. (2025)] enforce an all-or-nothing paradigm: applying a reference style requires accepting all its visual attributes simultaneously, which severely restricts artistic freedom and practical applicability. To the best of our knowledge, only one prior work addresses disentangled stylization in 2D [Qin et al. (2025)], yet it cannot be generalized to 3D, as style embeddings from separate references cannot simply be composed in 3D latent space. This leaves the problem of fine-grained, decoupled 3D stylization entirely open.

To address these limitations, we introduce Disentangled 3D Stylization (Disen3D), which aims to decompose reference styles into independently controllable color and texture attributes, enabling artists to selectively transfer specific style elements while preserving content geometry. We further propose Direct Injection with color-texture DEcoupling (DiDE), the first training-free framework for this task, which takes three inputs — a content image, a texture reference, and a color reference — processed through dedicated branches. To achieve this, We build on prior findings [Qu et al. (2025)] showing that feature channels of image-to-3D models [Xiang et al. (2025b)] can be decomposed into style- and content-significant subsets, with one branch dedicated to style and another to content. However, directly extending this framework with an additional branch for color is non-trivial: combining two style branches through the same attention pathway leads to feature interference, making disentangled control of texture and color difficult. To address this problem, we further show that texture information occupies only a subset of the style-significant channels, leaving additional feature capacity available for encoding an independent color attribute. We allocate those informative channels from the texture branch, while populating the remaining free channels with color features from a separate color reference branch. Finally, this partition is applied at every self-attention layer of the texture generation stage, enabling composable, interference-free injection of texture and color while preserving full 3D consistency.

Since no existing method addresses the disentangled stylization problem directly in 3D, we evaluate against complementary baselines on our proposed Disen3D-Bench benchmark: SADis [Qin et al. (2025)], the only prior work on color-texture disentanglement but operating in 2D, and StyleSculptor [Qu et al. (2025)] and MorphAny3D [Sun et al. (2026)], which perform 3D stylization but without attribute disentanglement. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce Disentangled 3D Stylization (Disen3D), a novel problem formulation that decomposes reference styles into independently controllable color and texture attributes, which is neglected in prior works.

  • •

    We are the first to identify and exploit the overcomplete nature of the structured latent space in image-to-3D models, demonstrating that texture information saturates only a small subset of channels, leaving a free subspace available for independent color and texture injection.

  • •

    We present Direct Inject with color-texture DEcoupling (DiDE), the first tuning-free color-texture disentanglement framework for 3D stylization, which exploits this overcomplete structure via a channel partition mechanism to enable composable, interference-free style control while preserving content geometry.

  • •

    Experimental results demonstrate that DiDE consistently outperforms existing 2D and 3D stylization baselines in color fidelity, texture transfer, and content preservation on our new collected multi-reference disentangled 3D stylization benchmark Disen3D-Bench.

    • 2 Related Work

    3D Generative Models. Two dominant paradigms have been established for high-quality 3D asset generation. The first focuses on distilling useful priors from pretrained 2D generative models into feed-forward 3D reconstruction algorithms. They either fine-tune 2D models to synthesize multi-view images [Shi et al. (2024); Shriram et al. (2025); Yu et al. (2025)], which are further reconstructed into 3D assets via techniques such as 3D Gaussian splatting [Kerbl et al. (2023)]; or directly guides 3D optimization through gradient signals from 2D diffusion models [Poole et al. (2023)]. Despite their effectiveness, they lack an explicit latent 3D space to achieve fine-grained structural control. To overcome this limitation, the second paradigm pursues unified native 3D generative models trained from scratch. Inspired by the remarkable success of diffusion models in visual synthesis [Ho et al. (2020); Khachatryan et al. (2023); Rombach et al. (2022)], recent methods [Cheng et al. (2023); Ren et al. (2024); Vahdat et al. (2022); Zeng et al. (2024)] learn compact latent representations and perform generation within this compressed latent space, significantly advancing 3D generative modeling. Benefiting from large-scale 3D datasets [Deitke et al. (2023a); Deitke et al. (2023b)], modern 3D foundation models [Chen et al. (2025b); Hong et al. (2024); Li et al. (2025); Team (2025b)] have been developed to capture strong geometric priors, enabling not only high-quality generation across diverse object categories but also various downstream applications [Du et al. (2025); Hu et al. (2024)]. However, most existing native 3D generators are restricted to either explicit representations or implicit formulations. TRELLIS [Xiang et al. (2025b)] addresses this constraint by introducing a Structured Latent Representation (SLAT) that supports flexible multi-format 3D generation, whose versatility we inherit to accommodate diverse 3D modalities in our framework. Although these 3D foundation models exhibit strong generalization abilities, they mainly generate samples from a learned data distribution and lack dedicated mechanisms for example-driven control. In this work, we leverage the powerful priors from the 3D foundation model TRELLIS [Xiang et al. (2025b)] and introduce a decoupled personalization framework. Our approach enables flexible adaptation of both geometry and appearance, while fully retaining the high-quality generative capacity of the underlying models.

    Controllable 3D Generation. Recent methods have been developed to enable image-guided control for 3D generation [Dong et al. (2024); Gao et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2023)]. Among these, some approaches inject explicit shape priors to regulate the geometric attributes of synthesized 3D content. In parallel, another line of work unifies the stylistic appearance of generated objects by leveraging reference images [Richardson et al. (2023); Song et al. (2024); Xie et al. (2024); Yeh et al. (2024)]. However, such style-guided 3D generation pipelines typically require users to provide predefined 3D geometry such as meshes, and enforce fixed geometric structures throughout generation to maintain spatial consistency. This strong restriction confines their controllability to texture style only, while leaving geometric style—another critical dimension of 3D asset customization—unchanged and fully uncontrollable. In this work, we employ TRELLIS as our backbone model, taking advantage of its expressive 3D latent representations that comprehensively encode both geometric structure and textural appearance. Built on these latent features, we achieve zero-shot style-guided 3D generation that supports simultaneous control over both texture and geometric style.

    Image-based 3D Stylization. Given a style reference input and a target content shape, 3D stylization is defined as the task of distilling stylistic patterns from the reference and transferring these patterns to the target geometry to synthesize stylistically aligned 3D assets. This problem has been investigated across diverse 3D representation frameworks, including explicit meshes [Hertz et al. (2020); Höllein et al. (2022); Hu et al. (2024)], neural implicit fields, and Gaussian splatting [Huang et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2022)]. To enhance generalizability, a prominent line of recent work [Chen et al. (2025a); Dong et al. (2024); Xie et al. (2024)] harnesses powerful 2D priors from large-scale image diffusion models [Rombach et al. (2022)] for 3D stylization. Concurrently, StyleSculptor [Qu et al. (2025)] leverages strong 3D priors [Xiang et al. (2025b)] to achieve view-consistent stylization. However, all these approaches share a critical limitation: contemporary 3D stylization methods [Hu et al. (2026); Qu et al. (2025)] enforce an all-or-nothing paradigm, where adopting a reference style necessitates the simultaneous incorporation of all its visual attributes. This inherent constraint severely limits the methods’ practical utility in real-world content creation scenarios.

    3 Methods

    To address the Disen3D problem, we propose a disentangled 3D style transfer framework DiDE built upon the TRELLIS backbone. Given a content image I_cnt, a texture reference Iₜₓᵤ, and a color reference I_col, our goal is to generate a 3D asset that (i) preserves the geometric structure of I_cnt, (ii) inherits texture from Iₜₓᵤ, and (iii) adopts color from I_col, while maintaining cross-view consistency. Unlike conventional 2D style transfer, our approach performs disentangled style modeling in the 3D latent space and injects style during rectified flow-based refinement.

    3.1 Preliminaries

    TRELLIS[Xiang et al. (2025b)] is a foundation model for conditional 3D asset generation that synthesizes assets in multiple representations (e.g., NeRF, 3DGS, mesh) from text or image inputs. It adopts a two-stage rectified flow framework to progressively transform noise into structured 3D representations: Stage I predicts a sparse geometric structure, and Stage II refines per-voxel latent features for texture and material details.

    Following this pipeline, we keep the first-stage sparse structure prediction unchanged to preserve geometric fidelity. Given an input image I_cnt, we use the DINOv2 model [Oquab et al. (2023)] to encode it into a latent z_c=𝔼(I_cnt). The Voxel Flow Transformer VFT then predicts a sparse voxel set

    P={pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^L, pᵢ∈{0,1,…,N-1}³

    		(1)

    where pᵢ is the positional index of an active voxel in the 3D grid intersecting with the surface of object, L is the total number of active voxels, and N is the maximum voxel index per dimension. We feed the coarse location information obtained in the first stage, along with the image embedding, into Stage II to generate features for each voxel. In the second stage, we complete the style transfer.

    3.2 Overcompleteness of the TRELLIS Feature Space

    StyleSculptor [Qu et al. (2025)] showed that TRELLIS feature channels can be decomposed into style and content-relevant subsets via patch-wise variance. However, their formulation assumes a single style reference. In our setting, texture and color must be injected independently into the same style branch, which can lead to feature interference. We therefore investigate whether the style-significant channels are overcomplete, asking whether all of them are actually required to faithfully encode texture. We conduct a channel ablation experiment in which we progressively reduce the number of channels used for texture injection at every DiT block of TRELLIS stage II, retaining only the top-k highest-variance channels from the style branch of Stage II. For each value of k, we generate outputs across the full set of style references from StyleSculptor [Qu et al. (2025)] using a fixed content image, render a single view, and measure DINOv2 cosine similarity between the mean patch features of the rendered output and the corresponding style reference image. As shown in Fig. 3, DINOv2 texture similarity is ≈0.6125 when only a small fraction of channels is retained, rises to ≈0.625–0.63 once more than 25% of the channels are retained, and remains within this range up to 100%. To further support this finding, we conduct a PCA reconstruction analysis (see appendix), confirming the low intrinsic dimensionality of texture within the TRELLIS feature space, and validating that style-significant channels contain a large free subspace that can be independently allocated to a second style attribute.

    3.3 Color-Texture Attributes Embedding

    Given a content image I_cnt, a texture reference Iₜₓᵤ, and a color reference I_col, our framework processes each input through a dedicated branch. The content branch is kept unchanged from the standard image-to-3D pipeline [Xiang et al. (2025b)] to preserve geometric structure, while the texture and color branches apply dedicated preprocessing to extract disentangled style embeddings, as described below.

    Texture Reference. We convert the texture reference image Iₜₓᵤ into grayscale to suppress color information, yielding Iₜₓᵤᵍʳᵃʸ. This grayscale image is then fed into the DINOv2 [Oquab et al. (2023)] encoder to obtain the texture embedding fₜₓᵤ=𝔼(Iₜₓᵤᵍʳᵃʸ).

    Color Reference. Our method supports two types of color reference inputs: reference images, common in style transfer applications, and color palettes, widely used in multimedia and design workflows. Both are processed to isolate color information from texture structure before encoding.

    When a reference image is used as the color reference, we extract its low-frequency components via a Fourier transform while suppressing high-frequency signals. Intuitively, high-frequency components primarily encode textural details (e.g., edges and fine patterns), whereas low-frequency components capture global color distributions. By filtering out high-frequency signals, our method enforces a structure-invariant color conditioning, thereby improving the disentanglement between color and texture.

    Given a color palette {cₖ}ₖ₌₁^n_colors, we construct a spatially varied image Iᵥₒᵣ via Voronoi tessellation: we sample random seeds over the image plane, assign each a palette color, and map every pixel x to its nearest seed:

    Iᵥₒᵣ(x)=c_a_j^*(x), j^*(x)=\arg\minⱼ∥x-sⱼ∥₂².

    		(2)

    This produces an image that encodes the palette’s color distribution without any texture structure. In both cases, the processed image is encoded via DINOv2 [Oquab et al. (2023)] to obtain the color embedding f_col=𝔼(Iᵥₒᵣ).

    3.4 Disentangled 3D Style Transfer (Disen3D)

    DiDE runs three parallel branches through the transformer blocks of Stage II — one for the content image, one for the texture reference, and one for the color reference — each processing its input through independent self-attention layers. At every transformer block, the texture and color branches produce separate attention outputs, which are composed via a channel partition mechanism into a single fused representation. This fused output is then injected into the content branch, overwriting its self-attention output before the residual update. We describe each step in detail below.

    Per-Branch Self-Attention. Given an input feature sequence X∈ℝ^N×d, a standard self-attention layer computes as:

    Attn(X)=Softmax ((QK^⊤)/(√d))V, Q=XW_Q, K=XW_K, V=XW_V.

    		(3)

    Prior 3D stylization methods [Qu et al. (2025)] adopt a cross-attention formulation in which the query is derived from the content image while keys and values come from the style reference. As shown in Fig. 3, this leads to structural leakage: the content query biases the output toward the content geometry and weakens style transfer.

    We instead run each style branch with its own standard self-attention, using query, key, and value all derived from the same branch input:

    SAₜₓᵤ=Attn(Qₜₓᵤ,Kₜₓᵤ,Vₜₓᵤ),(4)
    SA_col=Attn(Q_col,K_col,V_col).(5)

    This ensures that each branch faithfully encodes the style of its own reference without contamination from the content image.

    Texture-Color Composition. Building on our finding that texture information saturates only a subset of the style-significant channels (Sec. 3.2), we exploit the remaining free channels to encode an independent color attribute. This channel-wise decomposition is applied at every transformer block of Stage II, as illustrated in Fig. 4 (right).

    We introduce a channel selection operator S, where S(h)⊂{1,…,C} denotes the indices of the top k% highest-variance channels of a feature map with C channels. These channels are allocated to the texture branch, while the complementary set is allocated to the color branch. We construct a binary mask M∈{0,1}^C:

    M_c=\begincases1,&c∈S(h), 0,&otherwise,\endcases

    		(6)

    and define the fused attention output as:

    SA_fusion=Attn (Qₜₓᵤ,Kₜₓᵤ,M⊙Vₜₓᵤ)+λ Attn (Q_col,K_col,(1-M)⊙V_col),(7)

    where ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication broadcast along the sequence dimension, and λ>0 is a scalar hyperparameter that controls the trade-off between the color and texture branch.

    Injection into the Content Branch. The fused representation SA_fusion is injected into the content branch by replacing its self-attention output at each transformer block. Following the standard gated residual mechanism of the DiT blocks in TRELLIS, the content features are updated as:

    X_cnt^′=X_cnt+α_cnt⊙SA_fusion,

    		(8)

    where α_cnt∈ℝᵈ is the learned per-channel gate derived from the content branch’s adaptive layer norm conditioning, following the AdaLN-zero parameterization [Peebles and Xie (2023)]. This preserves the spatial structure and diffusion conditioning of the content branch while fully transferring the composed style signal, keeping the generated geometry faithful to the content image throughout the generation.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    We conduct extensive experiments to validate three core claims of DiDE: (i) effective disentanglement of color and texture in the generated 3D assets, (ii) faithful preservation of the content geometry, and (iii) competitive style fidelity against existing methods. Since no prior benchmark addresses the Disen3D setting, we introduce Disen3D-Bench and compare against representative 2D and 3D stylization baselines.

    Datasets. We collected 37 images to form a novel multi-image style transfer dataset named Disen3D-Bench for the Disen3D setup. These images include 10 content images, 12 texture reference images, and 15 palette images. The content images and texture reference images were selected from Stylesculptor [Qu et al. (2025)] and Morph3D [Sun et al. (2026)], and each palette image contains 3-5 different colors. These image combinations generate 1,800 3D assets for subsequent evaluation.

    Implementation Details. We mainly build our method DiDE upon TRELLIS [Xiang et al. (2025b)] while also verified on TRELLIS.2 [Xiang et al. (2025a)]. For the hyperparameters, we set k=25,λ=1.2. Both stages use a CFG strength of 3.0, with 25 inference steps. The reproducing code will be released after the peer review process. All experiments are conducted on a NVIDIA A40 GPU.

    Baseline Methods. We compare against three representative training-free stylization approaches, each adapted to the Disen3D two-reference setting to the best extent their architectures permit. SADis [Qin et al. (2025)] is the only prior method addressing color-texture disentanglement, though in 2D: we apply it to the content image and lift the stylized result to 3D using TRELLIS. MorphAny3D [Sun et al. (2026)] natively supports two image inputs via its dual-target morphing setting, which we use to provide the texture and color references directly. StyleSculptor [Qu et al. (2025)], originally designed for a single content-texture pair, is adapted by adding an extra reference branch for the color reference; the self-attention outputs of the texture and color branches are then summed to produce the fused style representation. We emphasize that StyleSculptor and MorphAny3D were not designed for disentangled two-reference stylization; these adaptations represent the closest reasonable comparison points rather than intended use cases. SADis, while designed for color-texture disentanglement, operates in 2D and requires an additional lifting step to produce 3D assets. Additional details on the experimental setup are provided in the appendix.

    Evaluation Metrics. We adopt several quantitative metrics across four axes: (1) For Geometry Semantics, CLIP-I [Radford et al. (2021)] measures semantic similarity between the generated asset and the content image; and Chamfer Distance and Hausdorff Distance are used to measure the geometric difference between two assets. (2) For Texture preservation: LPIPS [Zhang et al. (2018)] captures perceptual distortion and potential style leakage; and SSIM [Wang et al. (2003)] evaluates structural similarity. (3) For color fidelity: MS-SWD [He et al. (2024)] measures color distance between the generated asset and the color reference, and C-Hist computes the distance between color histograms. (4) Finally, we employ VLM-based evaluation using InternVL2.5-8B [Chen et al. (2024)], which performs binary judgments on texture consistency (whether the generated asset shares structural style with the texture reference, ignoring color) and color fidelity (whether colors absent from the color reference are introduced). Full prompts and scoring protocol are provided in Appendix B. All metrics are computed over 1,800 generated assets.

    4.2 Experimental Results

    Qualitative Results. In our evaluation of generation quality, visual results are presented in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6. For SADis, the method exhibits subpar object detail preservation, while introducing redundant textures and color artifacts in the background region. After 3D rendering, the reconstructed textures and colors also fail to align closely with the reference images. For StyleSculptor, the model fails to achieve full disentanglement of texture and color. The generated 3D assets exhibit a mixed color distribution derived from both reference images; furthermore, the results often suffer from style bias, tending to favor either the texture reference or the color reference rather than achieving balanced, independent control over both attributes. Regarding MorphAny3D, its Morphing Cross-Attention mechanism causes the colors and styles inherent in the content image to exert a significant influence on the final generation result. Additionally, the method generates spurious colors that are not present in the provided color palette images. In contrast, our DiDE enables precise decoupling of texture structure and color attributes. For instance, we can accurately align the cutout structure of the texture reference with the target color— a capability not achievable by other baseline methods. Simultaneously, our method DiDE ensures that the generated 3D asset remains consistent with the content image, free from distortions, flips, or other visual artifacts.

    Quantitative Results. Table 1 reports the full results. DiDE achieves the best CLIP-I score (0.75), indicating superior semantic alignment with the content image. For Geometry, DiDE achieves the lowest Chamfer (15.38) and Hausdorff (7.87) distances, improving over StyleSculptor by approximately 14.1% and 6.1%, respectively. Although SADis obtains a comparable Chamfer distance, its substantially higher Hausdorff distance reveals larger worst-case local deviations, showing that DiDE better preserves both global surface structure and local geometry. For color fidelity, DiDE leads on C-Hist (0.87) and by a large margin on VLM color accuracy (70.94 vs. 40.05 for the next best method), confirming faithful and disentangled color transfer. While MorphAny3D and SADis yield slightly better MS-SWD scores (18.31 and 18.38 vs. 20.40), this comes at the cost of degraded texture structure, as reflected in their lower SSIM scores. For texture quality, DiDE attains the highest SSIM (125.19) and VLM texture accuracy (30.72 vs. 23.22 for StyleSculptor), demonstrating superior structural preservation and texture fidelity. LPIPS scores are comparable across all methods (0.65–0.69), suggesting similar levels of perceptual distortion relative to the content image.

    4.3 Ablation Study

    Effect of Branch Preprocessing. We ablate the two key preprocessing components of DiDE — grayscale conversion of the texture reference and Voronoi tessellation of the color palette — by removing each in turn while keeping the rest of the pipeline unchanged. As shown in Fig. 7, removing grayscale conversion leaves residual color information in the texture branch, introducing undesired color interference in the generated output. Removing Voronoi tessellation causes color leakage, producing colors that deviate from the reference palette.

    Model Adaptability. To verify the generalizability of DiDE beyond the base TRELLIS backbone, we apply it to TRELLIS.2 [Xiang et al. (2025a)], which extends TRELLIS with a three-stage pipeline where texture and color features are processed in separate stages. As illustrated in Fig. 8, DiDE maintains robust and consistent disentanglement performance on TRELLIS.2, confirming that our channel partition mechanism transfers across model variants. The natural stage-wise separation in TRELLIS.2 further aligns with our texture-color decoupling design, making the adaptation straightforward.

    Channel Selection. In DiDE, channel variance is computed from the texture branch to determine the channel partition. To assess the sensitivity of this design choice, we ablate by computing variance from the color branch instead, swapping which branch drives the partition. As shown in Fig. 9, both settings achieve consistent texture-color disentanglement, with only minor differences in color saturation. This robustness to the choice of variance source corroborates our earlier finding (Sec. 3.2) that the latent feature space is overcomplete, with texture and color information redundantly distributed across channels regardless of which branch is used for estimation. We use texture-branch variance as default since it produces marginally more faithful color rendition in practice.

    Hyperparameter λ. We ablate the color branch weight λ in Eq. 7 by sweeping over the range [0.5,2.0]. All results are averaged over 600 randomly samples. As reported in Table 2, too small a value of λ weakens color transfer fidelity, while too large a value begins to compromise texture quality. This reflects the expected trade-off between the two branches, and λ=1.2 strikes the best balance, achieving the lowest C-Hist (0.89) and MS-SWD (19.25) while maintaining competitive texture scores.

    User Study. Our method received the highest preference rates across all three aspects, with 51.7% for geometry preservation, 58.2% for texture consistency, and 72.4% for color consistency. These results provide complementary perceptual evidence that the quantitative improvements of our method translate into noticeable visual benefits, including better preservation of content geometry and more faithful, disentangled transfer of texture and color.

    Failure Cases. We further show a failure case in Fig. 10. Our method is sensitive to the luminance distribution of the texture reference. While the original texture reference produces reasonable texture and color transfer, increasing its brightness by 1.5× causes the generated 3D assets to become nearly white, with substantial loss of both texture and color details. This indicates that large brightness shifts in the reference image remain a limitation of our current appearance-transfer formulation.

    5 Conclusion

    This work addresses a fundamental limitation in existing 3D stylization methods: the inability to independently control distinct stylistic attributes such as color and texture. We formalize this gap as Disentangled 3D Stylization (Disen3D) and propose Direct Injection with color-texture DEcoupling (DiDE), the first training-free framework to address it. DiDE decouples texture and color by processing each reference through a dedicated branch with tailored preprocessing and composes them via a channel partition mechanism injected into the self-attention layers of a pretrained image-to-3D model, preserving content geometry throughout. Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations on Disen3D-Bench confirm that DiDE outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in disentangled color and texture control. We hope this work opens the door to finer-grained artistic control in 3D content creation and inspires future research on multi-attribute style disentanglement.

    Appendix A Statements

    Limitations. While DiDE effectively mitigates detail attenuation and enhances fine-grained texture fidelity for training-free disentangled 3D stylization, it has several limitations: the framework is only validated on rectified flow-matching based native 3D diffusion models (the TRELLIS/TRELLIS.2 family) and has not been tested for generalization to other mainstream 3D generation paradigms, including voxel-based models, signed distance field (SDF) generators, 3D Gaussian splatting diffusion pipelines, and knowledge distillation-based image-to-3D methods. Furthermore, although the computational overhead is negligible, the low-noise restart refinement step adds mild extra inference operations, restricting direct deployment on extremely memory-constrained edge devices. Finally, DiDE focuses on color-texture decoupling and texture enhancement without a dedicated geometric refinement module, so the geometric quality of the generated 3D assets is inherently dependent on the geometric reconstruction capability of the underlying pre-trained 3D foundation model; and the current design only supports independent control of color and texture, without extending to multi-attribute disentanglement (e.g., material, lighting, geometric style), which limits its flexibility for complex artistic creation.

    Broader Impacts.DiDE advances controllable 3D content creation and delivers widespread practical value by enabling training-free, disentangled color-texture control for 3D stylization, which drastically lowers the technical barrier and production cost for generating high-fidelity and customizable 3D assets, benefiting diverse industries and scenarios including game development, film and television virtual production, industrial design, cultural heritage digitization, robotic perception, and metaverse content construction, empowering both professional creators and non-expert users to flexibly customize 3D assets with independent style control, improving creative efficiency and diversifying content supply; on the other hand, the strong detail-preserving and high-fidelity texture transfer capability of DiDE introduces potential intellectual property and ethical risks, as the model could be misused for unauthorized duplication, counterfeiting, or commercial exploitation of copyrighted objects, branded products, real-world artifacts, or cultural heritage items without permission, and to address such risks, we advocate for the responsible deployment of the technology, enforcing content authentication for generated assets, establishing clear usage norms and legal compliance guidelines, and promoting ethical adoption across industries to ensure that DiDE creates public value while minimizing harms from misuse.

    Ethical Statement. We acknowledge the potential ethical implications associated with generative image-to-3D technologies, including risks related to privacy, impersonation, and misuse of synthetic 3D assets. All models used in this work are trained on publicly available datasets and follow the usage policies of those datasets. To promote transparency and responsible research, we will release the implementation details necessary to reproduce our results. We encourage researchers and practitioners to use DiDE responsibly and to consider the broader societal implications when deploying image-to-3D synthesis .

    Reproducibility Statement. To ensure reproducibility, we will release the source code and training scripts required to reproduce the experimental results reported in this paper after the peer review process. All experiments are conducted using publicly available datasets, and detailed descriptions of the model architecture, training configuration, and evaluation procedures are provided in the main paper and appendices.

    Inference efficiency Table 4 compares the average inference time per sample. Our method is the fastest among the evaluated methods, requiring 21.96 seconds per sample, a 13.5% reduction compared to the fastest baseline, SADis.

    Appendix B VLM-based Evaluation Protocol

    Overview. To quantitatively evaluate the quality of generated images, we employ the InternVL2.5-8B [3] model as an automatic evaluator. The vision-language model (VLM) performs binary judgments on two complementary aspects:

  • •

    Style Consistency: structural similarity between images while being invariant to color differences.

  • •

    Color Fidelity: whether the generated image faithfully preserves the reference color distribution without introducing extraneous colors.

    • This enables semantic-level evaluation without requiring human annotation.

    Input Construction. Given a generated image I_gen, we construct paired inputs with different references:

  • •

    Iₜₓᵤ: texture reference image

  • •

    I_col: color reference image

    • Each image is converted into a sequence of visual tokens (patches) using a vision encoder. Let:

    V_gen, Vₜₓᵤ, V_col

    		(9)

    denote the corresponding token representations. We concatenate tokens as:

    V=[V_ref,V_gen]

    		(10)

    and provide the number of patches per image to preserve image boundaries:

    \textttnum_patches_list=[|V_ref|,|V_gen|]

    		(11)

    Style Consistency Evaluation. To assess whether the generated image preserves structural/style characteristics, we prompt the VLM with:

    Image-1:
    Image-2:
    Ignoring color differences, are the structures or styles of these two images similar? Answer yes or no.

    The input pair is (Iₜₓᵤ,I_gen), and the model outputs:

    y_style∈{yes,no}

    		(12)

    We define the style consistency score over N samples as:

    S_style=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N1(y_style⁽ⁱ⁾=yes)

    		(13)

    Color Novelty Evaluation. To evaluate whether new colors are introduced, we use the prompt:

    Image-1:
    Image-2:
    If the second image shows a color that is not present in the first image, answer yes; otherwise, answer no.

    The input pair is (I_col,I_gen), and the output is:

    y_color∈{yes,no}

    		(14)

    We compute the color novelty score as:

    S_color=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N1(y_color⁽ⁱ⁾=no)

    		(15)

    Appendix C Hyperparameter visualization

    We further analyze the influence of the hyperparameter λ in Equ. 7 on disentangled generation quality. Specifically, λ controls the contribution of the color branch during feature fusion. We evaluate five settings, λ∈0.5,1.0,1.2,1.5,2.0, and visualize the corresponding results in Fig. 11. As shown in the figure, smaller values of λ (e.g., 0.5) lead to insufficient color guidance, causing the generated 3D assets to inherit excessive appearance information from the texture branch. In contrast, excessively large values of λ (e.g., 1.5 or 2.0) overemphasize color features, which weakens texture fidelity and introduces structural inconsistencies. We observe that λ=1.2 achieves the best balance between texture preservation and color controllability. Under this setting, the generated results faithfully maintain the structural patterns from the texture reference while accurately matching the target color distribution, leading to the most visually coherent disentangled generation results.

    Appendix D Ablation on k

    We conduct an ablation study by varying k∈{0,25,50,75,100}, where only the top-k channels are retained and the features of the remaining channels are set to zero. Fig. 12 shows that even when k=25, the generated 3D assets already exhibit clearly recognizable texture patterns, indicating that a relatively small subset of channels is sufficient to preserve most of the texture information, which further demonstrates the overcompleteness of the TRELLIS feature space.

    Appendix E Additional Visualization Results

    we provide additional qualitative results to further demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method across diverse texture and color references. As shown in Fig. 13, our method consistently achieves effective disentanglement between texture structure and color attributes under various challenging scenarios. Specifically, the generated 3D assets faithfully preserve the structural patterns and geometric details from the texture reference while accurately matching the target color distribution from the color reference image. Moreover, our method maintains strong content consistency without introducing noticeable distortions, structural artifacts, or undesired color leakage. These additional visualizations further validate the generalization capability and stability of DiDE for controllable disentangled 3D generation.

    Appendix F PCA Reconstruction Analysis

    To further validate the overcompleteness claim of Sec. 3.2, we perform a PCA analysis on the style-significant channels of the TRELLIS Stage II features. We project the style branch features onto an increasing number of principal components and measure DINOv2 cosine similarity between the rendered output and the texture reference. As shown in Fig. 14, similarity stabilizes after retaining as few as 10 principal components, despite the full channel dimensionality being much larger. This confirms that texture occupies an extremely low-dimensional subspace, leaving the majority of the feature space free to be independently repurposed for color encoding — directly motivating our channel partition design.

一句话：现有「全有或全无」的迁移方式没法单独调色；解耦后按风格需求分别注入。

要点：

  • 背景：基于 rectified flow 的图生 3D 模型已经能生成高质量资产，随之出现一批「训练无关」的风格化方法，把参考图的视觉属性迁移到生成资产上
  • 现有方法的通病是「全有或全无」：颜色与纹理被联合迁移，没有任何机制能分别控制——作者把这个限制形式化为 Disentangled 3D Stylization 问题
  • DiDE 用「直接注入 + 颜色/纹理解耦」来解决：颜色与纹理作为两条可控通道分别作用到 3D 资产上

为什么值得看：关卡与角色经常需要「同一套模型、换一套配色」——美术叫它调色板复用。如果风格迁移能把颜色与纹理拆开，就等于让 AI 生成也支持这种最常用的资产复用方式，而不是每次都重生成。

中文摘要：基于 rectified flow 的图像生成 3D 模型已经能产出高保真资产，随之出现一类「训练无关」的风格化做法：把参考图的视觉属性迁移到生成好的 3D 资产上。但现有方法采取的是全有或全无的策略——颜色与纹理被联合迁移，没有机制能独立控制二者，作者把这个限制形式化为 Disentangled 3D Stylization 问题。DiDE 用「直接注入 + 颜色纹理解耦」来应对：颜色与纹理作为两条可分别控制的通道作用于 3D 资产，从而支持「只换配色、保留材质细节」或反之。对需要调色板复用与批量变体的资产管线，这是最贴近美术工作方式的控制粒度。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-11-01

DiDE:Direct Injection with Color-Texture DEcoupling for 3D Stylization

Abstract

Recent advances in rectified flow-based image-to-3D generative models have enabled high-fidelity 3D asset generation. Building on this, a growing line of work has exploited these strong 3D priors for training-free stylization, transferring visual attributes from a reference image onto a generated 3D asset. However, existing methods enforce an all-or-nothing paradigm: color and texture are transferred jointly, with no mechanism to control them independently — a limitation we formalize as Disentangled 3D Stylization (Disen3D). To address this, we propose DiDE, the first training-free framework for Disen3D. Key to our approach is the observation that the structured latent space of image-to-3D models is overcomplete with respect to texture: texture information occupies only a small subset of the style-significant channels, leaving a free subspace available for independent color encoding. DiDE exploits this via a channel partition mechanism that processes a content image, a texture reference, and a color reference through dedicated branches and composes both style signals interference-free at every self-attention layer, preserving content geometry throughout. Experiments on Disen3D-Bench, our newly collected multi-reference benchmark, show that DiDE consistently outperforms 2D and 3D stylization baselines in color fidelity, texture transfer, and content preservation.

1 Introduction

Generative models for 3D asset creation have witnessed significant advancements  [Team (2024); Team (2025a); Xiang et al. (2025a)], facilitating their widespread adoption across diverse domains, including entertainment [Xu et al. (2024)], robotics [Ke et al. (2024)] and healthcare [Khader et al. (2023)]. In particular, recent rectified flow-based approaches [Lipman et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023); Team (2025b)], exemplified by TRELLIS [Xiang et al. (2025a); Xiang et al. (2025b)], have demonstrated the ability to generate high-fidelity 3D objects by jointly modeling sparse structural representations and appearance features within a unified latent space, while explicitly disentangling geometric structures from appearance attributes. Beyond 3D asset generation, a growing line of work has extended generative models to support 3D stylization[Hu et al. (2026); Qu et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026)] — the task of transferring stylistic attributes from a reference image onto a generated 3D asset. By conditioning generation on a style reference, these methods allow the produced asset to inherit visual properties such as surface material, color palette, and structural texture, while remaining semantically aligned with a content image. This capability carries significant practical value: a single base geometry can be re-stylized for different artistic contexts, production pipelines, or brand identities without requiring manual re-authoring. Although existing stylized 3D generation methods [Qu et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2026)] have achieved promising results, they still exhibit a critical limitation: style attributes (such as texture and color) cannot be controlled independently, which severely restricts artistic freedom in practice.

In practice, content creators rarely want to adopt a single reference style. Instead, they often wish to selectively borrow specific components while preserving the core of their own artistic vision [Epstein et al. (2023); Hertzmann (2022)]. Color palettes play an essential role in this process: they are carefully designed to convey specific emotions or maintain brand consistency, and a creator may wish to preserve their own color scheme while borrowing surface texture from a reference. Equally, one might want to adopt the rough, weathered texture of aged stone from one reference while keeping the warm tones of an entirely different palette. These two attributes — color and texture — are visually and semantically distinct, yet current 3D stylization approaches [Hu et al. (2026); Qu et al. (2025)] enforce an all-or-nothing paradigm: applying a reference style requires accepting all its visual attributes simultaneously, which severely restricts artistic freedom and practical applicability. To the best of our knowledge, only one prior work addresses disentangled stylization in 2D [Qin et al. (2025)], yet it cannot be generalized to 3D, as style embeddings from separate references cannot simply be composed in 3D latent space. This leaves the problem of fine-grained, decoupled 3D stylization entirely open.
