More importantly, both heuristic [21] and learning-based methods [9] have largely focused on finding the best view of a whole object, rather than a view tailored to a task-relevant part or inter-object relation. This makes them poorly suited to long-horizon tasks, where visualization needs change across action phases: one step may require a close-up of a manipulated part, while the next may require a wider view to reveal its effect on surrounding structure or another object. Learning-based approaches can adapt more flexibly, but they depend on collected training data, and obtaining labels with sufficient spatial coverage over the viewpoint space is expensive and difficult. Their behavior is therefore tied to the training distribution, with limited control over which visualization criteria are actually being optimized. In our setting, we instead seek a planner that can adapt to each task state, remain directly steerable by explicit visualization goals, and optimize views for task-relevant parts and relations rather than whole-object preference.

    These limitations motivate a differentiable formulation of viewpoint planning. Instead of discretizing the camera space and exhaustively evaluating a predefined set of candidate views, we express viewpoint quality using image-space objectives and optimize continuous camera parameters directly through gradients. This allows the optimizer to progressively adjust the camera toward a better view without requiring dense enumeration of the full viewpoint space. Equally importantly, each visualization requirement remains an explicit and interpretable objective, allowing us to specify which properties a good view should satisfy. The resulting formulation therefore combines continuous camera optimization with direct control over the task-dependent criteria being optimized, rather than relying on fixed camera rules or expecting explanatory behavior to emerge implicitly from training data.

    We formulate adaptive camera control as a visualization policy that selects a sequence of camera configurations

    V={vₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, vₜ=(θₜ,φₜ,rₜ,rollₜ),

    		(3)

    where θₜ and φₜ denote the azimuth and elevation around the action-dependent camera anchor c_aₜ, rₜ denotes the viewing distance, and rollₜ denotes the in-plane camera rotation around the viewing axis. The objective is therefore not to find one generic best view of an entire object, but to optimize a sequence of viewpoints whose targets and required context evolve with the task.

    III-BDesign Goals and Viewpoint-Quality Metrics

    We optimize each camera configuration according to five complementary design goals informed by prior work on visibility, structural informativeness, functional perception, importance-driven attention, and animated transitions [42, 21, 33, 27, 43, 18, 19]. Rather than defining these goals separately from their mathematical realizations, we introduce each goal together with the metric used to operationalize it.

    G1: Target Legibility - Visible Coverage (fᵥᵢₛ): Prior work on viewpoint quality has shown that visibility and projected size are central factors in whether a view is informative and perceptually useful  [42, 27]. In our setting, however, the relevant unit is often not the whole object but the task-relevant part on which an action or state change occurs. We therefore measure whether this target is visible, unoccluded, and sufficiently large in the rendered image.

    fᵥᵢₛ(v)=1/HW∑_(i,j)∈Ωmᵥᵢₛ(i,j;v),

    		(4)

    where Ω is the H×W image grid, and (i,j)∈Ω denotes a pixel location. The binary mask mᵥᵢₛ(i,j;v)∈{0,1} equals 1 if the target is visible and unoccluded at pixel (i,j) under viewpoint v, and 0 otherwise. Thus, fᵥᵢₛ(v) measures measures the fraction of the rendered image occupied by visible target content. A higher value indicates that the target is more prominently presented, whereas the score decreases when the target becomes smaller, moves outside the field of view, or is occluded by surrounding geometry.

    Semantic Directional Frame: To represent the target from functionally meaningful directions, we construct a semantic directional frame that captures its front-back, top-bottom, and side-to-side orientations. This frame provides a shared directional reference for evaluating both the structural diversity revealed by a viewpoint and its alignment with the target’s functional orientation. We first construct three orthogonal candidate axes using one of two supported policies. The AABB policy uses the three world-aligned axes of the target’s axis-aligned bounding box, while the PCA OBB policy [44] estimates three object-oriented axes from the target mesh using area-weighted PCA. Both policies produce six opposing candidate directions {±a₁,±a₂,±a₃}.

    We render the target from these six directions and provide the direction-labeled images to a VLM, which identifies the functional front and top directions. For an individual part, each candidate direction is represented by two images: an isolated rendering showing only the part and an in-context rendering in which the part is highlighted within the complete parent object. The isolated views expose local geometry, while the contextual views help the VLM determine how the part is positioned and typically approached during interaction. For each candidate direction, the camera is placed on the corresponding ray from the target’s bounding-box center at twice the target bounding-box diagonal for isolated views and 1.2 times the parent bounding-box diagonal for contextual views.

    Let d̂_front and d̂ᵤₚ denote the resulting target-level front and up directions. After orthogonalizing the predicted up direction with respect to the front direction, we construct a side direction and obtain the semantic frame {±d_f,±dᵤ,±dₛ} where d_f, dᵤ, and dₛ denote the semantic front, up, and side axes, respectively.

    This semantic frame serves two complementary purposes in the following metric definitions: it provides the directional partition used to measure the structural diversity revealed by a viewpoint, and it provides the functional front and upright references used to evaluate camera alignment. Detailed prompts of VLM are provided in the Supplementary Material-Section 1.

    G2: Structural Informativeness — Patch Entropy (fₑₙₜ): Prior work on viewpoint entropy and related informativeness measures suggests that informative viewpoints should reveal meaningful structural evidence of the underlying 3D object rather than collapse it into a degenerate or uninformative projection [21]. For long-horizon task visualization, this means that the selected view should preserve sufficient structural evidence of the task-relevant target for its three-dimensional form and state to remain interpretable.

    Classical viewpoint entropy measures structural informativeness by computing entropy over visible polygons [21]. However, polygon-level formulations are sensitive to mesh triangulation [12] and may primarily reflect geometric discretization rather than task-relevant surface diversity. We therefore compute entropy over a fixed vocabulary of six semantic directional patches, front, back, top, bottom, left, and right, defined by the semantic frame above.

    Each mesh triangle f is assigned to one directional group according to

    s(f,m)=α⟨n_f,dₘ⟩+(1-α)⟨ĉ_f,dₘ⟩,

    		(5)

    where n_f is the outward triangle normal, ĉ_f is the normalized triangle-centroid location, dₘ is the m-th canonical direction, and α=0.5. The orientation term groups similarly facing surfaces, while the location term disambiguates curved or oblique surfaces. All triangles assigned to the same direction form one patch.

    For viewpoint v, let

    Aₙ(v)=∑_(i,j)∈Ωmₙ(i,j;v)

    		(6)

    denote the visible pixel area belonging to patch Pₙ, where mₙ(i,j;v) is the visibility indicator of patch Pₙ at pixel (i,j). We define

    πₙ(v)=(Aₙ(v))/(∑_n^′=1^NA_n^′(v))

    		(7)

    and compute normalized patch entropy as

    fₑₙₜ(v)=-(1)/(\logN)∑ₙ₌₁^Nπₙ(v)\logπₙ(v).

    		(8)

    Full implementation details and comparisons with alternative patch assignment policies are provided in the Supplementary Material Section 2.

    G3: Functional Alignment (f_func): Studies on active and task-dependent perception suggest that object understanding benefits from viewpoints selected relative to the observer’s goal and the functional properties of the object, rather than from generic canonical views alone [43]. In our setting, some directions are more informative because they better reveal how a part is normally observed or operated, such as the front of a button, the readable face of a dial, or the operational side of a handle.

    Let d̂_front and d̂ᵤₚ denote the resulting target-level front and up directions. Let ĉ(v) denote the unit direction from the target toward the camera, and let û_cam(v) denote the camera up vector. We define

    f_func(v)=\max (⟨ĉ(v),d̂_front⟩,0)·\max (⟨û_cam(v),d̂ᵤₚ⟩,0).

    		(9)

    The first factor favors cameras located on the functional front side of the target, while the second maintains an upright and semantically interpretable image orientation. Although Functional Alignment and Patch Entropy use the same semantic frame, they capture different properties. Functional Alignment determines whether the camera follows a functionally meaningful direction, whereas Patch Entropy evaluates whether the viewpoint reveals multiple directional surface regions of the target.

    G4: Context-Aware Focus (f_foc): Prior work on importance-driven focus of attention suggests that a viewpoint should allocate image-space emphasis according to the relative importance of scene elements rather than treat all visible content equally [33]. In long-horizon tasks, however, importance depends not only on individual objects, but also on the contextual information needed to interpret the manipulated target and its relation to the surrounding scene.

    We therefore measure whether the current viewpoint allocates image space among the target and its surrounding entities according to their task-dependent importance. The objective is not to maximize target area alone: an excessively close view may remove the context needed to interpret the target’s role, whereas a view containing too much surrounding structure may make the target too small to inspect.

    For each entity e∈E, let

    Aₑ(v)=∑_(i,j)∈Ωmₑ(i,j;v)

    		(10)

    denote the number of rendered pixels occupied by e. We then define the visual distribution induced by the current view as

    p(e|v)=(Aₑ(v))/(∑_e^′∈EA_e^′(v)).

    		(11)

    Let q(e) denote a task-importance distribution specifying how visual attention should ideally be allocated across entities at the current action step. The context-aware focus score is defined as

    f_foc(v)=\exp (-D_JS(p(·|v) ∥ q(·))),

    		(12)

    with

    D_JS(p∥q)=1/2D_KL(p∥m)+1/2D_KL(q∥m), m=1/2(p+q),

    		(13)

    with D_KL being the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

    This score is high when the current view allocates screen space across the target and its context in a way that matches their task-dependent importance. We use Jensen–Shannon divergence because it provides a symmetric and bounded measure of distribution mismatch, which is more suitable than a single KL divergence for comparing task-dependent attention allocations.

    G5: Temporal Continuity (fₜᵣₐₙₛ): Prior work on animated transitions and event understanding has shown that coherent visual changes help viewers preserve spatial context, maintain orientation, and follow evolving processes over time [18, 19]. For long-horizon task visualization, consecutive camera states should therefore be connected without unnecessarily large changes in viewpoint. Let vₜ₋₁ and vₜ denote the camera configurations associated with two consecutive action steps, and let pₜ₋₁ and pₜ denote their corresponding camera positions. Let ℓ(pₜ₋₁,pₜ) denote the length of the transition path connecting these positions. We define

    fₜᵣₐₙₛ(vₜ₋₁,vₜ)=\exp (-(ℓ(pₜ₋₁,pₜ))/(d_ref)),

    		(14)

    where d_ref>0 is a reference distance used to normalize the path length. A higher score favors nearby camera configurations connected by shorter viewpoint transitions.

    As a proof of concept, we use path length as a lightweight geometric proxy for temporal continuity. This formulation encourages spatially compact transitions but does not directly model higher-order camera-motion or perceptual properties, such as velocity, acceleration, screen-space target displacement, optical flow, or visual correspondence. The visualizations of each metric are listed in Figure 3.

    IV Image-Space Optimization via Differentiable Rasterization

    Previous section defines five complementary viewpoint-quality metrics. Among them, Visible Coverage, Patch Entropy, and Context-Aware Focus rely on binary visibility masks, discrete pixel ownership, and projected image-space areas. These rendering quantities are not directly differentiable with respect to the camera parameters: their values may remain unchanged under small camera perturbations and change abruptly when visibility or occlusion boundaries are crossed. Functional Alignment is already expressed as an analytic function of the camera orientation, while Temporal Continuity depends on the transition path between consecutive camera states.

    In this section, we construct a shared differentiable camera-to-image mapping for these metrics. Rather than redefining their semantic objectives, we replace hard rendering quantities with soft image-space attributes produced through differentiable projection, rasterization, interpolation, and antialiasing. This allows gradients from the viewpoint-quality objective to propagate directly to the continuous camera parameters.

    IV-ADifferentiable Camera-to-Image Mapping

    We instantiate our viewpoint optimization on top of a standard differentiable rasterization pipeline [45]. Our role here is not to introduce a new renderer, but to define a camera parameterization and a set of task-specific attribute encodings that expose differentiable image-space signals for evaluating candidate views.

    The camera position p(vₜ) is parameterized using Equation 15

    p(vₜ)=c_aₜ+rₜ\beginbmatrix\cosφₜ\cosθₜ \cosφₜ\sinθₜ \sinφₜ\endbmatrix.

    		(15)

    Together with a viewing direction towards target center c_aₜ and roll-dependent in-plane rotation, this defines a differentiable view matrix V(vₜ). Let P denote the perspective projection matrix. For a mesh vertex xᵢ, the clip-space coordinate is x̃ᵢ(vₜ)=P V(vₜ) xᵢ. Since both the camera transform and projection are smooth functions of v, the projected geometry is differentiable with respect to the camera parameters.

    IV-BSoft Rasterized Attributes

    Let Ω denote the image domain and let q=(i,j)∈Ω denote a pixel. Each mesh vertex ℓ is assigned an attribute vector a_ℓ∈ℝ^K. For a pixel covered by the front-most triangle τ_q=(ℓ₀,ℓ₁,ℓ₂), let βₖ(q;vₜ) denote its perspective-correct barycentric coordinates. The point-sampled per-pixel attribute is

    aᵖᵗ(q;vₜ)=\begincases∑ₖ₌₀²βₖ(q;vₜ) a_ℓₖ,&qis covered byτ_q, [5.0pt] 0,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(16)

    We define the soft per-pixel attribute as

    ã(q;vₜ)=A (aᵖᵗ(·;vₜ),{x̃_ℓ(vₜ)},F)(q),

    		(17)

    where F is the triangle set and A denotes geometry-aware differentiable antialiasing. The operator approximates pixel coverage at silhouette and visibility boundaries, producing fractional attribute values at boundary pixels while preserving the interpolated attributes in triangle interiors.

    For binary target membership, target vertices are assigned 1 and all other vertices are assigned 0, so that ã(q;vₜ)∈[0,1] represents the fractional target coverage of pixel q. For categorical attributes such as entity identity or patch identity, a_ℓ is a one-hot vector rather than an integer label. Consequently, ã(q;vₜ) represents the soft per-pixel membership across the corresponding categories.

    This construction defines the differentiable mapping

    vₜ \longrightarrow {x̃_ℓ(vₜ)} \longrightarrow {ã(q;vₜ)}_q∈Ω,

    		(18)

    allowing gradients from image-space objectives to flow back to the camera parameters.

    Visibility is determined by the front-most surface returned by the rasterizer. Because target, entity are interpolated only from the front-most triangle at each pixel, the resulting channels already account for occlusion by the parent object and other scene geometry. Differentiable antialiasing provides fractional coverage near projected boundaries, allowing small camera changes around these boundaries to produce continuous changes in the corresponding image-space attributes.

    IV-CDifferentiable Realization of the Metrics

    With the soft rasterized attributes defined above, we obtain differentiable counterparts of the three rendering-based metrics introduced in Section III. Their semantic definitions remain unchanged; binary masks and hard projected areas are replaced by soft image-space quantities that vary continuously with the camera configuration vₜ. Functional Alignment is already an analytic function of the camera orientation, while Temporal Continuity is computed from a differentiable approximation of the transition-path length.

    Visible coverage: We define the visible coverage of the target by integrating the soft visibility mask over the image domain:

    f̃ᵥᵢₛ(vₜ)=(1)/(|Ω|)∑_q∈Ωm̃ᵥᵢₛ(q;vₜ).

    		(19)

    This term increases when a larger visible portion of the target occupies the image, and decreases under occlusion or shrinkage in projection. In practice, however, maximizing visible coverage without bound is not always desirable, since an excessively large target region may reduce surrounding context. We therefore apply a saturation function

    f̂ᵥᵢₛ(v)=\min ((f̃ᵥᵢₛ(v))/(fᵥᵢₛᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ), 1)\exp (-k \max (f̃ᵥᵢₛ(v)-fᵥᵢₛᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ, 0)),

    		(20)

    where fᵥᵢₛᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ is a manually specified target coverage. This design encourages the optimizer to maintain sufficient target visibility while avoiding overly zoomed-in views.

    Patch entropy: To measure structural informativeness, we partition the target surface into N semantic or geometric patches. Let w̃ₙ(q;v)∈[0,1] denote the soft contribution of patch n at pixel (i,j), obtained by rasterizing patch-identity attributes into image space. The soft projected area of patch n is

    Ãₙ(vₜ)=∑_q∈Ωw̃ₙ(q;vₜ),

    		(21)

    which induces the normalized image-space patch distribution

    π̃ₙ(vₜ)=(Ãₙ(vₜ))/(∑_n^′=1^NÃ_n^′(vₜ)).

    		(22)

    The differentiable entropy objective is then

    f̃ₑₙₜ(v)=-(1)/(\logN)∑ₙ₌₁^Nπ̃ₙ(v)\log (π̃ₙ(v)),

    		(23)

    This term favors views that reveal multiple target patches with balanced visibility, thereby increasing structural informativeness.

    Context-aware focus: Let E denote the set of relevant entities, including the target, its parent, and other contextual elements. For each entity e∈E, let m̃ₑ(u;v)∈[0,1] denote its soft image-space occupancy. The soft projected area of entity e is

    Ãₑ(vₜ)=∑_q∈Ωm̃ₑ(q;vₜ).

    		(24)

    These areas define a differentiable visual distribution

    p̃(e|vₜ)=(Ãₑ(vₜ))/(∑_e^′∈EÃ_e^′(vₜ)).

    		(25)

    Given a target importance distribution q(e) determined by task semantics, we compute the focus term by comparing p̃(e|v) with q(e). Using the Jensen–Shannon form introduced earlier, we define

    f̃_foc(v)=\exp (-D_JS(p̃(·|v),q(·))).

    		(26)

    This term is maximized when the image-space pixel allocation matches the importance distribution of current task state.

    Temporal continuity: To encourage smooth and safe viewpoint changes over time, we define a differentiable transition term between the previous camera position pₜ₋₁ and the current one pₜ. We represent the camera path as a cubic Bézier curve

    B(τ)=(1-τ)³P₀+3(1-τ)²τP₁+3(1-τ)τ²P₂+τ³P₃,

    		(27)

    where P₀=pₜ₋₁ and P₃=pₜ, and P₁,P₂ are fixed intermediate control points determined by a collision-aware path construction.

    We measure path efficiency by the arc length

    ℓ=∑ᵢ₌₁^N∥B(τᵢ)-B(τᵢ₋₁)∥₂, τᵢ=i/N,

    		(28)

    IV-DUnified Objective and Optimization

    We combine the above terms into a unified viewpoint quality function:

    Q(v)=f̃ᵥᵢₛ(v)^w₁·f̃ₑₙₜ(v)^w₂·f_func(v)^w₃·f̃_foc(v)^w₄·fₜᵣₐₙₛ(v;vₜ₋₁)^w₅,

    		(29)

    where wᵢ≥0 controls the contribution of each design goal. The multiplicative form ensures that severe failure on any one objective, such as complete occlusion of the target, cannot be fully compensated by gains on unrelated terms.

    For optimization, we minimize the equivalent negative log-form objective. To account for action dynamics, we sample K intermediate states along the execution of action aₜ and evaluate the four per-view metrics under the same camera configuration vₜ at each sampled state. Their losses are averaged across the sampled states, while the temporal-continuity term is evaluated once between vₜ₋₁ and vₜ. This motion-aware formulation encourages the selected viewpoint to remain informative throughout the action rather than only at a single static instant.

    Lₜ(vₜ)=-1/K∑ₖ₌₁^K∑ᵢ₌₁⁵wᵢ\log (fᵢ⁽ᵏ⁾(vₜ)),

    		(30)

    Here, fᵢ⁽ᵏ⁾ denotes the i-th viewpoint-quality metric evaluated at the k-th sampled action state. Since temporal continuity depends only on consecutive camera configurations, its value is shared across all K sampled states.

    V Implementation Details

    We implement VISTA in Isaac Sim 4.5 [46] as an interactive extension built on the Omniverse Kit framework. The extension integrates the viewpoint planner into the simulator’s user interface, rendering pipeline, and articulated-object control system. We evaluate VISTA using mesh-based assets from three sources. RealAppliance [10] contains high-fidelity appliance models with articulated physical and electronic mechanisms and action logic consistent with their manuals. The Chevrolet C8 model [47] provides a high-fidelity vehicle model with articulated parts.The built-in Isaac Sim asset library provides the articulated Forklift [48] model, which contains movable components and part-level geometry. Each dataset provides a list of actions supported for each part. To reduce rasterization cost for geometrically complex components, we construct level-of-detail meshes for selected target parts.

    V-ASemantic Direction Extraction

    For semantic-face identification, we use a fixed version of GPT-5.4-2026-03-05[49]. The model identifies the functionally meaningful front and top directions of whole objects and target parts. These directions are cached and used to instantiate the functional alignment and semantic patch objectives. The optimization pipeline is implemented using PyTorch and nvdiffrast [45], with differentiable rasterization performed at a resolution of 64×64 pixels.

    V-BCamera Configuration

    The camera anchor c_aₜ is selected according to the action-conditioned target type and remains fixed throughout the corresponding action. For object–part actions, such as pressing, rotating, opening, and closing, the anchor is placed at the center of the manipulated part. For relational actions, such as picking, moving, and placing, the anchor is placed at the center of the parent object to preserve the surrounding interaction context. The manipulated object and, when applicable, the destination entity remain separate visual targets. The camera is oriented toward c_aₜ together with the optimized in-plane roll. Independent camera panning and look-at offsets are not optimized in the current implementation.

    V-CDifferentiable Optimization

    We use multi-start initialization to reduce sensitivity to local optima. By default, 15 initial camera positions are distributed over the admissible azimuth and elevation domain. All initial candidates are evaluated, and the three candidates with the lowest objective losses are refined using Adam. The default learning rate is 0.08, and each candidate is optimized for at most 80 iterations. Optimization terminates early when the best objective value does not improve by more than 10⁻⁶ for five consecutive iterations. For motion-aware optimization, we sample three states along the articulated motion, including the start and end states, and aggregate their metric values when optimizing the viewpoint for the complete action motion.

    V-DObjective Configuration

    The five objective weights for visible coverage, patch entropy, context-aware focus, functional alignment, and temporal continuity are set to 1.0 by default. A metric can be disabled by setting its weight to zero. The default visible-coverage target is 0.2, which provides an empirical balance between target legibility and preservation of the surrounding context.

    For context-aware focus, we distinguish three types of entities: the manipulated target, the parent object that provides global structural context, and other parts of the model that provide local task context. By default, the task-importance distribution is derived from the relative visible projected areas of these entities under the functional front view determined by the semantic directional frame. This distribution preserves the relative visual prominence of the task-relevant entities under a semantically meaningful frontal composition. Users may override these default values to emphasize particular targets or contextual entities. The objective weights, entity-importance values, target visible coverage, number of initial candidates, number of refined candidates, learning rate, iteration limit, and number of motion samples are exposed through the graphical interface and configuration files. VISTA can therefore be adapted to different objects, actions, and visualization requirements without modifying the optimization code. By tuning these parameters, users can obtain higher-quality views for specific tasks.

    V-ERuntime

    All visualization results are recorded on a machine equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. The reported wall-clock optimization time for a single action includes multi-start candidate evaluation and Adam refinement, while offline LOD construction and cached VLM semantic-face inference are excluded. Optimization requires approximately 5–10 seconds per action for RealAppliance and approximately 20 seconds for the Chevrolet C8 and Forklift model. The resulting long-horizon animations are provided in the supplementary video.

    VI Use Case

    We demonstrate VISTA in Figure 4 through a long-horizon cooking task with an air fryer. The input to our system is an action sequence:

    open(basket); pick(chicken); move(chicken, basket); place(chicken, basket); close(basket); rotate(timer knob, 90); rotate(temperature knob, 90); open(basket); pick(chicken). For each action, VISTA automatically identifies the task-relevant target and optimizes a viewpoint that best explains the ongoing manipulation.

    For open(basket), the action belongs to the first interaction type, object-part pair (o,p), where the target is a single manipulated part. Here, the basket is defined as the target part, and the whole object is the air fryer. The selected viewpoint should therefore make the basket clearly visible and provide the essential context around the basket.

    In contrast, move(chicken, basket) belongs to the second interaction type, namely the relational tuple (o₁,p,o₂), where the task depends on the spatial relationship between two entities. In this case, the chicken and the basket are jointly treated as target meshes, while the whole object remains the air fryer. These two targets are explicitly incorporated into different viewpoint quality metrics. The selected viewpoint should therefore simultaneously present the food item, the basket, and their relation, so that the moving process is easy to interpret.

    Figure 3illustrates one rendered image together with the visualizations of three metrics for that image. In this example, the target part is the timer knob. Therefore, in 3(b), both target pixels and parent pixels are shown, as this metric measures the ratio of visible target pixels in the full image; the orange pixels indicate the target region. In 3(c), only the target is rendered, since parent occlusion is not considered in the patch entropy computation. Three semantic patches are shown in the patch entropy visualization, where the partition is determined by the semantic information. 3(d) illustrates the visualization of the context-aware focus metric. This metric considers pixels from all parts as well as the parent pixels, and is computed as the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the observed pixel distribution and the desired context-focus distribution.

    VII Evaluation

    We evaluate VISTA in four stages. First, we assess the reliability of the VLM used to extract the semantic front and up directions required by patch entropy and functional alignment. Second, we conduct a qualitative leave-one-objective-out ablation to illustrate the complementary effects of the individual viewpoint-quality metrics. Third, we perform a user study to evaluate the perceptual quality of the optimized camera trajectories in terms of action visibility, spatial context, camera-motion smoothness, and overall preference. Finally, we introduce a VLM-based perceptual benchmark to measure how different camera strategies affect appliance-state recognition, goal reasoning, and closed-loop control. Together, these evaluations examine the reliability of the semantic inputs, the contributions of the objective terms, and the effectiveness of VISTA for both human-facing task visualization and agent-facing visual observation.

    VII-AVLM Semantic Direction Extraction Evaluation

    To evaluate the reliability of the semantic information extracted by the VLM, we manually annotated the front and top directions of the whole object and every functional part in ten RealAppliance models, resulting in 68 instances comprising 10 whole objects and 58 parts. Each whole object was represented by six axis-aligned views, while each part was provided with six isolated views and six contextual views showing its location within the appliance. Using identical inputs and a fixed structured-output prompt, GPT-5.4-2026-03-05 achieved 92.65% front accuracy, 95.59% top accuracy, and 92.65% joint accuracy, where joint accuracy requires both directions to be correct for the same instance. GPT-4o-2024-08-06 achieved 55.88%, 91.18%, and 55.88%, respectively. These results demonstrate that an advanced VLM can reliably extract the semantic and reference-direction information required by our camera optimization framework, while GPT-4o’s lower front-direction accuracy indicates that model selection remains important.

    VII-BQualitative Objective Ablation

    We conduct a qualitative leave-one-objective-out ablation to examine how the individual per-view metrics influence the optimized camera configuration. As shown in Figure 5, we optimize the viewpoint for the action open(basket) using the complete objective and four variants in which visible coverage, context-aware focus, patch entropy, or functional alignment is removed individually. Temporal continuity is not included in this single-view comparison because it is defined between consecutive camera configurations and therefore requires a sequence-level evaluation.

    The optimization curves in Figure 5 show that the individual metric scores improve while the weighted objective loss decreases during optimization. With the complete objective, VISTA produces a close and functionally aligned view that clearly presents the manipulated basket while retaining sufficient context from the surrounding appliance.

    Removing visible coverage results in a substantially more distant viewpoint, causing the manipulated basket to occupy only a small region of the image. This demonstrates the role of visible coverage in maintaining sufficient target prominence. Removing context-aware focus changes the relative image-space allocation between the basket and its parent appliance, producing a composition that does not preserve the same balance between local action detail and surrounding context. For example, as shown in the figure, removing context-aware focus causes the top knob, a task-relevant contextual part, to disappear from the resulting view.

    Without patch entropy, the optimizer produces a more oblique view with a less balanced presentation of the target’s directional surface regions. In contrast, removing functional alignment results in a viewpoint from obliquely below the object, without respecting its semantically meaningful front and up directions. Although patch entropy and functional alignment use the same semantic directional frame, these results illustrate their complementary roles: patch entropy encourages the exposure of diverse target surfaces, whereas functional alignment prevents semantically inappropriate viewing directions and favors an operationally meaningful composition.

    Overall, the complete objective provides the most balanced composition among target visibility, structural informativeness, functional orientation, and contextual presentation. This experiment is intended as a qualitative illustration of the behavior of the individual objective terms rather than a statistical analysis of their relative importance or weight sensitivity. A more comprehensive quantitative evaluation across actions, object categories, and objective-weight configurations remains an important direction for future work.

    VII-CUser Study

    We conducted a user study with 21 participants to evaluate the perceptual quality on the RealAppliance datasets. The camera trajectories are optimized by our method against two baselines: a fixed camera placement (Fixed) and a camera position selected using viewpoint entropy [21] (Entropy). The fixed camera position is obtained from the default position in the RealAppliance dataset. To obtain the viewpoint with the highest viewpoint entropy score, we sample candidate viewpoints on a sphere with a diameter of 1.5 times the object bounding box diagonal and select the one with the maximum entropy value.

    We did not include the learned human-preference baseline in the user study because, similar to viewpoint entropy, it produces a static whole-object view and does not adapt to changes in the action target. Because participants were required to watch, rate, and rank every camera trajectory, including both static optimized-view baselines would have increased the study duration and participant fatigue without introducing a substantially different camera strategy. We therefore retained entropy as a deterministic and interpretable representative of static optimized viewpoint selection. Our experiment was approved by our university’s IRB. At the start of the experiment, we obtained informed consent from all participants.

    We employed a within-subjects design, where every participant evaluated all three methods across all tasks, enabling direct comparison and reducing individual variability. Participants viewed camera-generated videos of five appliance interaction sequences: (1) airfryer, cook cycle, (2) bread machine, bake bread, (3) airfryer, air fry session, (4) oven, adjust controls, and (5) bread machine, bake cycle. Each task depicted the same interaction captured by all three camera methods. For each task, participants watched three videos (one per method) presented in a randomized order. They then rated each method on six criteria using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = worst, 5 = best) and ranked the three methods from best to worst. The presentation order of methods was randomized per task per participant across all six possible permutations to mitigate ordering bias.

    Participants rated each method on the following six criteria:

  • •

    Q1: How well the action is visible in the video.

  • •

    Q2: How well the camera provides spatial context.

  • •

    Q3: How natural and smooth the camera motion feels.

  • •

    Q4: How well the camera avoids occluding.

  • •

    Q5: General quality of the camera trajectory.

  • •

    Q6: Subjective preference for the method.

    • As shown in Figure 6, our method received significantly higher ratings than both baselines across all six evaluation criteria. Our method achieved a mean score of 4.53 (std = 0.88), compared to 2.24 (std = 1.20) for Fixed and 2.02 (std = 1.13) for Entropy. Participants ranked our method first in 96% of all tasks (101 out of 105), with a mean rank of 1.05 (1 = best). Fixed and Entropy received mean ranks of 2.42 and 2.53, respectively. (Figure 6).

    VII-DVLM Perceptual Benchmark

    Prior closed-loop benchmarks for embodied appliance manipulation [10] evaluate whether a VLM can predict the correct next action given a rendered observation, task instruction, the full task history, and product manuals. While this protocol evaluates end-to-end task performance, it inherently conflates perceptual quality with task reasoning. A model’s failure may stem either from ambiguous or insufficient visual observations or from a lack of procedural knowledge required to correctly sequence actions. Consequently, such benchmarks are not well suited for evaluating viewpoint quality, because their outcomes do not depend solely on the visual information provided by the camera, but also on the model’s ability to understand the task and reason about the required action. Moreover, given the overall complexity of these benchmarks relative to current VLM capabilities, models tend to rely heavily on semantic priors for decision-making. This tendency is further evidenced by our ablation study (see Supplementary Material Section 3), where models exhibit non-negligible performance even when provided with a completely black image.

    We therefore propose a new benchmark that isolates perceptual difficulty from task reasoning to measure the different viewpoints. The benchmark decouples appliance-state perception into three progressively complex tasks, each requiring only a single rendered image and a minimal contextual prompt, thereby reducing the influence of additional semantic information and encouraging the evaluation to depend primarily on the visual evidence provided by the viewpoint. This design makes performance differences between camera configurations directly attributable to viewpoint quality, not confounding factors.

    We formulate all tasks under a unified observation-state-action framework. Each appliance part is associated with a discrete state space S, defined by an ordered vocabulary (e.g., knob positions or binary states), and a rendering function R:S→O that maps states to RGB observations. Given an observation o∈O, the VLM is required to infer, compare, or control the underlying state.

    Task 1: State Recognition. This task evaluates direct perception as a mapping f:O→S, where the model predicts the current state ŝ=f(o). The metric is classification accuracy:

    Acc_T1=E_(o,s^*)[1(ŝ=s^*)].

    		(31)

    We denote the ground-truth state as s^*∈S and the predicted state as ŝ∈S. For example, consider an air fryer whose timer knob has vocabulary S=[\textttoff, \texttt10min, …, \texttt60min]. In a Task 1 example, the knob could be set to 30min and the VLM must read the label from a single image; a suboptimal viewpoint that blurs the dial markings could cause misclassification, e.g. "20min".

    Task 2: Goal Decision. Given an observation o∈O and a goal state g∈S, the model performs a binary judgment of whether the part has reached the specified goal f:O×S→{0,1} producing prediction ŷ=f(o,g). The ground-truth label is defined as y^*=1(s^*=g), where s^*∈S denotes the underlying state of the observation. For each (model, part, current-state) triple, one positive sample (goal =s^*) and one negative sample (goal selected as the state with the largest index distance from s^*) are generated, yielding a perfectly balanced 1:1 dataset. The metric is classification accuracy:

    Acc_T2=E_(o,g,y^*)[1(ŷ=y^*)].

    		(32)

    In Task 2, one image is paired with the goal "60min" and the model must answer state "60min" and YES; a model that cannot predict the correct state and reason whether the goal is achieved if it can not resolve the precise dial position.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有相机控制为静态物体设计，长任务里抓不住关键部件与状态变化。

要点：

  • 问题：交互式 3D 环境里的长时程物体级任务包含异质事件——细粒度操作、较大结构运动、微妙状态转换，用户需要看懂「动作如何导致结果」
  • 现有相机控制方法多针对静态物体设计，难以持续保证任务相关部件的可读性
  • VISTA 用可微的视角规划来处理：把「看得清关键部件与事件」写成可优化的目标，随时间规划相机路径

为什么值得看：自动运镜/演示录制在引擎里通常靠手写轨道。把「可读性」变成可微目标，意味着可以为长任务自动生成讲解镜头——对做录制回放、教学演示、自动化 QA 录像的团队都可复用。

中文摘要：交互式 3D 环境中的长时程、以物体为中心的任务，包含在时间与空间上展开的异质事件：细粒度操作、较大的结构性运动、以及微妙的状态转换。要帮助用户理解「动作如何随着时间导致结果」，有效的可视化很关键。然而现有 3D 系统中的相机控制方法大多是为静态物体设计的，往往无法持续保证与任务相关的部件与过程的可读性。VISTA 因此提出可微的视角规划方法：把「保持任务相关部件的可读性」写成可优化目标，随时间规划相机路径，从而在长时程任务中自动产出能讲清楚过程的镜头。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-10-30

本期推送：2026-11-01

VISTA: Differentiable Viewpoint Planning for Long-Horizon Task Visualization

PubID: pubid: 0000–0000/00$00.00 © 2021 IEEE

Abstract

Long-horizon object-centered tasks in interactive 3D environments involve heterogeneous events that unfold across time and space, including fine-grained manipulations, larger structural motions, and subtle state transitions. Effectively visualizing such processes is essential for helping users understand how actions lead to outcomes over time. However, existing camera control methods in 3D systems are commonly designed for static objects, and often fail to maintain the legibility of task-relevant components and their evolving relationships throughout long-horizon executions. We present VISTA, a differentiable viewpoint planning framework for long-horizon task visualization. We formulate camera control as a visualization policy that optimizes camera parameters under a unified rendering-based quality objective and we propose five quality metrics to satisfy our five design goals. To support both local part inspection and interaction-centric visualization centered on a primary object, our formulation handles targets defined either as object–part pairs or as relational tuples involving another interacting object. This allows the planner to reveal not only what part is important, but also how it functionally relates to surrounding structures during task execution. We demonstrate that the same planner supports two complementary use cases: presentation-driven narrative visualization for communicating how long-horizon tasks unfold to human viewers, and agent-driven active observation within an observe-act loop. Together, these results position differentiable viewpoint planning as a general mechanism for “how-things-work” visualization of long-horizon object-centered interactions in 3D environments.

Index Terms:

Informative Visualization, Visual Language Model, Agent

I Introduction

Visualization and illustration have long been effective at conveying how things look. A rich body of work [1, 2, 3] has developed techniques for depicting shape, appearance, spatial structure, and static relationships. By contrast, helping people understand functional behavior and state changes remains substantially more challenging [4, 5]. To communicate a process, a mechanism, or a long-horizon task, it is not enough to show the scene clearly at isolated moments. Viewers must be able to follow how relevant parts change over time, how actions transform states, and how local interactions accumulate into meaningful outcomes. In other words, “how-things-work” visualization requires not only visibility, but also a coherent visual narrative that unfolds progressively over time.

In this paper, we use long-horizon tasks to refer to temporally extended object-interaction processes composed of multiple semantically meaningful action steps. Such tasks require tracking how object parts, spatial relations, and task-relevant states evolve over time, rather than interpreting each moment in isolation [6, 7, 8]. We specifically focus on object-centered long-horizon tasks in interactive 3D environments, rather than broader scenarios involving full human activity understanding, social interaction, or whole-scene navigation. Prior work has demonstrated the value of computational methods for illustrating operation rather than static form alone, such as depicting how mechanical assemblies function, how fluid systems behave, or how geological structures evolve. These works highlight an important shift in emphasis: from showing what an object is to explaining what it does. Yet despite this progress, modern 3D visualization and simulation systems still provide limited support for constructing such process-oriented explanations. In many systems, camera control is treated as a fixed rendering choice [9, 10], a manually authored animation path [11], or a viewpoint optimization problem driven primarily by geometry [12].

While existing approaches may be adequate for short and atomic events, they become increasingly insufficient for long-horizon processes, defined here as multi-step processes that unfold over extended time spans and require viewers to track state changes, action dependencies, and spatially distributed interactions across successive stages. As tasks unfold, relevant parts may become too small, occluded, or drift outside the field of view. More fundamentally, viewpoints chosen only for instantaneous visibility often fail to preserve the continuity needed for understanding a process step by step. They may reveal what is visible in the current frame, yet fail to show what changed, why it changed, and how the current state relates to previous actions. As a result, viewers may perceive the scene but do not fully understand underlying mechanisms. This limitation is especially pronounced in object-centered manipulation tasks involving articulated or stateful objects, where an agent or system performs a sequence of actions that produces observable state changes over time. We use embodied tasks to refer to tasks situated in physical or simulated 3D environments, where an agent interacts with articulated or stateful objects, such as appliances, furniture, vehicles, and other household artifacts. In the agent-facing setting, these tasks become sequential decision-making problems: each action depends on visual observations of the current object state, the task goal, and the history of previous interactions. This scope is consistent with embodied AI and robotics benchmarks that model household activities as sequences of atomic actions and object-state transitions [6, 13, 7], articulated-object environments requiring part-level interaction [14], and long-horizon robot manipulation benchmarks [15, 8, 16].

We argue that camera control for long-horizon task visualization should be treated as a visualization policy. From this perspective, the camera is not merely a rendering parameter or a cinematographic afterthought; it is an active mechanism for organizing a linear visual narrative of the process. A useful camera policy should therefore help viewers follow the evolution of task-relevant states, maintain sufficient structural context across steps, and preserve the causal relationship between actions and outcomes [17, 18, 19]. Rather than optimizing only local visibility or aesthetic smoothness, it should support a temporally coherent visual explanation of how the process unfolds.

In this work, we present a differentiable viewpoint planning framework for long-horizon task visualization. Our method directly optimizes camera parameters under a unified projection-based quality objective. To support informative local views without losing global context, we introduce a state-aware formulation that jointly considers the target part, its parent structure, and the semantics of the ongoing action. The resulting planner produces adaptive viewpoints that evolve with the process while remaining temporally coherent. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach in two complementary settings. In a presentation-driven setting, given a long-horizon action sequence, the planner generates a camera trajectory and animation that visually narrate the task for human viewers, helping them understand how the process unfolds over time. In an agent-observation setting, the same planner provides a vision language model(VLM) agent with more informative viewpoints during observation, improving the visual evidence available for decision making in embodied tasks. These two settings highlight that our method supports both human-facing process understanding and agent-facing embodied decision making. To validate the perceptual quality of our generated camera trajectories, we conducted a user study with 21 participants comparing our method against a fixed camera baseline and an entropy-based approach. Our method was rated significantly higher across all evaluation criteria and was ranked first in 96% of all tasks. We show that camera viewpoint is a critical yet underexplored factor in VLM-based embodied tasks, and propose a benchmark (VISTA-Bench) that systematically evaluates the impact of viewpoint across perception (task 1), goal reasoning (task 2), and closed-loop control (task 3). Across diverse appliances and state-based tasks, our approach improves perception accuracy, goal decision, and, most notably, closed-loop control, achieving up to 2.1× higher success rates. These results highlight that adaptive viewpoint selection is essential for reliable sequential decision-making in embodied AI.

Our contributions are fourfold:

  • •

    We formulate viewpoint planning for object-centered long-horizon tasks around action-conditioned visual targets. Rather than selecting a generic best view of an entire object, each action instantiates either an object–part pair or a relational tuple, allowing different steps on the same object to emphasize different manipulated parts, interacting entities, and contextual structures.

  • •

    We translate these task-conditioned requirements into interpretable differentiable image-space objectives. In particular, we combine five metrics that jointly account for visibility, semantic relevance, and temporal coherence, enabling task-relevant visual criteria to be optimized directly with respect to continuous camera parameters.

  • •

    We implement the proposed metrics in VISTA, an interactive prototype for differentiable viewpoint planning. Through its graphical interface and configuration files, users can adjust the metric weights, task-importance distributions, target coverage, camera constraints, and optimization settings, enabling the planner to be configured for different objects, actions, and visualization requirements.

  • •

    We evaluate the VISTA for both human-facing narrative visualization and VLM-based active observation, and introduce VISTA-Bench to isolate the effect of viewpoint quality on perception, goal reasoning, and sequential control.

    • II Related Work

    II-AHeuristic View Quality Measures

    A substantial body of prior work studies viewpoint selection through hand-crafted heuristics and quality measures for static 3D objects. Early methods rely on geometric cues derived from rendered views, such as visible polygons and projected area [20, 21, 22, 12], silhouette shape [23, 24, 25], depth variation [26, 27], and saliency-related cues [28]. Beyond geometry, prior work has also discussed viewpoint preference in terms of canonicality, familiarity, functionality, and aesthetics [29, 30, 31, 32], suggesting that a “good” view depends not only on visibility but also on how an object is commonly perceived or used. In practice, however, most classical computational methods still optimize quantities that can be directly measured from geometry or rendering, such as visible area, contour complexity, saliency, or information content.

    Among these measures, viewpoint entropy is one of the most influential information-theoretic formulations. It measures how evenly the projected areas of visible polygons are distributed in the image and prefers views that expose many parts of the object in a balanced way [21, 22]. Using the standard notation over polygons z∈Z, viewpoint entropy is defined as

    VE(v)=-∑_z∈Z(a_z(v))/(aₜ(v))\log(a_z(v))/(aₜ(v))=-∑_z∈Zp(z|v)\logp(z|v),

    		(1)

    where a_z(v) is the projected area of polygon z from viewpoint v, aₜ(v) is the total projected area of the model, and p(z|v) is the normalized projected-area distribution. High entropy corresponds to views that show many polygons with relatively balanced visibility.

    A related but more expressive measure is viewpoint mutual information (VMI) [33], which evaluates the correlation between a viewpoint and the object’s polygon distribution. In its common form, VMI can be written as

    VMI(v)=∑_z∈Zp(z|v)\log(p(z|v))/(p(z)),

    		(2)

    where p(z) is the average projected-area distribution of polygon z over viewpoints. Intuitively, VMI compares the current viewpoint-dependent visibility distribution against a reference distribution and favors representative views with lower coupling to only a small subset of polygons. It can therefore also be interpreted as a KL-style divergence [12] between the visibility distribution under the current view and a target distribution over object parts.

    Similar heuristic principles have been extended to volume visualization. Bordoloi and Shen [34] propose a view-selection method for volume rendering that favors views where important voxels are highly visible, using visibility and importance to identify informative views or a compact set of representative views. Tao et al.[35] further introduce structure-aware viewpoint selection for volume visualization, defining shape and detail view descriptors to capture global structures and local boundary details from volume data. These methods broaden static view selection from surface visibility to volumetric visibility, importance, and structural characteristics.

    Despite their importance, heuristic viewpoint selection methods remain limited for our setting. Most are designed to select a single best or representative view of a static object through dense sampling and repeated rendering over candidate viewpoints, making best-view search costly. Moreover, many measures emphasize one dominant cue at a time: geometric methods focus on visible area, contour, or depth; information-theoretic measures such as VE and VMI rely on projected visibility distributions [33]; and higher-level criteria such as familiarity or functionality are difficult to encode in a unified optimization framework. As a result, a view may score highly while failing to emphasize semantically critical regions relevant to the current task. Although VMI is more stable than viewpoint entropy and can incorporate object-level importance, it still operates on static visibility distributions and does not explicitly model action phases, interaction semantics, or temporal continuity. Overall, these methods provide valuable geometric and information-theoretic foundations, but they remain single-view quality criteria rather than policies for organizing long-horizon visual explanations. Our setting instead requires viewpoint planning for long-horizon task visualization, where the camera must jointly account for semantic focus, structural context, and temporal coherence over time. In addition, while some prior work focuses on volume data, our work primarily targets mesh-based objects and their task-driven state transitions.

    II-BLearning-Based Viewpoint Selection

    Learning-based viewpoint selection has recently emerged as an alternative to brute-force evaluation of handcrafted quality measures. Schelling et al. propose a dynamic-label-generation framework that predicts high-quality viewpoints directly from 3D models, reducing the reliance of traditional measures on clean surface meshes and costly rendering-based search [36]. Their method also addresses the ambiguity of non-unique optimal views, such as those caused by object symmetries, by adapting the supervision target during training. Another line of work learns viewpoint quality from human preferences rather than predefined geometric criteria. Hartwig et al. show that preferred views depend not only on engineered measures such as entropy or occupancy, but also on category knowledge and familiar depictions, and train a neural view-quality model from large-scale crowdsourced pairwise comparisons [9].

    Related learning-based prediction has also been studied in interactive volume visualization. Sun et al.[37] propose RmdnCache, a dual-space RNN–MDN model that predicts the next POV and its uncertainty range from user exploration trajectories for data prefetching in large-scale volume rendering. However, its goal is to reduce cache misses and input latency, rather than to estimate viewpoint quality or plan informative viewpoints. Overall, these works improve the efficiency and flexibility of view prediction, but they still focus on static best-view estimation, preference modeling, or system-level prefetching. In contrast, our work formulates viewpoint selection as a differentiable long-horizon planning problem, where the camera must reveal state transitions, preserve context across actions, and support action–outcome attribution over time.

    II-CDynamic Camera Planning and Visibility-Aware Control

    Beyond static viewpoint selection, prior work has explored camera control as a task-driven and optimization-based process. Ji et al.[38] propose dynamic view selection for time-varying volumes by first evaluating static view quality using opacity, color, and curvature distributions, and then applying dynamic programming to select a smooth viewing path that maximizes perceived information over time. Similarly, Mitra et al.[4] generate visual explanations of dynamic processes, such as exploded views and step-by-step assembly visualizations, emphasizing functional behavior and action sequences rather than purely geometric visibility.

    The computer graphics and animation community has also developed formal models for camera control. Christie et al.[39] survey camera control techniques that formulate camera placement and motion as constraint- and optimization-driven problems, balancing visibility, framing, smoothness, and narrative constraints. Hsu et al.[3] similarly optimize camera trajectories for volume data animation under multiple criteria, including feature visibility, importance, and temporal smoothness. These works show that camera planning is inherently multi-objective.

    However, existing approaches typically target short sequences, predefined animations, or fixed optimization objectives. They do not explicitly formulate camera control as a continuous, differentiable policy over long-horizon tasks. In contrast, our work casts viewpoint planning as a unified differentiable optimization problem that encodes task-dependent visualization goals and produces temporally coherent viewpoint sequences for evolving processes.

    III Design Goals and Unified Camera Quality Objective

    Long-horizon task visualization requires the camera to do more than merely keep a target visible, as illustrated in  Figure 2. As a task unfolds, the viewpoint must adapt to changing explanatory demands: it should make the task-relevant component and its state changes clearly legible, preserve sufficient surrounding structure for those changes to be interpreted, and maintain visual continuity across successive action stages  [17, 18, 40, 41]. We therefore formulate camera control as a visualization policy over a long-horizon action sequence. For each action, the policy constructs an action-conditioned visualization target and optimizes continuous camera parameters according to explicit viewpoint-quality objectives.

    III-AAction-Conditioned Visualization Targets

    To capture these requirements, we formulate adaptive viewpoint planning over an input action sequence A={a₁,…,a_T} describing a long-horizon task. Since different actions impose different visualization demands, we consider two common target configurations in long-horizon tasks, illustrated in the middle panel of Figure 2. The first type is an object–part target (o,p), where p is a salient part of object o and the main goal is to clearly inspect a local manipulation or state change on that part. The second type is a relational target (o₁,p,o₂), where part p of object o₁ interacts with, affects, or should be interpreted relative to another object o₂. This type is used when understanding the action requires not only the manipulated part itself, but also its spatial or functional relation to another object. These two configurations cover the primary cases considered in this work, but are not intended as an exhaustive taxonomy of all possible task targets.

    For each action aₜ, our goal is to determine a camera configuration vₜ that best supports the corresponding visualization target. The selected view should make the target legible, preserve sufficient object-level context, and, when applicable, reveal the relation between the involved entities. Optimizing one viewpoint for each action produces a temporally ordered sequence that supports both local part inspection and interaction-centric visualization.

    These requirements are difficult to satisfy with existing viewpoint selection paradigms. Hand-crafted heuristic methods [21, 33] typically optimize fixed geometric cues and commonly rely on a discrete candidate-search procedure: they sample a large number of viewpoints over the camera space, render and evaluate each candidate independently, and select the one with the highest score. More importantly, both heuristic [21] and learning-based methods [9] have largely focused on finding the best view of a whole object, rather than a view tailored to a task-relevant part or inter-object relation. This makes them poorly suited to long-horizon tasks, where visualization needs change across action phases: one step may require a close-up of a manipulated part, while the next may require a wider view to reveal its effect on surrounding structure or another object. Learning-based approaches can adapt more flexibly, but they depend on collected training data, and obtaining labels with sufficient spatial coverage over the viewpoint space is expensive and difficult. Their behavior is therefore tied to the training distribution, with limited control over which visualization criteria are actually being optimized. In our setting, we instead seek a planner that can adapt to each task state, remain directly steerable by explicit visualization goals, and optimize views for task-relevant parts and relations rather than whole-object preference.

    These limitations motivate a differentiable formulation of viewpoint planning. Instead of discretizing the camera space and exhaustively evaluating a predefined set of candidate views, we express viewpoint quality using image-space objectives and optimize continuous camera parameters directly through gradients. This allows the optimizer to progressively adjust the camera toward a better view without requiring dense enumeration of the full viewpoint space. Equally importantly, each visualization requirement remains an explicit and interpretable objective, allowing us to specify which properties a good view should satisfy. The resulting formulation therefore combines continuous camera optimization with direct control over the task-dependent criteria being optimized, rather than relying on fixed camera rules or expecting explanatory behavior to emerge implicitly from training data.

    We formulate adaptive camera control as a visualization policy that selects a sequence of camera configurations

    V={vₜ}ₜ₌₁ᵀ, vₜ=(θₜ,φₜ,rₜ,rollₜ),

    		(3)

    where θₜ and φₜ denote the azimuth and elevation around the action-dependent camera anchor c_aₜ, rₜ denotes the viewing distance, and rollₜ denotes the in-plane camera rotation around the viewing axis. The objective is therefore not to find one generic best view of an entire object, but to optimize a sequence of viewpoints whose targets and required context evolve with the task.

    III-BDesign Goals and Viewpoint-Quality Metrics

    We optimize each camera configuration according to five complementary design goals informed by prior work on visibility, structural informativeness, functional perception, importance-driven attention, and animated transitions [42, 21, 33, 27, 43, 18, 19]. Rather than defining these goals separately from their mathematical realizations, we introduce each goal together with the metric used to operationalize it.

    G1: Target Legibility - Visible Coverage (fᵥᵢₛ): Prior work on viewpoint quality has shown that visibility and projected size are central factors in whether a view is informative and perceptually useful  [42, 27]. In our setting, however, the relevant unit is often not the whole object but the task-relevant part on which an action or state change occurs. We therefore measure whether this target is visible, unoccluded, and sufficiently large in the rendered image.

    fᵥᵢₛ(v)=1/HW∑_(i,j)∈Ωmᵥᵢₛ(i,j;v),

    		(4)

    where Ω is the H×W image grid, and (i,j)∈Ω denotes a pixel location. The binary mask mᵥᵢₛ(i,j;v)∈{0,1} equals 1 if the target is visible and unoccluded at pixel (i,j) under viewpoint v, and 0 otherwise. Thus, fᵥᵢₛ(v) measures measures the fraction of the rendered image occupied by visible target content. A higher value indicates that the target is more prominently presented, whereas the score decreases when the target becomes smaller, moves outside the field of view, or is occluded by surrounding geometry.

    Semantic Directional Frame: To represent the target from functionally meaningful directions, we construct a semantic directional frame that captures its front-back, top-bottom, and side-to-side orientations. This frame provides a shared directional reference for evaluating both the structural diversity revealed by a viewpoint and its alignment with the target’s functional orientation. We first construct three orthogonal candidate axes using one of two supported policies. The AABB policy uses the three world-aligned axes of the target’s axis-aligned bounding box, while the PCA OBB policy [44] estimates three object-oriented axes from the target mesh using area-weighted PCA. Both policies produce six opposing candidate directions {±a₁,±a₂,±a₃}.

    We render the target from these six directions and provide the direction-labeled images to a VLM, which identifies the functional front and top directions. For an individual part, each candidate direction is represented by two images: an isolated rendering showing only the part and an in-context rendering in which the part is highlighted within the complete parent object. The isolated views expose local geometry, while the contextual views help the VLM determine how the part is positioned and typically approached during interaction. For each candidate direction, the camera is placed on the corresponding ray from the target’s bounding-box center at twice the target bounding-box diagonal for isolated views and 1.2 times the parent bounding-box diagonal for contextual views.

    Let d̂_front and d̂ᵤₚ denote the resulting target-level front and up directions. After orthogonalizing the predicted up direction with respect to the front direction, we construct a side direction and obtain the semantic frame {±d_f,±dᵤ,±dₛ} where d_f, dᵤ, and dₛ denote the semantic front, up, and side axes, respectively.

    This semantic frame serves two complementary purposes in the following metric definitions: it provides the directional partition used to measure the structural diversity revealed by a viewpoint, and it provides the functional front and upright references used to evaluate camera alignment. Detailed prompts of VLM are provided in the Supplementary Material-Section 1.

    G2: Structural Informativeness — Patch Entropy (fₑₙₜ): Prior work on viewpoint entropy and related informativeness measures suggests that informative viewpoints should reveal meaningful structural evidence of the underlying 3D object rather than collapse it into a degenerate or uninformative projection [21]. For long-horizon task visualization, this means that the selected view should preserve sufficient structural evidence of the task-relevant target for its three-dimensional form and state to remain interpretable.

    Classical viewpoint entropy measures structural informativeness by computing entropy over visible polygons [21]. However, polygon-level formulations are sensitive to mesh triangulation [12] and may primarily reflect geometric discretization rather than task-relevant surface diversity. We therefore compute entropy over a fixed vocabulary of six semantic directional patches, front, back, top, bottom, left, and right, defined by the semantic frame above.

    Each mesh triangle f is assigned to one directional group according to

    s(f,m)=α⟨n_f,dₘ⟩+(1-α)⟨ĉ_f,dₘ⟩,

    		(5)

    where n_f is the outward triangle normal, ĉ_f is the normalized triangle-centroid location, dₘ is the m-th canonical direction, and α=0.5. The orientation term groups similarly facing surfaces, while the location term disambiguates curved or oblique surfaces. All triangles assigned to the same direction form one patch.

    For viewpoint v, let

    Aₙ(v)=∑_(i,j)∈Ωmₙ(i,j;v)

    		(6)

    denote the visible pixel area belonging to patch Pₙ, where mₙ(i,j;v) is the visibility indicator of patch Pₙ at pixel (i,j). We define

    πₙ(v)=(Aₙ(v))/(∑_n^′=1^NA_n^′(v))

    		(7)

    and compute normalized patch entropy as

    fₑₙₜ(v)=-(1)/(\logN)∑ₙ₌₁^Nπₙ(v)\logπₙ(v).

    		(8)

    Full implementation details and comparisons with alternative patch assignment policies are provided in the Supplementary Material Section 2.

    G3: Functional Alignment (f_func): Studies on active and task-dependent perception suggest that object understanding benefits from viewpoints selected relative to the observer’s goal and the functional properties of the object, rather than from generic canonical views alone [43]. In our setting, some directions are more informative because they better reveal how a part is normally observed or operated, such as the front of a button, the readable face of a dial, or the operational side of a handle.

    Let d̂_front and d̂ᵤₚ denote the resulting target-level front and up directions. Let ĉ(v) denote the unit direction from the target toward the camera, and let û_cam(v) denote the camera up vector. We define

    f_func(v)=\max (⟨ĉ(v),d̂_front⟩,0)·\max (⟨û_cam(v),d̂ᵤₚ⟩,0).

    		(9)

    The first factor favors cameras located on the functional front side of the target, while the second maintains an upright and semantically interpretable image orientation. Although Functional Alignment and Patch Entropy use the same semantic frame, they capture different properties. Functional Alignment determines whether the camera follows a functionally meaningful direction, whereas Patch Entropy evaluates whether the viewpoint reveals multiple directional surface regions of the target.

    G4: Context-Aware Focus (f_foc): Prior work on importance-driven focus of attention suggests that a viewpoint should allocate image-space emphasis according to the relative importance of scene elements rather than treat all visible content equally [33]. In long-horizon tasks, however, importance depends not only on individual objects, but also on the contextual information needed to interpret the manipulated target and its relation to the surrounding scene.

    We therefore measure whether the current viewpoint allocates image space among the target and its surrounding entities according to their task-dependent importance. The objective is not to maximize target area alone: an excessively close view may remove the context needed to interpret the target’s role, whereas a view containing too much surrounding structure may make the target too small to inspect.

    For each entity e∈E, let

    Aₑ(v)=∑_(i,j)∈Ωmₑ(i,j;v)

    		(10)

    denote the number of rendered pixels occupied by e. We then define the visual distribution induced by the current view as

    p(e|v)=(Aₑ(v))/(∑_e^′∈EA_e^′(v)).

    		(11)

    Let q(e) denote a task-importance distribution specifying how visual attention should ideally be allocated across entities at the current action step. The context-aware focus score is defined as

    f_foc(v)=\exp (-D_JS(p(·|v) ∥ q(·))),

    		(12)

    with

    D_JS(p∥q)=1/2D_KL(p∥m)+1/2D_KL(q∥m), m=1/2(p+q),

    		(13)

    with D_KL being the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

    This score is high when the current view allocates screen space across the target and its context in a way that matches their task-dependent importance. We use Jensen–Shannon divergence because it provides a symmetric and bounded measure of distribution mismatch, which is more suitable than a single KL divergence for comparing task-dependent attention allocations.

    G5: Temporal Continuity (fₜᵣₐₙₛ): Prior work on animated transitions and event understanding has shown that coherent visual changes help viewers preserve spatial context, maintain orientation, and follow evolving processes over time [18, 19]. For long-horizon task visualization, consecutive camera states should therefore be connected without unnecessarily large changes in viewpoint. Let vₜ₋₁ and vₜ denote the camera configurations associated with two consecutive action steps, and let pₜ₋₁ and pₜ denote their corresponding camera positions. Let ℓ(pₜ₋₁,pₜ) denote the length of the transition path connecting these positions. We define

    fₜᵣₐₙₛ(vₜ₋₁,vₜ)=\exp (-(ℓ(pₜ₋₁,pₜ))/(d_ref)),

    		(14)

    where d_ref>0 is a reference distance used to normalize the path length. A higher score favors nearby camera configurations connected by shorter viewpoint transitions.

    As a proof of concept, we use path length as a lightweight geometric proxy for temporal continuity. This formulation encourages spatially compact transitions but does not directly model higher-order camera-motion or perceptual properties, such as velocity, acceleration, screen-space target displacement, optical flow, or visual correspondence. The visualizations of each metric are listed in Figure 3.

    IV Image-Space Optimization via Differentiable Rasterization

    Previous section defines five complementary viewpoint-quality metrics. Among them, Visible Coverage, Patch Entropy, and Context-Aware Focus rely on binary visibility masks, discrete pixel ownership, and projected image-space areas. These rendering quantities are not directly differentiable with respect to the camera parameters: their values may remain unchanged under small camera perturbations and change abruptly when visibility or occlusion boundaries are crossed. Functional Alignment is already expressed as an analytic function of the camera orientation, while Temporal Continuity depends on the transition path between consecutive camera states.

    In this section, we construct a shared differentiable camera-to-image mapping for these metrics. Rather than redefining their semantic objectives, we replace hard rendering quantities with soft image-space attributes produced through differentiable projection, rasterization, interpolation, and antialiasing. This allows gradients from the viewpoint-quality objective to propagate directly to the continuous camera parameters.

    IV-ADifferentiable Camera-to-Image Mapping

    We instantiate our viewpoint optimization on top of a standard differentiable rasterization pipeline [45]. Our role here is not to introduce a new renderer, but to define a camera parameterization and a set of task-specific attribute encodings that expose differentiable image-space signals for evaluating candidate views.

    The camera position p(vₜ) is parameterized using Equation 15

    p(vₜ)=c_aₜ+rₜ\beginbmatrix\cosφₜ\cosθₜ \cosφₜ\sinθₜ \sinφₜ\endbmatrix.

    		(15)

    Together with a viewing direction towards target center c_aₜ and roll-dependent in-plane rotation, this defines a differentiable view matrix V(vₜ). Let P denote the perspective projection matrix. For a mesh vertex xᵢ, the clip-space coordinate is x̃ᵢ(vₜ)=P V(vₜ) xᵢ. Since both the camera transform and projection are smooth functions of v, the projected geometry is differentiable with respect to the camera parameters.

    IV-BSoft Rasterized Attributes

    Let Ω denote the image domain and let q=(i,j)∈Ω denote a pixel. Each mesh vertex ℓ is assigned an attribute vector a_ℓ∈ℝ^K. For a pixel covered by the front-most triangle τ_q=(ℓ₀,ℓ₁,ℓ₂), let βₖ(q;vₜ) denote its perspective-correct barycentric coordinates. The point-sampled per-pixel attribute is

    aᵖᵗ(q;vₜ)=\begincases∑ₖ₌₀²βₖ(q;vₜ) a_ℓₖ,&qis covered byτ_q, [5.0pt] 0,&otherwise.\endcases

    		(16)

    We define the soft per-pixel attribute as

    ã(q;vₜ)=A (aᵖᵗ(·;vₜ),{x̃_ℓ(vₜ)},F)(q),

    		(17)

    where F is the triangle set and A denotes geometry-aware differentiable antialiasing. The operator approximates pixel coverage at silhouette and visibility boundaries, producing fractional attribute values at boundary pixels while preserving the interpolated attributes in triangle interiors.

    For binary target membership, target vertices are assigned 1 and all other vertices are assigned 0, so that ã(q;vₜ)∈[0,1] represents the fractional target coverage of pixel q. For categorical attributes such as entity identity or patch identity, a_ℓ is a one-hot vector rather than an integer label. Consequently, ã(q;vₜ) represents the soft per-pixel membership across the corresponding categories.

    This construction defines the differentiable mapping

    vₜ \longrightarrow {x̃_ℓ(vₜ)} \longrightarrow {ã(q;vₜ)}_q∈Ω,

    		(18)

    allowing gradients from image-space objectives to flow back to the camera parameters.

    Visibility is determined by the front-most surface returned by the rasterizer. Because target, entity are interpolated only from the front-most triangle at each pixel, the resulting channels already account for occlusion by the parent object and other scene geometry. Differentiable antialiasing provides fractional coverage near projected boundaries, allowing small camera changes around these boundaries to produce continuous changes in the corresponding image-space attributes.

    IV-CDifferentiable Realization of the Metrics

    With the soft rasterized attributes defined above, we obtain differentiable counterparts of the three rendering-based metrics introduced in Section III. Their semantic definitions remain unchanged; binary masks and hard projected areas are replaced by soft image-space quantities that vary continuously with the camera configuration vₜ. Functional Alignment is already an analytic function of the camera orientation, while Temporal Continuity is computed from a differentiable approximation of the transition-path length.

    Visible coverage: We define the visible coverage of the target by integrating the soft visibility mask over the image domain:

    f̃ᵥᵢₛ(vₜ)=(1)/(|Ω|)∑_q∈Ωm̃ᵥᵢₛ(q;vₜ).

    		(19)

    This term increases when a larger visible portion of the target occupies the image, and decreases under occlusion or shrinkage in projection. In practice, however, maximizing visible coverage without bound is not always desirable, since an excessively large target region may reduce surrounding context. We therefore apply a saturation function

    f̂ᵥᵢₛ(v)=\min ((f̃ᵥᵢₛ(v))/(fᵥᵢₛᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ), 1)\exp (-k \max (f̃ᵥᵢₛ(v)-fᵥᵢₛᵗᵃʳᵍᵉᵗ, 0)),

    		(20)
